I recommend this course for anybody who wants to know what private equity is about and the challenges they face. A lot of the cases are drawn from the instructors' past projects as well as guest speakers'. As one would expect, private equity people are not the nicest people and you get that sense from the speakers that come to class so if that's not your cup of tea, stay away. Class discussion is managed well and centers on cold and warm calls so preparation is key. Absolutely! If you are interested in the alternative asset class of VC, Growth Equity or PE Buyouts - this is a must take class.
Yes. It is a good introduction into PE and I like the case style of the class. Professors are extremely well-prepared - very impressive!

Absolutely, this is a must-take class in the MBA program. Even if you're not focused on finance or don't come from a financial background, you'll learn how to create value by sticking to core business fundamentals, thinking creatively, and being extremely disciplined in execution. The workload is heavy, but it's more than worth it for the quality of learning and practical insight you gain.

Highly recommended! This class will challenge and push you. Not only do you gain great knowledge about PE and LBO, but you become a more confident and well rounded business person. This is the type of MBA class I was looking for.

Yes, I would recommend both professors to fellow students. They have a rapid fire and sharp angle in engaging the class that it closes the gap that can be felt especially via a zoom class. Their insight into the industry is a goldmine that they both share with the class.

I would recommend this course if you are looking for a boot-camp style crash course on PE. This class and the professors will challenge you to defend your stance on every case. It's a lot of work but in the end you will have learned a lot about PE and potential career opportunities.
Yes, I would because it is very interactive and at least give me a taste of what is PE LBO.
Yes, more than theory of investment, the real life challenges associated with investment thesis are clearly taught. Goes to show that there are lot more than excel calculations when making a deal
Yes I would

Yes I would. This class was super valuable for anyone who is interested in Private Equity, or finance generally. Also, many of the learnings and takeaways are applicable to the corporate world and entrepreneurship. Great class! Yes I would. The workload is significant with a lot of reading, but both professors have a lot of experience to share. The strategy, insights and anecdotes form working on deals is invaluable. This narrative isn't available in online modeling classes or other finance mba classes. The subject matter is very specific but high value for anyone looking to work in the field.

I'd definitely recommend this course to anyone interested in PE or adjacent industries; the content and perspectives are fantastic. That said, people should be aware that the workload is heavier than you'd expect for a 2-unit class, and in my experience it was actually more work than some of the toughest 3-unit courses.
Yeees! Very valuable and no other class at haas similar

It's hard to give a simple recommendation. On one hand, the course prepares you extremely well and you truly learn a lot. But you have to be the type of student who doesn't mind spending a significant amount of time on cases — even when it might be more efficient to focus on the core concepts rather than spending twenty minutes or more on a single case while another still waits. There are definitely more efficient ways to teach the material, and given how much there is to absorb in an MBA program, it may make more sense to focus on the highest-value concepts and dive deep, rather than working through two cases when one of them doesn't add much.
I would recommend the course if you're aiming for IB or PE and have the time to dedicate to it. It's tougher for part- time MBA students who are balancing work, life, and other classes.

The professor himself is legendary. A major part of the appeal is simply the chance to learn from him. Just don't expect hands-on work with detailed models. I would suggest that he provide the underlying models and walk the class through them — that would create a real playbook for how to approach the analysis and allow us to experiment with the assumptions.

One more important point: the slides and materials he prepares for each class are fantastic. He clearly cares about what you learn, and the quality of the content reflects that. He consistently brings in great speakers as well. It will be a sad day when he retires.
I would definitely recommend this course to other students. You will be challenged and will grow more than you expect.

If you're not seriously considering a PE career, then my answer is no. It didn't really give me practical LBO modeling skills, and I felt that the learning I got didn't justify the amount of time and energy it required.

sections.goodFor: Students with no accounting background who want the fundamentals; non-finance career switchers who want to read financial statements.
sections.notFor: Anyone who already studied accounting (MBA Math, undergrad) - repeatedly called basic; one says the content is textbook-learnable and the discussion adds little.
sections.workloadNote: In-class practice problems plus assignments; one student says class time and assignments cut into recruiting time. No hours given.
sections.gradingBasis: Class participation is scored; one student notes she weighs effort over final results.
sections.redFlags: Several say it is too basic if you have prior accounting; one says participation scoring forces attendance time away from recruiting; one calls delivery dry.
sections.quote: I would recommend the course to people with a caveat; only for those who haven't previously studied accounting.
comments: Yes. Professor Wu is extremely kind, takes the time to break down material, allows us to practice the material within the class. She's also extremely flexible, which I appreciate as a busy MBA student.
I would recommend the professor to another student because she's very eager for people to learn and does a great job explaining. She also incorporates feedback readily and makes sure we're heard.
I thought this course was helpful in explaining the core concepts of accounting.
Yes

Yes! This was a great course to understand fundamentals of accounting, given my previous knowledge of 0, and it allows me to understand better how business is done. i was surprised at how important accounting was to making investment decisions, which I should have known earlier.
Yes. They make accounting straightforward and simple
I would recommend this class to anyone who hasn't taken accounting before and wants to see how businesses today use accounting
Yes I would!
Yes, its important to understand accounting for career development and professor Wu is good on teaching it, she is clear and practical.
Professor does well at explaining super basic level of accounting
Yes! She was lots of fun.

I would recommend the course to people with a caveat; only for those who haven't previously studied accounting. If you have studied in a pre-MBA course like MBA Math and are reasonably confident, class time and assignments will unfortunately detract from your available time to put towards more critical activities like recruiting. The class participation scoring, while generally helpful, does mean that you have to make a decision
Yes
I recommend this course if you want to have a solid accounting foundation.
Yes! It was helpful for me as someone who came from non-finance background.
Yes - supportive, accessible, smart, brings subject matter to life
Explains the material well enough, but it's all a bit dry
Probably no. Many things can be learned through textbooks and I found having discussions with each other is more important for the MBA class.
Yes, she's a great teacher
Yes absolutely!!! Prof Wu is so kind and knowledgable and patient and can teach extremely complex concepts in very digestible formats, and its invaluable information for the business world.
Prof Wu is awesome, I recommend!
Yes! She really cares about us:)
Yes - Professor Xi really takes into account students needs and is always willing to help.
Yes and yes.
Yes!!

Yes. This is a fundamental class for all business. The concepts discussed underline every other class you will take. Yes, but I would recommend it to students without accounting background. For those who has, the class might be a little l basic.
Yes. She values our efforts more than that final result, which encourages me to do my best to learn as much accounting as possible without only focusing on the grade

Xi is the sweetest professor. She did a great job of making the course engaging and encouraging students. I loved the real world examples to contextualize concepts. By the end of the course the daunting and unfamiliar topic of accounting was made simple.

Yeah absolutely. The prof cares about us learning core accounting concepts and making it relevant to us no matter our future occupation. It's a fantastic intro to accounting and very doable to follow along even if you have no accounting background beforehand. She also shows fun shark tank videos which are always really funny.
Yes

Professor Wu's knowledge is clearly vast, but she does a great job of catering to different backgrounds regarding the topic of financial accounting. She is patient and understanding, and I highly recommend the course.

Yes. Accounting is the language of business and this course effectively taught me the foundation of that language. It feels basic at first but as you move along and experience other classes you really come to appreciate how foundational it is to all of your future studies at Haas. And Professor Wu is so nice!
Yes I highly recommend Professor Xi because you will learn the fundamentals of accounting and how it applies in the real world

rows.title: Haas@Work
rows.disagree: High rating, but comment tone is mixed or negative

sections.goodFor: Students exploring consulting or design thinking who want real client contact, storytelling practice and team dynamics; also recommended for I-School/MIMS students. Keeps you local.
sections.notFor: Anyone who cannot invest real energy outside class, or who wants a direct consulting course - it is more a design-thinking framework class than consulting proper.
sections.workloadNote: A team-based real client project run on a design-thinking process; substantial work outside class. Load varies a lot by project draw, and team leads report far more of it. Hours not stated.
sections.gradingBasis: unclear - no student mentions grading; the work centers on a client project, generating insights and presenting them.
sections.redFlags: Recurring (3): your experience depends heavily on project draw and team buy-in - some projects are far harder, and teammates who are not bought in make it hard work. Team leads carry noticeably more.
sections.quote: I would recommend the course. It's a great process to go through and understand. But caveat, if people are not bought into the project, it can be hard work.
comments: This was the most meaningful course of my first year. I absolutely loved being able to test and learn design thinking and consulting in such a growth-minded and fun environment. You will truly get as much out of this course as you put into it. The course's mantra of "trust the process, do the work", is something that I can't wait to apply for the rest of my life!
Yes
Yes, especially if you want a (relatively) chill Applied Innovation class that keeps you local
Yes - hugely applicable, great frameworks, repeatable process
Yes
Yes, absolutely! Both Haas and Ischool/ MIMS students should learn this method, how to work in diverse teams, the power of feedback, and would enhance their product design and management skills.
Great for someone that is looking to gain experience in engaging with clients

Great course. Highly practical. Good learning experience if you want to know how to present or interact to clients. It is not a direct consulting class, but if u have 0 prior experience this will give a good introduction. More a framework class to understand design thinking.

I would recommend the course. It's a great process to go through and understand. But caveat, if people are not bought into the project, it can be hard work. I'd encourage team buy in from the beginning

I would recommend this course as it helps get some relevant experience in design thinking and client work. However, some projects are more difficult than others, so it may require far more work. Be prepared to invest energy into this, especially if you are one of the team leads.

[REDACTED IN THE PUBLIC BUILD] A student described finding the team-lead role considerably harder and more emotionally draining than expected, and said they would not recommend it to others in their position. — Why: The original names the writer's race and gender. In a section this size that is potentially identifying, and it was written for a CalNet-gated audience.

This is a great course for any students exploring the consulting or design thinking spaces. It will give you plenty of practical experience and provide a boost to your resume when applying to jobs. This course does require a substantial amount of work outside the classroom, but it's worth it in the end!
Yes, helpful for navigating team and client dynamics.

Yes, it was great because you learn a ton about how to generate insights and communicate them, storytelling is a big part of this course and you get to practice it in real-time. It was also a great bonding experience with our team.

sections.goodFor: Students who want real client/consulting reps, design-thinking practice, and comfort with ambiguity; useful signal for consulting internships and leadership growth.
sections.notFor: Anyone who can't accept that the outcome rides on a randomly assigned team and client, or who wants structured skill instruction - it is learning by doing, not curriculum.
sections.workloadNote: Semester-long real-client consulting project with an internal team; called a fair amount of hands-on work. Evening sessions are short lectures plus team work time.
sections.gradingBasis: unclear; work centers on team client deliverables and a final client-facing output. Grading itself is not discussed.
sections.redFlags: Outcome hinges on your assigned team/client (3 mentions; one carried a lot of dead weight). 1: class time wildly inefficient, no instructor/TA help. one student reported the team-lead role was unexpectedly draining.
sections.quote: Ultimately, your experience is far, far, far too at the mercy of who you get grouped up with on your team.
comments: The frameworks and thought process that I learned from this class were something I immediately started applying at my job, and I'm sure I will continue using them. It forces you to think in unconventional ways, to explore alternatives and to validate ideas. Working so closely with a team for a semester is also one of the best experiences I've had at Haas. I would definitely recommend the course.
I got a lot out of this course. I had fun, I learned a lot.

8 times out of 10, I would absolutely NOT recommend this course to a fellow student, unless they indicated to me that they would benefit from going through the type of consulting project that this course offers. Ultimately, your experience is far, far, far too at the mercy of who you get grouped up with on your team. While I had some great team members, I'm exhausted from carrying a LOT of dead weight.
Yes
Yes. This course is helpful in case you're looking for an internship and/or looking to work with a client without fear of failure

Haas@Work is a signature course at Haas for a reason and brings human-centered design and innovation principles into practice with real clients. The class combines consulting, product management, AI, strategy, and client work together in a hands on class. Even though it meets in the evenings, I found every class to be valuable time to work with my team and learn consulting and innovation skills that apply in any job context. I loved this class and highly recommend it, although it is a fair amount of hands on work with the internal team and client!

I highly recommend this course to anyone looking to work in the consulting industry. It involves real client needs and helps solve their actual pain points. The entire process closely reflects what real consulting work is actually like. Yes, absolutely; it was very hands on and helped me develop tools for dealing with ambiguous problems and helped in understanding how to " trust the process "
I probably wouldn't recommend the course. With the rise of AI tools today, I feel like part of the course's value proposition has become less compelling

Yes, this class is great if you're looking for hands-on client experience, experience with design thinking methodology, or growth in leadership (internal or client-facing). The experience can be mixed based on the client project you are assigned to, however. It's also less about structured learning and skill sets and more about learning through doing and getting comfortable with navigating ambiguous, complex problem spaces.

Yes, I would recommend both the course and professor. I appreciated the open creative space that was created for us to work in, the lectures were relevant and helpful, but short enough to leave time for group work. I enjoyed working on a real project with real clients and appreciate the structure of this course for making that possible.
No. The class time felt wildly inefficient and I didn't feel like the instructors or TAs stepped in to help or push us along when needed

Yes, you will remember the experience
Yes! This class will provide you with a strong foundation to solve ambiguous challenges and allow you to build confidence in tackling challenges in areas you may not be familiar with.
no

sections.goodFor: Anyone interested in any corner of US healthcare (digital health, pharma, services) - Macpherson's network and guest speakers are repeatedly cited, including for internships.
sections.notFor: Students wanting frameworks and structured instruction - after the first few weeks it runs as a speaker series; the merely curious with no healthcare background may struggle to keep up.
sections.workloadNote: Bimodal: three case assignments described as 'a TON of work' plus a heavy final project, sprinkled through the semester; outside those the course is not much work.
sections.gradingBasis: Three case write-ups plus a final project; students call the assignments fair.
sections.redFlags: Two to three say Kim largely stops teaching after the first few weeks and it becomes a speaker series with limited practical frameworks and little discussion time; the three cases are very heavy.
sections.quote: Outside of the first few weeks of the course though Kim doesn't really teach the class, it functions more like a speaker series.
comments: For those interested in understanding the US healthcare landscape this is a class someone should strongly consider taking.

This course gave a great overview of the complexities of the healthcare system in an engaging and digestible way for students who range in level of past experience in healthcare. I'd recommend the class as it is well-organized and fair in terms of assignments. Kim's passion and enthusiasm for the subject comes across in her lecturing style. She is up- to-date in what's going on in the healthcare world which lends itself well to the material/curriculum that she updates every year. She is also well-connected to people in industry and brings in stellar guest lecturers. Although cases require a significant amount of time, there are only a few sprinkled out through the semester and stimulating to think about and apply learnings from class. If interested in any aspects of American healthcare (digital health, pharma, healthcare services, etc.), I'd recommend taking the class.

This class brings in amazing speakers from healthcare companies shaping the industry. Kim's connections go hard and you can get a lot out of them. Outside of the first few weeks of the course though Kim doesn't really teach the class, it functions more like a speaker series. As awesome as the speakers were I was hoping for a bit more practical instruction and frameworks. The three cases you have to complete are a TON of work. But they are very interesting and relevant and I learned a lot from them that I've taken into networking sessions. Outside of the three cases and final project which are all a heavy lift, the course is not a lot of work.
Yes, I thought it was good - tons of very good speakers, but not a lot of time to engage and discuss as a class. Kim is very good.

Yes, with the qualifier that this is a very different class structure than most MBA classes and can be harder in that sense. Kim is incredibly smart, well-informed in the space, and well-connected, which can help you get an internship over the summer if that is what you are looking for
Absolutely! If you have any interest in Healthcare at all this is an amazing class to take!
Yes! one of the must-take course here at Haas
Yes, great for intro to healthcare, but would warn students to be weary of the workload for each case

Yes, I have no background in healthcare and this class gave a good baseline understanding of the whole industry Absolutely! Kim is so knowledgable, and you get to ask questions and get access to just a sampler of Kim's network, who I would have never met otherwise. I came in with a very surface level understanding of American healthcare, and came out with more context and understanding about the nuances of the US Healthcare System.
Absolutely, anyone who wants to understand the players of US healthcare in greater detail and have engaging guest lectures should join the class!
Only if you are truly interested in healthcare. If you are curious about it but have no healthcare background, it may be difficult to keep up with the content.
This course provides a comprehensive overview and insights into the Healthcare value chain, as well as the US and global markets.

sections.goodFor: Students interested in people, management, human capital, HR, or data broadly; several non-quantitative students said it unexpectedly became their favorite class. Commenters also flag the AI/ML, algorithmic-bias, and experiment-design content as relevant well beyond HR.
sections.workloadNote: One commenter noted the learning was substantial relative to the amount of work required, implying a manageable load.
sections.quote: Absolutely. This class was highly informative with a strong professor leading the course. The amount of learning was substantial for the amount of work needed to be put into the class.

rows.title: Finding Your Place in Real Estate

sections.goodFor: First-years and anyone curious about real estate careers with little prior exposure - commercial acquisitions, asset management, affordable housing, investment - and wanting to meet practitioners.
sections.notFor: Students who already know the industry or want technical/financial skills; this is career exploration, and several say it is most useful in the first year.
sections.workloadNote: Explicitly described as 'a valuable class for low effort'; format is a speaker-driven survey of real estate career paths. No hour figures given.
sections.gradingBasis: unclear
sections.quote: Yes, a valuable class for low effort. Really allows you to understand real estate career options.
comments: Yes it was informative and had a lot of speakers
Yes
I would recommend this class to anybody especially anyone in their first year at Haas! Abigail's an amazing professor, and the class was very engaging with a lot of diverse speakers!
Yes. I would recommend this class for those interested in real estate. So many different areas covered in detail and with esteemed experts. Amazing course.
Yes. It is very practical
Yes, very valuable and great for learning about real estate.
Yes, but most useful for first year students
Yes great class to meet real estate folk!

Yes, I would definitely recommend this course. It's an excellent introduction for anyone who is curious about real estate but doesn't yet have a deep understanding of how the industry works in the U.S. Most people initially think of real estate only in terms of development or residential brokerage. This course opens your eyes to the much broader set of career paths available — including commercial acquisitions, asset management, affordable housing, and real estate investment, among others.

Hearing directly from experienced professionals provides a realistic picture of the work involved, the types of skills that matter, and the lifestyle and compensation considerations in each area. By the end of the course, you'll have a clear, high-level view of where you might fit within the real estate ecosystem, whether you're considering it as a full-time career or a future side investment.

I would recommend this course for anyone who is tangentially interested in real estate but has limited experience. Yes, a valuable class for low effort. Really allows you to understand real estate career options. Professor is wonderful and genuinely cares about her students.
DEFINITELY!!!
Highly recommend this course for someone who is interested in real estate
Yes definitely if you're interested in RE it's a great way to learn about different areas

sections.goodFor: Students headed into nonprofit, social sector or impact investing work, or anyone who has to measure hard-to-quantify outcomes; also good from a public health angle.
sections.notFor: Students not going into social impact say relevance drops off; the all-case, participation-required format can get boring, and the course largely endorses metrics rather than critiquing them.
sections.workloadNote: Weekly cases and readings; students specifically say assignments are fair with no busy work and that they reinforce the class concepts. Hours not stated.
sections.gradingBasis: Case discussion with participation required, weekly readings, and assignments students call fair with no busy work.
sections.redFlags: Two of 15 say relevance falls off sharply if you're not entering the social sector; one found the all-case format boring at times; one wanted a more critical take on the limits of metrics.
sections.quote: At times, it can be a little boring because it's all case-based with discussions in class and participation is necessary.
comments: I would recommend this course as Colin is an effective lecturer engaging students in thought-provoking discussions. He applies theory to the real-world and walks through specific case studies that enable critical learning. Yes, if they are interested in a career in social impact. I think it's less relevant to me than I was expecting but I still found the learnings and frameworks for critiquing study design interesting.
Yes absolutely!

Yes, absolutely. I'd highly recommend this course — especially for anyone interested in working in the social sector or tackling problems where good measurement really matters. Social Impact Metrics gives you practical tools you can apply immediately, and Colin's teaching style makes even the tougher analytical concepts feel clear, engaging, and surprisingly fun.
Colin is very engaging, approachable, and passionate! He was effective at facilitating case discussions in a way that didn't just feel like a regurgitation of case facts.

Colin is an incredible professor. Super knowledgeable about the subject and the class is structured in a way that really facilitates learning. Assignments are fair, there's no busy work, and I felt the assignments helped me gain a better understanding of the concepts discussed in class. I thought the cases were very informative and interesting as well! Would recommend.
definitely!! great guy all around, funny and very knowledgeable on the subject

I would recommend this class for someone who is definitely going to go into non-profit or social impact work. I sometimes felt like it lost the forest for the trees: is non-profit work really the place to make the most impact or do we need to figure out how to change private companies to shift more in this direction as well? I felt that the class could have been a little more critical of using metrics rather than fully endorsing them as an always excellent tool. I would absolutely recommend this course to anyone interested in social impact! Professor Boyle has amazing insights and course content is extremely applicable and helpful for any social impact professional.
Colin Boyle is a wonderful professor! I really enjoyed this course and consider it a must-take if you're interested in the social sector.

Great class if you're interested in social impact, especially if you're interested in data and metrics. Colin is a extremely knowledgeable and has a great personality. He really cares about the information and the class is structured well. At times, it can be a little boring because it's all case-based with discussions in class and participation is necessary. Yes, this can help you understand a less traditional way of thinking to help us be better, more rounded out leaders in the future

Yes, Colin was a true facilitator of insightful conversation for each week's case, challenging students to dig deeper to question why certain social impact decisions were made by organizations and how to best evaluate outcomes from a data-driven perspective. The class provided a very unbiased perspective and allowed people like me (who have little social impact experience) to better understand the complexities of investing and decision-making within the industry. I would recommend this class if you are interested in social impact work -- it gives a good foundation for how to think about measuring impact and what the limitations and opportunities are for different metrics or study designs I would recommend this course to peers, because it gives a strong foundation in critical thinking about impact, evaluation, and the intersection of the two. Colin crafted an insightful, engaging, and valuable course that raised important considerations for both the theory and practice of impact evaluation. The class readings were helpful in diving into the topic we discussed and lecture & discussion of underlying assumptions was great for uncovering the why evaluation happens and how to get the most out of the process. I thought the course was well structured and that Colin does a great job facilitating discussion to support student learning.
yes

Yes for professor Boyle I would give him the highest of recommendation. For the class I think it is great for everyone who is interested in working with some sort of measurement, even if not Social Impact. A lot of the ideas can transfer to other fields where outcomes can be difficult to measure.
Yes, it is useful for real-world decision making. This is one of the best class I've taken so far.

This course is a great complement to other Haas classes in that it helps evaluate the effectiveness of initiatives not focused on profit. It's a great lens to be able to use in your career and personal life.
I would. I think it is a unique and valuable opportunity to explore a new area, particularly coming from a public health perspective.

sections.goodFor: Students new to entrepreneurship and venture capital who want a hands-on crash course, and anyone who values networking with international MBA students from other schools; the guest panels, pitching from both founder and VC sides, and site visits get consistent praise.
sections.notFor: Students who already have entrepreneurship or VC experience say it will not move the needle, and some expected more Bay Area company visits than the mostly classroom format delivered. One remote-year student also warned about coordinating group work across time zones.
sections.workloadNote: A compressed one-week intensive that students call intense, with back-to-back entrepreneur and VC deep dives and group assignments on very short turnarounds.
sections.redFlags: Recurring (3 comments): too introductory for anyone with prior entrepreneurship or VC exposure. Recurring (2 comments): fewer company visits than the course title suggests.
sections.quote: Yes, amazing course. You get to meet so many incredible people from around the world and get a deep insight into the silicon valley ecosystem.

rows.title: Sales Force Management and Channel Strategy

sections.goodFor: Anyone going into sales, go-to-market, channel/partner strategy or biz dev - especially at-scale selling rather than startup scrappiness. Praised by tech and engineering backgrounds.
sections.notFor: Students who already worked in sales or channel-partner teams; one says most of the course will feel basic, though the strategy/leadership angle may still add value.
sections.workloadNote: Coursework requires solid PowerPoint skills (though not necessarily presenting); assignments called thought-provoking and practical. Guest speakers and cases feature heavily. Hours not stated.
sections.gradingBasis: unclear - PowerPoint-based assignments and cases are mentioned, but no exams or grading breakdown are discussed.
sections.redFlags: Little recurring criticism. One says those with prior sales/channel experience will find it basic; one found a guest speaker's delivery unexciting; Azhar's dry humor takes a class or two to get used to.
sections.quote: If you have prior experience working in sales/channel partner teams or experience closely collaborating with these teams then you may find most of the course basic for you.
comments: This class is invaluable for those who work directly with a sales team or who plan to manage/create one in the future. The coursework requires a solid understanding of creating PowerPoint presentations (though not necessarily presenting them). I would highly recommend this class, even if it is solely to understand the incentivization and structuring of a sales team.
Yes, fantastic class

I would highly recommend this course and professor to my fellow students. I had no prior knowledge of sales teams and channels, yet came away with a great understanding of how their success is paramount to a company's operations.
Some of the guest speakers that I consider paramount to our learning:
-Abde Tambawalla
-Joshua Sivaslian
-Yamini Rangan
I thought that Chris Jones' presentation was not very exciting, but I really appreciated his case, as well as his POV. It is very interesting to learn about his perspective as a VAR.

Many Haas classes teach scrappy startup sales, but companies at scale operate way differently. This class is essential for anyone wanting to work on the "revenue side" of a company (where everyone should want to work...) This course has been an amazing learning experience for me. Coming from technology background, I had very limited exposure to sales. The course helped me understand the principles and strategies that the sales and marketing teams employ in planning go to market strategies.
Yes
Absolutely Yes
This class is essential for anyone aiming to develop expertise in sales and channel strategy.

It covers several foundational marketing concepts that every business or marketing student should understand. Fantastic class - take it. Really different perspective on go to market than any other class at haas. Take it with Wasim - dry sense of humor make take a class or two to get used to but he is the GOAT for a reason... you learn about how to set up a sales motion and what types of sales teams work for different kinds of products and markets. Strong focus on channels and especially how to work with partners which is somewhat unique and not that common to have a specific class on. Prof is just a good person to learn from, period.

Prof Azhar is amazing; super knowledgable and a great instructor. This course broadly covers salesforce management and channel strategy and you get an overview of the key challenges and dynamics. The course had some really great speakers; learnt a lot from them and you get to interact on a personal level.

If you have prior experience working in sales/channel partner teams or experience closely collaborating with these teams then you may find most of the course basic for you. However, you can still learn to sharpen your strategic and leadership skills in those domains.

This has been one of the best courses I have taken at Haas. It provides a deep dive into channel strategy and the principles required to design, manage, and scale successful go-to-market organizations. Coming from an engineering background, the course opened an entirely new world for me and fundamentally shifted how I think about business development, pivots, and growth strategy.

The assignments were thought provoking and reinforced the concepts in a practical, engaging way. Professor Azhar is extremely approachable, fosters rich class discussion, and drives down to the crux of the concept. The guest speakers were outstanding — experienced, relevant, and deeply current. They covered a wide range of topics, from GTM design to sales force management, and offered insights that were both inspirational and aspirational.

Yes. Good 101 class. Not a lot of workload. Gives a wide perspective of Sales. Professor knows a lot

YES

yes! one of the best classes at Haas

the professor is really structure on how he is teaching, and answer all the questions. He is really engaging. Yes I would definitely encourage this class as it gives a great overview of the sales world and how to manage and grow one.

Professor and course are good. Not too much outside work, and I think it was an overall benefit to my education. Absolutely. Like others have said, great intro to sales class. yes definitely it actually significantly helped my internship search

Yes!
Yes. definitely. This is a masterclass on leadership!

Yes, especially if you want an " MBA-like " learning experience.

Amy's classes are always fantastic and some of the most valuable time you can spend at haas. She is great at facilitating discussions and the people she brings in are such heavy hitters it's kind of insane.

Yes, I highly recommend to those who are looking for practical lessons that can be applied to real-life situations Yes, I think so! Yes - very interesting class!

Amy is a fantastic professor, genuinely one of the best I have had at Haas. Amy is the BEST!!!
definitely! great guest speakers, engaging material

sections.notFor: MBAs wanting consulting or entrepreneurship practice - one says other Haas experiential courses do it better. You carry teams of masters students with 0-2 years of experience, across an age gap.
sections.workloadNote: Thin evidence (5 comments), contested: two say workload is 3x the unit count - interviews, weekly assignments, deliverables, several presentation rounds; one calls the class reasonably laidback.
sections.gradingBasis: weekly assignments, project deliverables, and mid-term, alumni-night and final demo-day presentations
sections.redFlags: 2 students: business students hard-carry teams of young masters students as pseudo-coaches, and workload far exceeds the unit count. Experience swings on client and teammate engagement and assigned industry.
sections.quote: The workload is much higher than you think, because the teams are usually Masters students who are fresh out of undergrad with <2 years of work experience
comments: Not if you're a business student, unless you are making a hard pivot and are seriously in need of a hands-on client project on your resume, and you're willing to put in the time and unpaid labour for it. It's a good project to talk about during interviews, but that can easily be achieved through other Haas Experiential Learning courses or an in-semester internship. The workload is much higher than you think, because the teams are usually Masters students who are fresh out of undergrad with <2 years of work experience (often 0 or 1 year), so it's much more work than you'd think to coordinate with them and work with them to get the material up to a standard that you're willing to present and put your name on. The projects are usually a business question at its core (market entry, commercialisation, pricing, etc) and most groups this year had max 1 business school student, so as a business student you'll be hard-carrying most of the analysis and being a pseudo-coach for the rest of your team trying to grapple with business content that they might be learning for the first time.

Also be aware that there is usually an age gap, so if you're above the median age for business school students, be prepared to have sufficient patience to work with other students in the 22 to 25 year old range.

One advantage of this course is that the networking nights are truly impressive. Lots of VCs, serial entrepreneurs, and folks from all backgrounds (e.g. ex-military, someone who used to work at a large insurer and now is a GTM specialist for healthtech startups). The quality of contacts here is higher than the average business school networking event, so it does have value if you're interested in continuing in the deep tech space. Networking nights happen ~3 times per term (mid-term presentation, alumni night, and final demo day, though along the way you sometimes get connected with one-time "mentors" that you can speak to about your project too).

The course is a great opportunity to leaarn about the path to commercializing frontier "deep tech" innovations (frontier technologies). Profs Rappaport and Bowman are great and have experience, especially on the patent and regulation side of things. The course is a great opportunity to connect with industry professionals and experts that may open up future opportunities. That said, be ready for an extremely heavy workload. The class easily takes 3x the time suggested by the unit count and requires managing interviews, project deliverables, weekly assignments, and several rounds of presentations. The experience is also heavily team-dependent and teams are formed based on interest and past experience (plus availability)

I think this course has a lot to offer. It gives you exposure and experience to working at an early stage startup. Prof Rappaport and the GSIs offer a reasonably laidback class, and I think any complaints of the course are probably centered on their teams or startups. I enjoyed the course and would recommend it whole heartedly.

sections.redFlags: Guest speakers eat ~half of nearly every class, crowding out teaching (4+); assignments posted 2-3 days before due, students chased the teaching team (2); pro forma guidance too high-level (3).
sections.quote: 90 minutes of almost every class was scattershot guest speakers talking about their various developments across the country that didn't add much to my learning.
comments: Highly recommend this course to those who look to learn fundamental and systematic real estate investment and development
Nancy has a lot to teach, but i think half of the time was spent on guest speakers which ate up the time to learn some really practical skills in real estate investment/finance

I would recommend this to folks who are serious or seriously curious about going into commercial real estate, but not for anybody else. I came in thinking this would be a nice foundation for future personal real estate investments, giving me the ability to evaluate the profitability of, say, buying a house or a small set of apartments. I also was hoping for in depth evaluation of the state of the real estate industry in the climate transition and where / how it needed to move faster. Unfortunately, neither of these were the case. We quickly dove into jargon and nuances of commercial real estate, which was good for the half of the class who had taken real estate classes already, but which made it difficult for me to engage. I do think the lineup of speakers were quite cool (e.g., the developers of Hudson Yards in NYC), but again, very focused on larger scale commercial real estate.

There's a slight disconnect among real estate classes. We learn how to build a proforma multiple times. There should be a foundational pro forma building course, giving other courses more time to go deeper into their specific real estate topic.

"Highly recommended! If you're a student interested in project development — whether from the business side or the engineering/architecture side — this class is extremely valuable. It equips you with the tools to plan, execute, and finance a project effectively."

Yes. It is definitely tailored for students already working in real estate or pursuing jobs in real estate, but it was well taught and the guest lecturers and panels were all incredibly additive to the course experience.
This class is worth what you put into it. I found immense value in the guest speakers, and as a gateway to the real estate industry.

I recommend taking this class for anybody interested in commercial real estate development. Professor Wallace is a great professor and has her pulse on the market, able to convey difficult concepts simply. Ed McFarlane supplements Nancy's lectures well, as an Architect he adds a practical element to classes and between the both of them can answer any question you may have. Each class starts with guest speakers, who are industry practitioners. This alone is great exposure and worth attending the class. What you get out of this class is very reliant on what you put in. As someone working in Real Estate, I can firmly say I learned some new things and got some great ideas.

Yes I would recommend this course to fellow students as think the insights from professionals were great to have in class and the exercises in the class helped develop real estate analysis skills I didn't have before.
Yes, good class to learn how real estate development numbers work
Would definitely recommend for anybody interested in real estate finance and how to view it from a sustainability lense!
Yes, I would, if the person was interested in pursuing a career in real estate. The material can be a bit overwhelming if a students does not know about the fundamentals of real estate investments.

This is good class to take if you are interested in learning more about real estate - the professors are both experts in this field - and are willing to look towards the future of where it should be going. However, the first few weeks will feel like getting thrown into the deep end - but it's actually quite manageable! I'd recommend. Real estate is something you should have given a bit of thought before graduating from business school (it is the biggest asset class in the US after all).

I loved Nancy Wallace as a knowledgeable professional but I would not recommend this course. I had hoped to get more practical financial skills in this course, but felt that ultimately very little teaching happened. 90 minutes of almost every class was scattershot guest speakers talking about their various developments across the country that didn't add much to my learning. And the other 90 min was often student presentations advancing towards the final project...but that left little time to do any real teaching/skill-building.

Also the course felt disorganized. The curriculum felt haphazard with topics not often progressing logically from one to the next, and assignments (and their accompanying details) wouldn't be created on BCourses until often 2-3 days before they were due. We would often have to remind the teaching team to post assignments (things that were vaguely labeled in the Syllabus like "Progress Report 2") and to give us details about what to submit, and then scramble to get those materials together on time. This is especially surprising in a 30-person course with two Readers that could have been supporting.

I would recommend as a very introductory class for real estate. It goes through most of the topics, but if someone wants something more technical or specific about the financials, this is not the class. Overall, speakers were great. Would liked to have more concrete learnings about applying sustainable features into real estate.

Yes. This class is a must for whoever used to, wants, or is about to work in the Real Estate industry. Professors are super professional and knowledgeable in this area. This class provides a hands on experience in Real Estate and cover almost every aspect of the industry from financial pro-forma to sustainability. If you don't have any finance or real estate background like me, this class might be a bit challenging but still manageable.

I would recommend this class as a great intro to real estate development and understanding the high level levers that could be utilized. Covers key topics and familiarizes you with different projects and companies within the ecosystem. I would recommend this course if you are interested in the built environment. That said, if you are only casually interested then this may be too technical/heavy on the finance side of things. The course has some heavy hitters as guest speakers who have implemented projects all over the country.

I would recommend this course for students who already have a good understanding of real estate or who are willing to put in extra time and effort outside of class to get up to speed on the concepts and fundamentals. Instructors were not the most organized and often were delayed in communicating expectations for class assignments. Half of the lecture time for almost each class was reserved for guest speakers, which was sometimes useful and interesting but not always. Almost half the grade is based on the final project and there is very little guidance on how to actually work through the pro forma model, complete the research, etc. (guidance is very high level).
I would recommend this course to students who want to dive deeper into the financial side of sustainable

development. This introductory course would require someone to have heard certain terminology from real estate to make this course more worthwhile. Other than terminology, coming from an engineering background, I was able to share sustainable strategies and was able to correlate how efficiency affects financial results.

I wouldn't recommend this to an EWMBA student. I didn't enjoy the low opportunity to share experiences and knowledge that other students had. This course is great prep for some one seeking a career in commercial real estate. However, as a someone with no background in real estate this course lacks breadth. I still don't understand how to develop a commercial real estate project. I get a few concepts like pro-forma and pitching projects to LPs.

sections.goodFor: Anyone interested in real estate development/investment or sustainability in the built environment, or wanting GP/LP incentives, pro formas, industry lingo and strong networking access.
sections.notFor: Students without finance or modeling experience - one warns it can be VERY difficult with lingo and concepts coming fast. One says do not pay for it, audit instead.
sections.workloadNote: Experiential 3-unit course: pro forma modeling through case studies plus a final team project, with a heavy guest-speaker roster. One warns there is a lot to absorb very quickly.
sections.gradingBasis: unclear - case studies and a final team project are described, but no exams or grading breakdown are mentioned.
sections.redFlags: One student says most of the class is listening to guest lectures with the two professors hardly lecturing themselves, and would audit rather than pay. Pace and modeling demands are heavy for finance novices.
sections.quote: This is definitely a 3 unit and requires a lot of time and effort. Make sure you have a good, collaborative, communicative group because you will need to lean on them a lot
comments: I would highly recommend this instructor and course, especially for students interested in real estate. Regardless of whether you have a prior background in the field, the instructor is very supportive and makes a strong effort to help students understand the material. The course includes a project based on real-world scenarios, which provides a valuable and comprehensive experience of the real estate process. It allows students to engage with the challenges, opportunities, and complexities of real estate development in a meaningful way. Overall, it is a very rewarding and insightful course.
Yes, highly recommend this course. This course helps student to understand the real estate principle a lot if you are interested.

Whether you're interested in a career in real estate or just want to understand what defines a good real estate investment, you should take MBA280. This is a foundational course for anyone curious about the built environment. Nancy Wallace and Ed McFarlan are Berkeley's best and are complemented by an excellent roster of guest speakers. This is an experiential course so students should come prepared to work hard because they'll only get as much out of the class as they're willing to put in.
Yes, if they are interested in GP/LP real estate side of the business. it is very useful to understand the incentives for the built environment.
Yes, for the connections and networking opportunities the class affords.

Terrific course, the professors (especially Professor Wallace) add so much insight and context atop the great guest speakers. If you're interested in sustainability in the built environment and/or real estate development I highly recommend this class
Yes, if you're interested in real estate. this is one that should be taken.
Yes I would. The professors and guest speakers were wonderful and really deepened my understanding of the real estate industry.

I would not recommend paying for this class. If you are able to audit it, that would be much better. Most of the class is listening to guest lectures and the two professors hardly do any lectures themselves.

Yes, I would recommend this class if you are interested in a career in real estate. It provides a solid introduction to pro formas and financial modeling, taught by two stellar professors who are genuinely passionate about teaching and eager to help students learn. They emphasize gaining hands-on development experience while incorporating

sustainability principles. I learned a lot despite having very little pro forma experience when I entered the class, and my knowledge of pro formas grew significantly during the course through practice with case studies and the final team project (the Professors provided a lot of support). Both professors are very approachable and make themselves available. office hours, responding promptly over email. They are thoughtful in bringing a stellar lineup of industry guests, developers, investors, and other professionals, who share their experiences. This greatly enhances the classroom experience and offers a valuable opportunity to connect with industry leaders. You will leave with useful tools, industry terminology, and connections, as both professors are well-connected and encourage students to reach out to speakers and contacts. This was my favorite class during Haas, and I only regret not being able to take more classes with Professors Wallace and Ed.

I definitely recommend this course to folks, especially if you are looking to develop or hone your real estate skills. If you don't have muc h modeling experience or finance background, this course could be VERY difficult for you. There is A LOT to absorb very quickly, including industry lingo but also concepts. This is definitely a 3 unit and requires a lot of time and effort. Make sure you have a good, collaborative, communicative group because you will need to lean on them a lot with the case studies and projects. I'm not kidding. But it is worth it and you will feel prepared to talk shop about real estate after this class. I took away a lot, even if I don't plan to go into a real estate job after my MBA.

yes, especially for those who do not come from a finance background and wants to deep dive into the world of real estate finance. this course will help you understand an evaluate financial deals and structures used in the market Yes

I highly recommend this course. Professor McQuade starts the course by providing a succinct history to explain our modern real estate finance system. The sessions go from there, as he dives into bond math, REITs, and private equity, culminating into mortgage backed securities.
I am someone with extensive experience in commercial real estate, and I can say that this is one of the classes that defines why I came to business school at Haas.

Yes I would recomend it for students interested in general bond math and the real estate market. It is one of the more technical courses I've taken, so be prepared to spend some time in excel understanding a cash flow

Definitely yes. It is one of a kind course that gets you to think differently. As someone who comes from a non mba background, I really was exposed to a lot of new ideas and way of thinking.

Because this is an applied innovation class where we work with clients to solve a problem, I thought that more of the focus of the class would be on how to actually solve those problems and gain important business skills such as: understanding market landscape and market size, how to do research for startup businesses or nonprofits, skill building on being professional when working with clients (which is something I felt my team really needed), designing a go-to-market strategy, etc. Instead, this class was mostly about why animal agriculture is bad and plant-centric diets are important, and taught us very very little about how to do the actual work we are supposed to do for our clients.

Because the teams are made up of a mix of undergrads and people from different graduate programs, I was the only MBA student on our team. We were working with a startup and asked to do market sizing, competitor landscape research, profitability analysis, create a pitch deck for funders, etc. No one on my team had any idea to do this, except me who had a very baseline idea. Instead of learning this in the class, I was responsible for TEACHING my team how to do it. I was also the only one with experience working with clients, and felt I had to teach my team how to be professional and responsive. It felt like herding cats, and a big part of the workload for me was effectively being a PM trying to wrangle undergrads. It was horrible.

I wish the course had focused more on actually building our business skills and teaching less experienced folks how to be professional, given it's a Haas class, and less focused on why it's important to be plant-centric. That's valuable info and it's good to have a few lectures on that, but not the whole class.

Yes for sure. If students were interested in plant-based movement or the food system in general this class gives a really good overview/mix of topics related to both of the field mentioned. There are graduate/MBA students that I didn't know this class combined.
Yes, but more for undergrad then MBA

Definitely take this class. The community is awesome, and getting three units of credit to work on your own startup, with real time and resources to build momentum, is a pretty rare opportunity. The class also gives you credits for Lovable, AWS, Claude Pro, and other tools, which makes a real difference when you're building.

Compared to programs like Lean Launch Pad, which lean heavily on customer interviews alone with a tight weekly cadence of identical deliverables for every team, this is much more flexible. You'll still do customer discovery, but you'll also have the structure to leverage the newest AI tools and actually ship in parallel. Different startups can be at different stages — you can pivot, break up with your team and join a new one, start over, and run customer discovery and building in parallel. This structure also reflects how products are actually getting built today. Software is so much cheaper to ship now, so customer discovery and building can happen in parallel, not in the old waterfall sequence of research-then-build. The class mirrors how real startups operate, which makes the experience much more applicable to the real world. Progress is defined in terms of what's actually moving the needle for your team's specific venture, not busywork deliverables. It feels like a real incubator, not a academic checklist.

How the class is structured: you're making real progress every week. Class sessions usually open with an hour topic overview from the professors, followed by a guest speaker, and then dedicated mentoring time where you can get advice from the week's in person mentors and collaborate with teammates and other peers on whatever challenges you're working through. The mentor program is a real highlight. There's a deep roster of mentors brought in from a wide range of backgrounds and industries, and you have choice in who you work with. Combined with the peer collaboration in class, the community feels built in and there to support everyone.

Set your expectations going in: if you're looking for a tightly structured curriculum with a lot of rigorous frameworks, this may not be that. But if you come in thinking of it as a great incubator community led by Omri (who's an exceptional teacher and infuses life lessons alongside entrepreneurship lesson) you'll get a ton out of it. He's beloved for good reason. One signal of how inspiring this community is: about 20 of the 27 teams from this cohort are continuing their ventures past the end of the class. That speaks for itself. Heads up that it's a lot of work, plan for it to take meaningful time and energy. But if you're game for that, you'll learn a ton.

Even if you're not sure entrepreneurship is your long-term path, this class is still worth taking. With AI, the lines between PM, engineer, designer, and user researcher are collapsing, we may not even have separate roles for much longer, just "builders." This class is one of the best opportunities at Haas to practice being an "AI builder", wearing all those hats at once. You'll do real customer research, real building, and real iteration alongside teammates with different perspectives, with your ideas challenged by real customers. The broader skills: flexible thinking, customer empathy, the ability to pivot and learn from your learnings, humility, the willingness to try different creative approaches, are applicable far beyond entrepreneurship. I'd recommend this for anyone with curiosity about AI, entrepreneurship, product, or even just what it's like to spend a semester working with a team on a creative project. I highly recommend taking this class because it gives you the opportunity to actually build a product and learn through practice. However, I suggest that students come in with a validated idea (for example, already having done 20–30 customer interviews); otherwise, you may end up spending half of the course on customer discovery, while teams that start with a concrete idea can use the time to build and iterate on their product. I would even recommend taking Lean Launchpad, which focuses heavily on customer discovery, before this class so that you can get the most benefit from the experience.

I definitely would recommend this class. Unless you have 0 curiosity in AI, I think this is a great way to spend 1 credit (and honestly I would have spent more).

Yes, I would recommend. The depth of knowledge and expertise on a frontier subject is not only timely, but if great value for students living through this transitionary paradigm.

sections.notFor: No criticism was raised. One notes people from large legacy firms find the startup perspective harder to relate to at first.

sections.gradingBasis: unclear
sections.quote: I would recommend this class to anyone who hasn't worked in a strategy or consulting role before... how to position a company within a market, how to build a new market, how to navigate regulation
comments: Yes. Absolutely! Very interesting class. You get more out of it than you realize just why be present and actively engaging in discussions, lectures, and conversations with guest presents. If you're interested in in the world of big tech, this is the class for you.

Yes, teaches you about Silicon Valley and the issues that entrepreneurs have, how to solve. Very informative Yes I would recommend. Jon Metzler has extreme insights into this area of study and students considering leading startup or even leading a new division at fast-growing firm will immensely benefit from this class
Yes, you will learn very important ascpects of how to build a startup from fundamentals, money, how to think. Also speakers are great
Yes
100% would recommend. He is really engaged and knowledgeable. Definitely worth your time and money!
yes!
Yes. This is a very enlightening course and the instructor made it interesting. Also the course contents and topic covered were very relevant most especially to people considering entrepreneurship.

Absolutely - the ability to recognize opportunity is more important now than ever before in the AI age. The principles that Jon focuses on are timeless and will sharpen our collective mental models on capitalizing on opportunities that could lead to outsized returns.

Yes, highly recommend Jon's classes, especially if you are interested in deep tech, semiconductors, foundational technologies, etc. Jon puts a huge amount of effort into the class and comes prepared with great stories and guest lecturers.

Absolutley, specifically anyone interested in the historical context of silicon valley and the tech industry, as well as what are the various "tech readiness level" equivalents of companies and startegies.

Great course for those with entrepreneurial mindset and goals. The guest speakers were wonderful and the network that Prof. Jon brought into the course was amazing. rows.title: Modeling for Energy and Infrastructure Project Finance

sections.goodFor: People targeting renewable energy or infrastructure development, or pivoting into energy project finance from an adjacent role; good on capital stack, deal terms and current market trends.
sections.notFor: Anyone expecting real modeling depth or with no energy/finance grounding. Several say a background is critical and that newcomers feel lost more than once.
sections.workloadNote: A 1-credit intensive run as two 8-hour Sundays; readings, a case study and a group project with four scenario options built around an Excel project-finance model. Content called dense.
sections.gradingBasis: A group project building a project finance model is the key deliverable, alongside readings and a case study; no exams mentioned.
sections.redFlags: Recurring: high-level overview, not a modeling course. One says the model taught is abbreviated and omits standard practice (DSCR, reserve accounts, lender sensitivities). Two 8-hour Sundays is very dense.
sections.quote: Yes, if you are looking for a high-level overview of project finance. If you want to learn modeling, then no.
comments: Yes, approachable and knowledgable

The essence of this course is building a project financing model by yourself, and it looks like an Excel heavy activity, but anyone who followed the classes with Matt can easily build their own financial model that they can utilize in their own project. Highly recommend and one of my best Sunday elective course.

I absolutely would. If you were interested in how the infrastructure of America and other countries are developed and financed from the perspective of all market participants, this course is perfect for you.

Yes! The course feels very "real world" in nature. If you are interested in energy / infra project finance or working for an (especially renewable) energy developer generally, this is a good course to take
Course is incredibly informative with real-world cases and guest lecturers. A background in financial modeling and/or energy is critical for success.

This is a good class for anyone that wants to understand how large physical projects are financed. The class is more geared towards finance professionals, but it is tractable for non-finance professionals with a little more work. Matt is a good instructor and the class is well structured and organized.

Yes but only if you already have a deep understanding of the clean energy financing landscape. It is very difficult to do the class without a general understanding of this space and the various financing nuances.
Yes, very helpful for those working or interested in the field. Also the policy, deal and terms discussiosn are very up to date.

For a one-credit course, I feel I got an incredible amount of learning out of this class. It helps that I'm really interested in the subject, so I did fully-engage with the class project in order to maximize my learning outside of the classroom as well. Matt Rogers brings an incredible amount of industry knowledge and was able to facilitate very valuable Q&A in addition to covering a large amount of lecture content. The readings, case study, and group project also greatly facilitated the learning. The 3 different guest speakers were all incredible - very informative and complementary perspectives. I only wish it were offered as a 2-credit class, so we could have had more time to dig deeper into different topics and get more practice with the financial modeling itself, although the 4 different options/project scenarios for the group project do provide a great opportunity for self-learning outside the classroom.
This was a really useful course and I would recommend it to anyone interested in energy infrastructure.

I would recommend this course generally if you're passionate about or curious about energy markets and project finance, but my caveat is that you should have realistic expectations of what you'll get out of it. As someone with little background on the topic, I learned a lot in the class by being exposed to the information and models, but I can't say I gained confidence in putting this learning into practice. If you're also new to the topic, and willing to put in a lot of extra work outside the class, you could perhaps build that confidence. Also, since a group project is the key deliverable of this course, your group will greatly shape your experience outside of class.
YES 100%
Overall, yes, I'd recommend this course to anyone interested in the financial side of the renewable energy industry and market development.

I would recommend this class to anyone interested in project finance. It is a higher level class (it doesn't dive into a ton of detail) but it does a great job of introducing you to many different topics.

I'd recommend this course to anyone looking to learn more about project finance and infrastructure. Provided a good overview about some of the technical details. the speakers were also good with a lot of industry knowledge

If you are looking to work in renewable energy development or a related field, I would highly recommend this course. It teaches practical basics for excel modeling of projects and gives a great overview of current market trends to be able to make informed business decisions.
Recommend the instructor but do not recommend the course. I felt that I barely learnt anything even though it is only a 1 credit course.
this is a good one if you already have finance basic

Yes! Professor Rogers is highly engaging!

I'd recommend this course to anyone looking to get an introduction to project finance, or looking to pivot into energy project finance from a similar role in another industry. Yes, this is great course to understand how Project Finance modelling impacts the undertaking of any energy project. I recommend this course because it gives you a chance to get a bigger picture of the project financing landscape in the energy industry, which is a field that is hard to understand on your own.

Matt is great The 2 Sunday format is not something I would recommend to a full time student but I would recommend the class to those interested in the energy space.

This course is fascinating and I would absolutely recommend, especially if you are interested in understanding how renewable energy projects are put together. Great professor with in-depth expertise in the industry that is still current and has a wealth of experience vertically and horizontally across energy and finance.
