comments: Absolutely!

YES!! This course is one of my favorites so far. You get practical experience to test the entrepreneurship journey along with solid advice, clear examples, and team support. It is a lot of work if you are truly passionate about your chosen project so do be aware of that. Especially if you are new to the VC/entrepreneurship space, I HIGHLY recommend taking this course. I learned so much that I can now directly apply as a possible entraphsip or really any new project. Both professors are so willing to help and also honest with their feedback which I so appreciate!
Great experience in taking that first step into becoming a founder. This class is a safe environment to test your VC's ideas, again VC ideas!

Yes, I would highly recommend this course to any MBA student, or those considering entrepreneurship. Its extremely hands on, so only take it if you are ready to engage and put the work in, especially at the end of the semester. The learnings are invaluable and whether or not you have an idea or business you want to work on now, this will help you learn how to think about problem spaces, validate ideas and progress through bringing a product/service to life. If you do have an idea or business now, this will be an opportunity for guided strategic development.

The course began on a strong note, with the first 3 – 4 weeks offering well-structured and valuable content. However, the quality and coherence of the course declined significantly afterward. The structure appeared to unintentionally encourage groupthink and popularity-driven decisions, often at the expense of better ideas. Strong projects were sometimes overlooked, while weaker or duplicate ideas advanced. While the professors aim to stay neutral in team formation and idea selection, some degree of intervention — especially when multiple teams are proposing near- identical or clearly underdeveloped concepts — might improve the overall experience and outcomes.

A more flexible team formation process would also be beneficial. Forcing students to join groups they may not be genuinely interested in, rather than allowing them to pursue topics they are passionate about, can limit engagement and stifle creativity.

Also I really want to emphasize how the GSI was unnecessarily strict and annoying about random things when they themselves were so disorganized. Many students, including myself, found the GSI to be overly rigid and

unapproachable. For instance, I was incorrectly marked absent from a session I clearly attended and signed in for. When I raised the issue, the GSI dismissed it without considering a correction. This kind of inflexibility and lack of responsiveness undermines trust and adds unnecessary frustration to the student experience. Given that most graduate students are working professionals, a more respectful and collaborative approach would have been more appropriate.

If you have not done anything in entrepreneurship before I think it is helpful framework. The final deliverables lacked clarity on what was expected and the fact that the class was a simulation goes against the seeming expectation for you to actually build a company. It is hard to tell if the expectation is an educational endeavor or for you to actually build a company which makes assignments difficult.

I would 100% recommend this course. It's fantastic from a learning perspective, I loved how the course was structured layer by layer to build up a business plan. I've already taken an entrepreneurship course, but this landed in a much bigger way.
I would say you get out what you put in. And your team is so important to making this an enjoyable process, so keep this in mind.

100% recommend it. The EWMBA version has more interesting students, and the teaching staff are both legends too. If you want to learn how to synthesize an and take it all the way to pitching it to VCs from Lightspeed, a16z, etc, this is the class for you.
Only if they have an idea that they are passionate about and want to launch.
Hands down I would certainly recommend this class to other students interested in exploring the world of entrepreneurship or VC.

I would, but this course is pretty disorganized and has a lot of busy work. They need to get rid of the weekly assignment/write ups because I didn't get much value from those. Instead, have check points related to our main project to keep teams on track. Also, it was really hard to reach the TA and professor, slow replies, and not always getting quality time

Definitely recommend. Even if you don't see yourself as an entrepreneur, this course can be helpful in understanding the start-up ecosystem and gaining knowledge about funding, business model, strategy etc.
I absolutely would. This should be a required course and is full of invaluable lessons for all.
yes, I would definitely recommend the class to someone interested in learning about startups and wanting to get a holistic view on the process of startups.
I would not because I could have learned so much more by having devoted class time to learn by doing rather than listening to lectures.
yes

No. The class was helpful the first few weeks when we were all working towards our own ideas and pitch. The class took a nosedive once Professor Beyer had to step out and Shiva stepped in. We didn't learn anything during the weeks Shiva instructed. The class workload is too heavy (essays every week) and wasn't helpful. This class would be more effective if each student continued working on their ideas throughout the semester.

There is a 35% chance I would only recommend this class to my fellow students. For most of them, it would be a no. Maybe this is because I had a sub-par experience with my team after Darwin Day, but after speaking with many of my fellow classmates, there was a lack of interest in the class across the board after Darin Day. The motivation to come to this class went down substantially for me and many of my classmates after Darin Day, but we all still came and felt unmotivated through the end of the semester.

sections.goodFor: Students who want Lean Startup framing for validating a new venture, or who value hearing directly from a few successful entrepreneur guests.
sections.notFor: Anyone wanting step-by-step guidance on starting a venture - one of two commenters attended every class and says lectures rambled and taught nothing beyond blue ocean strategy.
sections.workloadNote: Only 2 comments - evidence is very thin. Students pitch a startup idea, then work in teams on the ideas selected by vote/professor; one says no instruction accompanies that work.
sections.gradingBasis: unclear; student startup pitches and team work on selected ideas.
sections.redFlags: 1 of 2 commenters reports rambling lectures unrelated to assignments, no instruction to support the team startup work, and calls it a waste of credits and money.
sections.quote: I have attended all classes and walked away learning nothing but the definition of blue ocean strategy. Waste of credits and money.
comments: I would not recommend this course unless you are looking to hear from a couple of successful entrepreneurs. Majority of class does not teach anything, its more of rambling on topics unrelated to assignments or how to actually step by step start your own venture. Only one class "blue ocean strategy" is explained, and I could have googled it. We did not learn anything unfortunately. You create your own startup one day-which may or may not be chosen. You then are told to work with peers on the selected group ideas the professors pick or are based on student votes, and are not taught anything to help you with these startups. I have attended all classes and walked away learning nothing but the definition of blue ocean strategy. Waste of credits and money.
Yes, the focus on the "Lean Startup" methodology makes this course essential for anyone serious about validating a new venture.

sections.goodFor: Aspiring entrepreneurs, including people arriving without an idea; several cite a comprehensive framework from concept through go-to-market and fundraising. Take it in person.
sections.notFor: Students unwilling to work hard if their startup isn't picked, or who can't tolerate uneven teammates - one reports classmates checked out of group work because only their own idea mattered.
sections.workloadNote: Thin evidence (7 comments). Team-based work on selected startup ideas - everyone pitches a company idea - plus customer surveys, where one student reports conflicting guidance (200 responses vs 30).
sections.gradingBasis: unclear - a pitched company idea and team project work are described, but grading is never discussed.
sections.redFlags: One alleges opaque project selection, an unqualified TA teaching half the course (incorrect pricing lecture), and end 'VCs' largely from Beyer's own fund. Another says a co-lecturer was rude to female founders.
sections.quote: you should only take this course if you have intention in working hard independent of your startup getting picked
comments: I would definitely recommend Dr. Beyer to students who want to learn about entrepreneurship. I would additionally say that you should only take this course if you have intention in working hard independent of your startup getting picked. I'm a student who came in to learn about entrepreneurship, not because I had a pre-existing idea, and I left with a lot of learnings. But it was disheartening working with people who were checked out on group work, because they only were interested in themselves.

I think the course was well-designed overall. If Shiva continues to co-lecture, he needs to come better prepared to the sessions. Also, please do not bring back Niki; she was rude to all female founders.

I would certainly recommend this course to wanna be entrepreneurs as it provides a comprehensive framework to think of your business all the way from conceptualizing your idea, to going to market, raising funds and sustaining it. Quite a few of Kurt's students from this course have gone on to become successful entrepreneurs which in my opinion is a testimony to effectiveness and impact of this course on your entrepreneurial journeys.
I would 100% recommend this course if you are even remotely interested in becoming an entrepreneur. This was one of the most fun classes at haas.
YES!!! Take it in person, though. Wait to take the class until you feel like you have an entrepreneurship idea that you're really excited about, since everyone must pitch a company idea.
Yes, absolutely. I loved the class learnings.

I came away from this class not trusting Kurt Beyer or his TA, Shiven, who teaches literally half the course. From the unclear way in which projects were chosen ("We did it all by voting -- except for the last few, which we chose.") to letting someone HIGHY unqualified teach half the course (Shiven -- who gave a straight up incorrect lecture on pricing.) to Shiven saying that we needed 200 survey responses and then Kurt implying sometime later that we needed 30 to him saying that there would be a bunch of VCs at the end and it was all either people who weren't VCs or were part of his own fund, I don't trust this guy. He's self-serving. If you want to stroke someone's ego and hope that you get chosen for a project and want him as a VC even though he doesn't seem trustworthy, take the course. Otherwise, steer away.

rows.title: International Business Development for MBAs, IP course

sections.goodFor: Students who want international consulting experience and travel, and who can tolerate not knowing their country, team or client at sign-up. Several call it their favorite Haas experience.
sections.notFor: Anyone unwilling to work extra hours or take assignment uncertainty. Team leads do far more work with little recognition, and projects that aren't go-to-market fit the curriculum poorly.
sections.workloadNote: Not weekly-quantified but heavy: spring coursework, 80+ hours per week during the two-week in-country stint, plus assignments carried into the following fall for the last credit.
sections.gradingBasis: team client deliverables, a blog post and a final presentation; students say length guidelines were not enforced consistently
sections.redFlags: Credit-to-work mismatch is the loudest complaint (2 say it should be 4 credits given fall assignments); assignment instructions confusing, changing and unevenly enforced (2); class time not relevant to all projects (2).
sections.quote: Project, team, and country dependent. Super MBA experience and would recommend doing it. Team leads should expect to do a lot more work with little recognition.
comments: Absolutely. Amazing opportunity to get consulting experience while traveling the world.
This is a truly transformative experience. A lot of work, a lot of hard work!! But you get to learn so much, experience so much, and explore so much! I highly recommend this course????
I would. This was a GREAT course!!

This course, as many people know, carries a lot of uncertainty. When you sign up for the course, you have no knowledge about what experience you are doing to get (country, team, client), so it is definitely a risk. But that said, I think the whole experience was worth it once you are able to go to your country, experience a new culture, and meet your client in person.

There were a few issues with this course throughout the semester that I hope are addressed: 1. The class time was not always relevant to all projects and it seemed not the best use of time for all teams. I think sharing a variety of resources that might or might not be applicable to projects would be rather, rather than providing only one framework or way to do things and assume that all teams can use this in their project. 2. Especially at the end, guidelines provided for some assignments were not followed by all teams. For example, we were told to keep the blog post at certain length, or the final presentation at 3 slides and these guidelines seemed almost "optional" and not really enforced by all teams, creating an unfair advantage for those teams who did follow the guidelines. 3. This class should be 4 credits if they still make us do assignments in the fall semester. I think it is ridiculous that we only get 2 credits in the spring for the amount of work we put in, including traveling in country and working 80+ hours for two weeks while in- country. All other applied innovation classes that have client-facing work are 3 credits. The fact that we also need to do a presentation in the fall to get the final 1 credit out of the 3 does not make sense at all, and this should be 1 credit IN ADDITION to the 3 credits we should already be earning for all our work from January to May. I hope this changes for future classes.
Yes if they are willing to work extra hours
Project, team, and country dependent. Super MBA experience and would recommend doing it. Team leads should
expect to do a lot more work with little recognition.

It's a great course with plenty of opportunity. Well-organized but not all projects are Go To Market strategy, and that is all the course focuses on. Instructors are very helpful, but instructions for assignments are confusing and change constantly
Yes, this was my all time favorite experience at Haas. The in country travel was a once in a lifetime experience, and I made lifelong friendships with my teammates.
Yes for the travel and consulting case experience!! Bang for your buck

rows.title: Investment Management Series
rows.ghostNote: One-unit, six-week speaker series on investment management careers: asset managers, allocators and analysts.

sections.goodFor: Students in or heading into strategy, corporate strategic planning or futures work who want structured scenario-planning and outside-in tools for long-term thinking.
sections.notFor: Anyone wanting depth or hands-on application. Several call it vague, framework-heavy and low on actionable content; consultants may find little new. Not innovative enough given the name.
sections.workloadNote: 2-credit course dominated by guest lectures and group work with little actual lecture - one calls it more workshop than class. Frameworks land early then repeat; classes often start 15 min late.
sections.gradingBasis: unclear - group work and applying the scenario-planning frameworks are described, but grading is never discussed.
sections.redFlags: Recurring (4+): repetitive after ~week 4 once the full framework is introduced; too much guest lecture and group work with little lecture, so it feels light for 2 credits; classes often start 15 minutes late.
sections.quote: This course could've been shorter. Maybe one block week or two all day Sundays. It got a little repetitive after week 4.
comments: Instructor yes but course no unfortunately. It's framework focused and did not feel innovative enough despite the name

Olaf is very experienced in the area of deliberating about uncertain future scenarios for companies and this course allows students to learn and apply the frameworks he has developed. Recommend for FTMBAs although this class was mostly EW and EMBAs. They actually get stuff done.
Yes! It helped organize the way I think about scenario planning, especially the outside in approach. Great for people who want to start thinking critically about big ticket ideas
Course was a pleasant surprise and although was slightly different than expectations and what was described in the syllabus.

It's a very important topic and the material is very interesting. However, the course felt too light since the great majority of the class is guest lecture and group work so I felt like I did not get my money's worth for a 2-credit class. There was actually very little lecture material and it felt like a workshop. Classes also often start 15 minutes late. I still highly recommend the class though!

I think (or atleast I hope) there are better courses out there that could help in enhancing your overall learning specifically when you have been in challenging roles like Consulting or growing companies with good pathways to train leadership being available internally.
Yes

Not unless the course is redesigned as a 1-credit module. The scenario planning framework is valuable and thought- provoking, but the pacing made the latter sessions feel repetitive once the full framework was introduced early on. Condensing the content or rebalancing it with more hands-on coaching and application would make it far more impactful.

Yes. Olaf was one of my favorite at my time here at Haas. This course opens your eyes and gets you thinking long term and strategically, something all companies look for in a senior IC or leader. Highly recommend it.

The content is useful if you work in strategy or support the development of your organization's strategic planning efforts. This course could've been shorter. Maybe one block week or two all day Sundays. It got a little repetitive after week 4.

Yes. You'll learn scenario planning tools in this course and it can be applied to many fields in your life. Yes, I would. Disruption futures challenges your thinking and leverages concepts from strategy courses to envision what companies can do to position themselves for an ever changing business environment, both locally and globally. Yes!

Would definitely recommend this course to anyone who wants to pursue a career in any kind of strategy. This course will give a great framework to bring your strategy acumen to the fore and impress your stakeholders. All in all, great learning experience.

I'd recommend this course if you want to to learn about futures thinking and the role futurists/strategists play in their firms. His course brought in great guest speakers who are currently futurists at their firm. What was really helpful were the various consulting frameworks provided for thinking about how to address futures questions. Overall, this is an enjoyable class that will allow you to come away with frameworks for how to think towards the future. It helps bring together many of the things you may have learned in may of your other Haas classes as well. I'd recommend this course.
This class is immeasurably helpful, however, one must be prepared to leverage outside tools.

Yes I would definitely recommend peers taking this class. The class gave me an opportunity and the framework and tools to think bigger both for my work, career, and the industry I work in. Truly inspiring!
In the middle - I'd recommend for someone interested in strategy and future thinking course. Looking for industry information and general business knowledge.
I think it's to vague and not much actionable course
Would absolutely recommend this class. We are at Haas to 10x our careers, and this class teaches you how to and gives you the tools you need to plan and be successful
Great course to think above and beyond not only from a company perspective but also from the world's. Learned practical tools usage and also the role of futurist!

sections.goodFor: Students interested in human behavior, bias and self-reflection; a good complement to corporate finance for deepening finance understanding.
sections.notFor: Students who need substantive, rigorous content - one of five says another elective may be a better use of the slot.
sections.workloadNote: Thin evidence - only 5 comments. One explicitly calls it a light workload; no one describes assignments or hours.
sections.gradingBasis: unclear
sections.redFlags: One of only five commenters felt the class lacked enough substance to justify taking it over another elective.
sections.quote: Maybe, while it was very interesting I think there may be more substance required to make it worth taking over a different class.
comments: Absolutely, one of the best professors at Haas.

I believe taking this course in addition to corporate finance will deepen your understanding of finance. I would recommend this class to those who are interested in human behavior and constantly engage in self-reflective thinking. Many of the topics covered in this class have crossed my mind, and they can really impact you in the long run.
Prof is fun and the class sometimes feels like a stand-up comedy, light workload too.
Maybe, while it was very interesting I think there may be more substance required to make it worth taking over a different class.

Yes, I recommend the class to anyone looking to connect behavioral finance theory with real-world applications. Yes this is a great class for students who want to think about decision making and determine if you think rationally or irrationally. The research backed data he presents is pretty eye opening and proves that our biases play a huge factor in how we make decisions. Going forward, I plan to be more aware of these biases to make myself a better and more effective leader. Highly recommend this course

sections.goodFor: Students who want finance through a behavioral lens - biases, options strategy and corporate finance made digestible, with freedom to pick project topics.
sections.notFor: Students who need organization: bare bCourses site, slide decks unusable for review, ambiguous last-minute deadlines; one flags 'outlandish and problematic' takes in lecture.
sections.workloadNote: Thin evidence (7 comments). Main deliverable is a project with flexible, self-chosen topics; 3-hour sessions. Deadlines and expectations reported as ambiguous or last-minute.
sections.gradingBasis: A project with student-chosen topics; expectations described by one student as ambiguous.
sections.redFlags: One detailed comment (of 7): bare bCourses site, limited tech skills, slides that are graphs/pictures rather than study material, ambiguous or last-minute deadlines, some problematic takes.
sections.quote: Lastly, deadlines and assignments/expectations were ambiguous or given at the last minute. Despite all this, I found the course interesting and insightful
comments: Yes

Absolutely recommend! Great for connecting financial strategies (which can be complex, opaque, etc) to very relatable human experiences/biases/dynamics. There's life advice, financial strategies, and bonus info on salmon behavior that made it all together a really great class.
Yes, cool way to view finance outside of the traditional lens and explore why marketplaces are the way they are. Yes, definitely a great class and engaging professor.
Yes

I highly recommend this course for its holistic approach to complex subjects. Professor La Blanc presents markets, options strategy, and corporate finance in a very digestible manner that balances theory with practical understanding. Additionally, the flexibility provided on project topics allows students to explore personal areas of interest, making the assignments much more relevant and engaging

Prof La Blanc is a very engaged and impassioned speaker and knows a lot about behavioral economics. There is truly never a dull moment in his class, and you will be engaged for the full 3 hours of class. That said, some of his takes were very outlandish and problematic, and his technology skills were limited. The bCourse site was very bare. The slide decks were long and not the most helpful for review (mostly graphs and pictures pertaining to cases he discussed, not course concepts that you could use to study). Lastly, deadlines and assignments/expectations were ambiguous or given at the last minute. Despite all this, I found the course interesting and insightful, and I don't regret taking it.

rows.title: Managing the New Product Development Process

sections.goodFor: Students new to product management, or anyone who wants to build/found something and needs the fundamental PM frameworks with hands-on team practice.
sections.notFor: Students with existing product experience - one says content is mainly basic PM frameworks and your experience swings on which team you land in.
sections.workloadNote: Thin detail. Structure is frameworks plus hands-on team work solving a real problem; one student says the experience is heavily group dependent.
sections.gradingBasis: Team-based applied product project; not detailed further.
sections.redFlags: One student: content is mainly basic PM frameworks and the course experience is heavily dependent on your group.
sections.quote: Only take this course if you have no product experience or you have a personal interest in building a product (you have an idea OR want to think through one).
comments: Yes.
I strongly recommend it if you are interested in product management and development. It's a great class!! Great PM intro course
Yes! A clear expert in the field. This course is the perfect introduction to product management.

Yes, particularly those who are interested in product management and want to learn the fundamentals! Yes on both fronts. If you're remotely interested in product management and building/founding a company more broadly, this is the right Haas class for you.

Yes, I would definitely recommend this course, especially for students who are new to product and want hands-on experience working with a team to solve a real problem. The structure, guidance, and practical approach make it a great entry point into product development, and the balance between frameworks and applied work helps you learn by doing.
Yeeeeees
Yes

Only take this course if you have no product experience or you have a personal interest in building a product (you have an idea OR want to think through one). Course experience is heavily group dependent and course content is mainly basic product management frameworks
Yes! Vince is amazing and really approachable!
Yes I will
Definitely, Vince was great

rows.title: Fundamentals of Business

sections.goodFor: Students with little or no business-management experience who are eyeing leadership roles, especially early-career; commenters praised the engaging teaching style and discussion-driven format.
sections.workloadNote: Described as not too difficult, with results tracking the effort you put in.
sections.quote: Not too difficult, you get out what you put in, great professors.

rows.f26Day: These courses exist for the benefit of the rest of campus, or for populations other than our MBAs - not included on our schedule or in bidding.  However, MBA students may take these courses; they count toward your required MBA units for graduation when taken for letter grade. Please add/drop via CalCentral per campus deadlines and request information from the Instructors. These courses are not managed by the FTMBA Office.

sections.goodFor: Students new to food systems or plant-based business who want passionate instructors, strong guest speakers and industry connections in the food space.
sections.notFor: MBAs expecting business skill-building - one says it taught almost nothing about market sizing, GTM or client work while they coached undergrad teammates. Weak if you already know the space.
sections.workloadNote: Contested: one says not a ton of outside work, another describes a LOT of little busywork assignments plus an external client project. Zoom sessions with guest speakers, plus in-person potluck days.
sections.gradingBasis: many small assignments, pre-submitted guest speaker questions, and a team client project
sections.redFlags: 3 students call it one-sided advocacy ('vegan propaganda') rather than business content; mixed undergrad/grad teams leave the lone MBA carrying and coaching (2); many small busywork assignments (2); Zoom disengaging (2).
sections.quote: this class was mostly about why animal agriculture is bad and plant-centric diets are important, and taught us very very little about how to do the actual work
comments: This class is helpful if you are new to food systems and the plant-based world and it is a good learning experience about everything involved in animal agriculture processes and the negative impacts socially, environmentally, ethically ets. Lots of good guest speakers but signing up to ask a question before we heard them speak is not best, since we don't know exactly what they will talk about and usually the questions are already answered. The in-person potluck days are fun - I really enjoyed trying plant-based dishes from others. I would say as an MBA this was a LOT of little assignments that were a lot of busy work, in addition to project with an external client, so the class seems a little more geared towards undergraduates than graduate-level students, so I think less little required assignments should be required for this to be a 3-credit course with an experiential learning component.
Yes, engaging, so interesting, found my niche

Working with a client in a team setting is a great learning experience, which I would highly recommend. You get more out of this class if you're into food systems, obviously, but prior experience isn't super necessary at all. I would 100% recommend this course to a fellow student because of Miyoko and Brittanys' passion towards the topic. It is an excellent place to build teamwork strengths as you get to work with many different classmates and have so many opportunities to share ideas with each other. This class is also an excellent place to gain more connections if you intend to work in the food business because of the group projects that connect you to relavent food businesses and institutions and all the guest speakers as well.

Interesting class for students who have never taken a food systems or plant-based class in the past, but you won't gain too much additional information if you came in with prior knowledge. The speakers and semester-long partnerships are interesting, but do note that having Zoom discussions isn't the most engaging and you'll be working with undergraduates who may depend on your MBA knowledge to ensure project success.
The professors, Brittany and Miyoko, are extremely knowledgeable and great people to know. If you plan to work in food systems in the future, they can absolutely help to support!
I definitely would recommend this class to other people. Its super important and cool.

I do wish it was slightly less one sided and they talked about case studies of sustainable meat production, or at least discussed how that fits into a sustainable food system, because at times it felt too heavy on that "veganism woohoo!!!" type of education.
Yes, since it is very informative, ran by passionate instructors, and gives people great opportunities to hear from many different experts in the world of plant-based foods.

No, absolutely not. Do NOT take this class. I was warned by past 2nd years and did not listen. Because this is an applied innovation class where we work with clients to solve a problem, I thought that more of the focus of the class would be on how to actually solve those problems and gain important business skills such as: understanding market landscape and market size, how to do research for startup businesses or nonprofits, skill building on being professional when working with clients (which is something I felt my team really needed), designing a go-to-market strategy, etc. Instead, this class was mostly about why animal agriculture is bad and plant-centric diets are important, and taught us very very little about how to do the actual work we are supposed to do for our clients.

Because the teams are made up of a mix of undergrads and people from different graduate programs, I was the only MBA student on our team. We were working with a startup and asked to do market sizing, competitor landscape research, profitability analysis, create a pitch deck for funders, etc. No one on my team had any idea to do this, except me who had a very baseline idea. Instead of learning this in the class, I was responsible for TEACHING my team how to do it. I was also the only one with experience working with clients, and felt I had to teach my team how to be professional and responsive. It felt like herding cats, and a big part of the workload for me was effectively being a PM trying to wrangle undergrads. It was horrible.

I wish the course had focused more on actually building our business skills and teaching less experienced folks how to be professional, given it's a Haas class, and less focused on why it's important to be plant-centric. That's valuable info and it's good to have a few lectures on that, but not the whole class.

Yes for sure. If students were interested in plant-based movement or the food system in general this class gives a really good overview/mix of topics related to both of the field mentioned. There are graduate/MBA students that I didn't know this class combined.
Yes, but more for undergrad then MBA
Yes definitely, if you are passionate about challenging the societal norm and exploring food systems! But it would be better if in person.

This is an interesting applied innovation course, not a ton of outside work and cool guest speakers. I have changed my perspective on plant based eating quite a lot as a result of this class. A lot of the material is super interesting. Overall though, be prepared for the class to feel a bit like vegan propaganda at times - if youre aware and open to that, I think it's a great class and highly recommend.

Yes very much so. I have learned about foundations and habits that I will aspire to keep for the rest of my life surrounding my food choices. I think it's extremely important to learn about our food system and to inspire to make a change in the world.

Taking this class really depends on what you want to learn. I personally thought it would integrate business management and food systems a little more but that's my fault for not reading the description clearly. If someone wants to learn more about food systems and health impacts, they should definitely take it. It's also a good way to learn about food in general and since there aren't many of those classes at Berkeley, this would be a good one to take. yes

rows.title: Opportunity Recognition: Technology and Entrepreneurship in Silicon Valley

sections.goodFor: Students interested in entrepreneurship, VC, or tech strategy who want a light, discussion-based class on innovation frameworks and Silicon Valley history; Isaacs' engaging teaching, guest speakers, and cases featuring the actual protagonists are the draw.
sections.notFor: Students wanting current, hands-on, practical content; several found the deliberately older cases (1960s-90s) dated and theory-heavy with few practical takeaways, and a couple found sessions repetitive for the credit load.
sections.workloadNote: Consistently described as light and manageable; several call it an easy class, with some wishing it carried fewer credits or more coursework.
sections.gradingBasis: One term's students said weekly assignments graded by GSIs made up the whole grade; others simply called grading very fair.
sections.redFlags: Recurring (4+ comments): dated case material with limited real-world application; some sessions feel drawn out or repetitive; one comment flagged that grading ran entirely through GSI-graded weekly assignments.
sections.quote: Drew is a fantastic lecturer and makes class interesting and engaging - 3 hours flies by!

rows.title: Business Communication in Diverse Work Environments

sections.goodFor: Students who want a discussion-heavy, psychologically safe space to hear differing perspectives and practice hard conversations as future leaders.
sections.notFor: Students wanting practical business application (role-play, strategy) or a clear stated purpose; two say the course as-is does not belong in the core.
sections.workloadNote: Only one student addresses workload, warning there is 'a lot of writing so it's not easy'; otherwise not discussed.
sections.gradingBasis: unclear beyond one mention of substantial writing

rows.disagree: Modest rating, but comments are uniformly enthusiastic

sections.notFor: Students not focused on supply chain - two say the credit hours are better spent elsewhere; anyone wanting implementation tools or technical supply chain (try engineering).
sections.workloadNote: Weekly readings before class plus cases and simulations; front-loaded - 'pretty light after the first few weeks.' Manageable final project applying the concepts.
sections.gradingBasis: Participation weighted ~40% with cold calls on the readings, plus cases and a final project.
sections.redFlags: Two say the sustainability-only lens limits it and it doesn't give tools to actually implement responsible supply chains; two say non-supply-chain students should take something else.
sections.quote: Readings every week before class and you might get cold calls, participation heavy 40% so be ready to voice out your ideas
comments: I would only recommend this class, as it stands now, if you really want to focus on sustainability. If you are looking to learn about supply chains, you'd probably be better off taking an elective in one of the engineering departments. Amy is great and brings in very senior, knowledgeable guests, but I think a lot of the takeaways that aren't sustainability specific do relate more to concerns you might have 10 years down the line in a role, not in your first few years post- MBA.
yes, if you have any interest in learning about supply chains this is a beneficial class

Yes, absolutely — as the world moves towards strengthening sustainability initiatives across the world, supply chains are an area where environmental impacts can be extremely severe at scale, and this makes a great class to be more knowledgeable in how to apply real world solutions for future Haas MBAs.

I would recommend this course to other students. As it stands, this is the only supply chain class held at Haas and it was very well designed for a both a deep dive into core operations topics and more nuanced discussion about the realities of creating tangible products and value for businesses and communities. The guest speakers were varied in professional background and perspective and brought great context to the theory we had discussed in class. Assignments were manageable and like a value add.

If you aren't focusing your post-MBA career on supply chains, take another class for sure, as you'll gain more from other classes that have similar credit hours/ time in class. If you are focusing on supply chains, this is solely focused on responsible/ sustainable supply chains, and even within this subset of supply chain work doesn't necessarily give you the tools to implement them in your own firm. I'd take this class again if I were interested in this topic, needed to fill up credit hour requirements, or wanted a low-credit-hour class. But otherwise, I'd look elsewhere for your electives. Yes, for sure.

I would recommend this class to students who are not only interested in sustainable/responsible supply chains, but supply chains in general. I honestly feel I learned much more real world valuable insight than in Operations core. We also heard from speakers working in different facets of supply chains in CPG, Tech, Consulting, etc and that was great exposure

rows.title: Business and Labor Rights in Global Supply Chains
Tech and the City: How to Get Urban Innovation Right

sections.goodFor: Students who want their worldview challenged, and those in real estate, urban policy or tech who want a critical humanities-style seminar plus a strong practitioner speaker network.
sections.notFor: Anyone wanting practical frameworks to build or launch urban tech; the description misleads. Not for people who want to coast or dislike heavy reading, cold calls and a critical/pessimistic lens.
sections.workloadNote: Strongly front-loaded: an immense reading load in the first half, much lighter by around October. Heavy prep for discussion and participation throughout; the professor grades assignments herself.
sections.gradingBasis: Participation in discussion with cold calling, plus written assignments graded by the professor rather than a reader. Weights not discussed.
sections.redFlags: Misleading description - critical humanities seminar, not innovation frameworks (3). Reading heavier up front than advertised (5). One reports abrasive cold-call responses early on; 2 call discussion curated/biased.
sections.quote: Be prepared for heavy reading, especially in the first month. This feels more like a graduate seminar in urban studies than a typical MBA elective.
comments: Yes! Not enough courses at business school are asking tough, probing questions about technology and innovation, making this is a rare opportunity.

This was by far the most interesting topic and course material I've gotten to take at Haas. The course is structured with a ton of intention bringing lots of really interesting readings, guest speakers, and discussions to the table. It definitely requires critical thinking and some work, but I think it was worth it!
Yes I would, it's a good amount of work but it is very engaging, covers a lot of material and is very very engaging and exciting.

Mostly yes - it was the best class I took this semester but some moments were frustrating. The workload is heavy at first, and the expectations are very high to read everything and participate which can be a little stressful. The course balances out later, and there are some genuinely great classes and insights. Very discussion heavy, but sometimes it can feel overly curated to the point where you don't feel like it's worth participating.
This is a lot of work and sometimes a little arduous but I did learn a lot

I'd recommend this course with significant caveats about expectations. I enrolled thinking this would focus on how to innovate in urban spaces using technology — essentially a course on doing tech-driven urban innovation right. That's not what this is. Instead, this course takes a critical, humanities-oriented lens examining the ethical implications and unintended consequences of urban innovation. It's much more about understanding what goes wrong and why, rather than learning frameworks for designing and implementing urban tech solutions.

If you're interested in real estate or urban planning with a focus on responsible development and social impact, this course offers genuine value. The speaker series brings in interesting practitioners from Molly's extensive network, and you'll be exposed to thoughtful critiques of how technology intersects with cities. If you're approaching this from a tech or product management perspective (as I was), there's still something to gain — particularly in developing a more nuanced understanding of stakeholder impacts and ethical considerations. However, don't expect a course on innovation strategy or emerging urban technologies.
Be prepared for heavy reading, especially in the first month. This feels more like a graduate seminar in urban studies than a typical MBA elective.

Molly is exceptionally knowledgeable and clearly well-connected in this space. She knows her material deeply and brings real-world credibility. Whether you find her perspective convincing will likely depend on how closely your views align with hers going in, but you'll definitely be intellectually challenged.

Bottom line: Take this course if you're genuinely curious about the critical perspective on urban innovation and comfortable with a humanities-heavy approach. Skip it if you're looking for practical frameworks on how to build or launch urban tech products.

I found this course to be incredibly valuable as an MBA student preparing to enter the tech space. It made me consider how to think more critically about potential tech solutions, and if they really are solutions. Molly is very up front about the workload of the class -- be prepared that the first half of the course will be very reading/homework heavy, to set the foundation for the remainder of the course. If that is something you can commit to doing well, then I highly recommend the course. The second half of the semester is much lighter workload, as well.

Unsure. If you asked me after the first 7 weeks of class, I would have said no, but if you asked me after just the last seven weeks, I would say yes. At the beginning of the semester, Molly was intense, and there was an IMMENSE amount of reading with a lot of cold calling. After cold calling people, her responses to many students was abrasive and abrupt. I usually love learning, but in this class, it was harder to find that joy because I felt stressed and anxious. I feel like there is a way to ask questions, invite conversation, motivate students, and have debate without digging into people. During the second half of the semester, there was a big change. She relaxed more, and we had less reading and more interesting guest speakers. I think she really took our mid-semester feedback to heart and made changes. Looking at the semester as a whole now, Molly was incredibly organized, and she clearly cares a lot. She graded all of the assignments, not the reader, which is a ton of work. I think feedback is a gift, and she absolutely took the time to give thoughtful and detailed feedback. I do deeply appreciate that.

This is one of the best classes I took at Haas. Molly expects a lot. Don't take this class if you want to slack off, not go to class, not pay attention, not do the reading, etc. There are plenty of classes here where you can do that. Take this class if you want to learn. Molly has a nuanced, deep perspective on how tech and policy interact. She will equip you with knowledge of the history of cities and how you should think about it today. She will impart incredibly insightful lessons from decades of real work in this space. She is the real deal. The guest speakers she brings in are fantastic and she asks great questions of them. There are far too many classes that are just fluff pieces for guest speakers. Molly asks them to have and defend interesting perspectives. Your own perspectives may be challenged in this class. That's a great thing. But you should be ready for that if you're going to take it.

If you're looking for a course on urbanism, the challenges cities face and different solutions implemented around the world, this is NOT your course. This course focuses more on a bit of urbanism history in the Bay Area and mostly on managing the public policies challenges for urban tech startups.
Yes!
I would!! I think it is tough class but sometimes we need that here.

Molly was an amazing professor and this was the best elective I have taken at Haas. I appreciate that she created an environment where everyone was really focused - it's rare to see a class where no one was on their devices, and I think the reason for that is because of how engaging both the content and the guest speakers were. Molly is really knowledgeable about the subject matter and does a great job of sharing her expertise with the class - she has worked in this space for a long time and it shows. This class truly changed my worldview and has made me take different actions in my personal life - notably, to get more involved with local news and politics! The one thing to note is that their is a lot of work early in the semester (heavy reading load) but by October that totally goes away, and the class becomes much more manageable.
Front heavy with lots of readings! So be ready, but guests were very interesting and engaging
Highly recommended but the students should understand that the workload is relatively heavy.

discussion-driven class, but in practice the conversations can feel somewhat biased and there isn't always enough time for genuine, open debate among students. I would unequivocally recommend this course to anyone who wants to have their perspective challenged, and wants to come away with a unique set of viewpoints on the role of governments and venture capital in how start-ups can thrive. For me, it was a good way to learn new and different things because with business electives the incremental learnings arent that great
Yes. Very well designed class.
I would not. See previous comments. The course is to pessimistic

This course is a great option for students who are interested in developing a POV on urban problems and tech solutions in cities. It is a class that requires strong engagement in and outside of class, but Molly brings great guest speakers and is very intentional about the course design.

sections.goodFor: Students who want real international client consulting plus travel and cultural immersion, and who can tolerate not knowing their country, team or client when they sign up.
sections.notFor: Anyone needing to know the project/team/country in advance, unable to absorb heavy hours, or serving as team lead - leads report far more work, little recognition. Class only teaches go-to-market.
sections.workloadNote: Heavy: team consulting project running January-May plus assignments in the following fall semester, with 80+ hour weeks during two weeks of in-country work. Students dispute the 3-credit allocation.
sections.gradingBasis: Team consulting deliverables (blog post, final presentation) plus a fall presentation for the last credit; guidelines not enforced evenly.
sections.redFlags: Credit/workload mismatch (1 argues it should be 4 credits); assignment instructions confusing and constantly changing; guidelines unenforced, advantaging teams that ignore them; team leads carry far more work.
sections.quote: When you sign up for the course, you have no knowledge about what experience you are doing to get (country, team, client), so it is definitely a risk.
comments: Absolutely. Amazing opportunity to get consulting experience while traveling the world.
This is a truly transformative experience. A lot of work, a lot of hard work!! But you get to learn so much, experience so much, and explore so much! I highly recommend this course????
I would. This was a GREAT course!!

This course, as many people know, carries a lot of uncertainty. When you sign up for the course, you have no knowledge about what experience you are doing to get (country, team, client), so it is definitely a risk. But that said, I think the whole experience was worth it once you are able to go to your country, experience a new culture, and meet your client in person.

There were a few issues with this course throughout the semester that I hope are addressed: 1. The class time was not always relevant to all projects and it seemed not the best use of time for all teams. I think sharing a variety of resources that might or might not be applicable to projects would be rather, rather than providing only one framework or way to do things and assume that all teams can use this in their project. 2. Especially at the end, guidelines provided for some assignments were not followed by all teams. For example, we were told to keep the blog post at certain length, or the final presentation at 3 slides and these guidelines seemed almost "optional" and not really enforced by all teams, creating an unfair advantage for those teams who did follow the guidelines. 3. This class should be 4 credits if they still make us do assignments in the fall semester. I think it is ridiculous that we only get 2 credits in the spring for the amount of work we put in, including traveling in country and working 80+ hours for two weeks while in- country. All other applied innovation classes that have client-facing work are 3 credits. The fact that we also need to do a presentation in the fall to get the final 1 credit out of the 3 does not make sense at all, and this should be 1 credit IN ADDITION to the 3 credits we should already be earning for all our work from January to May. I hope this changes for future classes.
Yes if they are willing to work extra hours
Project, team, and country dependent. Super MBA experience and would recommend doing it. Team leads should
expect to do a lot more work with little recognition.

It's a great course with plenty of opportunity. Well-organized but not all projects are Go To Market strategy, and that is all the course focuses on. Instructors are very helpful, but instructions for assignments are confusing and change constantly
Yes, this was my all time favorite experience at Haas. The in country travel was a once in a lifetime experience, and I made lifelong friendships with my teammates.

rows.title: Sustainable Capitalism in the Nordics
rows.disagree: Modest rating, but comments are uniformly enthusiastic

sections.goodFor: Students interested in sustainability or the limits of American capitalism who want immersive company/exec access via Strand's deep Denmark network; strong for newcomers.
sections.notFor: Students already deep in sustainability - several say they learned little new; casual learners; and anyone who wants spring break free, since the week is packed.
sections.workloadNote: Front-loaded: weekly readings and assignments in the ~6 weeks before the trip, then an intensive spring-break week of Copenhagen site visits with class time only Mon am and Fri pm.
sections.gradingBasis: Pre-trip readings and weekly assignments plus in-class engagement during the trip; no exam mentioned.
sections.redFlags: Recurring (4+): pre-trip readings one-sided, repetitive and pitching the Nordic model without bridging to US business reality; some in-country sessions boring or filler; two say Strand is 'a little all over the place.'
sections.quote: I think this course can be insightful, but you will be pitched repeatedly on the Nordic model. Unfortunately a lot of it seems divorced from the reality
comments: Go on this trip! You should use all of your bid points! Robert is a fantastic teacher and does an excellent job planning the trip! Only thing to know is to expect a good amount of reading in the 6 weeks leading up to the trip. Yes!!! Highly recommend this course and professor. Learned so much, had really deep conversations on systems and society, and had a lot of fun. Don't miss this class.
Potentially. If you're interested in sustainability, Copenhagen and the Nordics, you'll enjoy the week. Otherwise, it's a class during spring break, so.. it's up to you.

Yes, absolutely! I highly recommend this course. It provided valuable insights and references about Nordic capitalism, sustainability, and the different paths we can take toward a more sustainable world. Having the chance to see things in person and engage directly with senior leaders driving sustainability efforts in their organizations was truly remarkable. If you're curious to draw your own conclusions and expand your reflections on " Is there a Sustainable Capitalism in the Nordics? ", this course is a must.
Yes, it's so inspiring to see the different attitude here towards sustainability. The real-life applications are a testament to ingenuity and gives me hope for humanity.
Yes! Very different course with real world learnings.
I would recommend this class to someone who is very interested in sustainability and is looking to pursue a career in it or in Denmark. As a casual learner, it was a bit less effective for me.

I think this course can be insightful, but you will be pitched repeatedly on the Nordic model. Unfortunately a lot of it seems divorced from the reality of how business works in the United States and not a lot of work put in to bridge that gap.
Yes! Robert's energy is infectious. An amazing course and amazing professor.

Highly recommend. Great conceptual lessons regarding corporate form and sustainable capitalism, including considerations for how ti actually works. Also great engagement with specific companies that are very relevant to the field of sustainability broadly.

Depends! It was super fun to travel with your class mates, but you will have class all during spring break and will not get to see and explore as much as you might have otherwise. Prior to class there are weekly readings and assignments that are interesting, but are also one-sided and repetitive and can be annoying. The class in Denmark mixed. Overall it was well planned but the sessions could be more concise to leave more time to explore the city. Less applicable learnings then I would have hoped, so depends if you are already well-informed.
Yes! A great way to think creatively and explore a different culture.

Yes, this course was one of the best experiences I had at Haas, from connecting with fellow students to immersing ourselves in the Copenhagen culture, it has been an amazing experience.
This is definitely the most valuable and interesting course I've ever had!

I cannot recommend this class enough if you are interested in Sustainability. Hearing from practitioners in industry was invaluable and Robert is a the perfect person to teach this course

I'd recommend this class to lift the veil of American capitalism from your eyes. I'd recommend adding structure to it yourself because Robert, though knowledgeable and energetic, is a little all over the place.
