The business and university visits provide a very unique and authentic opportunity to hear directly from people working in this space.
Yes! Very well organized course content and travel logistics. Curated company visit is well thoughout and echos with the course reading

Yes. I would be impossible to take this class and not be impacted by the exposure to the Nordics. I think the awareness will make you a greater business leader, more than a spring break bender (as fun as that can be)
Definitely! Incredibly passionate and he has done this class for 18 years and built very strong relationships in Denmark that make the class very worth while.
Fun class to travel and see a new country. Great discussions too. Do some of the readings though so you a get a better idea of what's heading your way

If you're even remotely on the fence, take the class. If you haven't very familiar with the Nordics / Scandinavian culture, take the class. It's invaluable that we get exposed and immersed in other business environments with different business structures. This class does a good job at whetting the appetite into learning more. Robert also has gone through incredible lengths arranging connections to key businesses and foundations in Denmark and Sweden during our visit, and these are hard to reproduce on your own.

This was the best class I've taken at Haas. Robert is an amazing instructor with deep knowledge of the subject matter and cares so much about the course and students. I'd highly recommend this course to anyone who is considering whether you know a lot about sustainable capitalism or not.
Absolutely! Robert is great and this topic is so relevant now.

sections.goodFor: Students interested in sustainability, comparative capitalism, policy or the Nordic model who want an immersive international experience over spring break.
sections.notFor: Students without spring bandwidth for heavy prework, or expecting business-model/finance content - the week skews to environmental sustainability, policy and industry site visits.
sections.workloadNote: Front-loaded: dense pre-trip readings and extensive discussion posts before the Copenhagen immersion week, then long days of site visits; prework exceeds comparable 2-unit trek courses.
sections.gradingBasis: Pre-trip readings and discussion posts plus participation in immersion-week site visits; other components not described.
sections.redFlags: Pre-trip reading/discussion load heavy and partly felt like busy work (6+ comments); learning objectives unclear (2); organization could be better (2); class grew to ~60 and feels unwieldy; you arrange your own housing.
sections.quote: I would recommend this course only if you have the bandwidth in the spring to take on 12-20+ hours of preparation material, as it has a lot of prework.
comments: Yes! This course gave a incredibly valuable global perspective on the topic of capitalism. The site visits are worth a hundred readings and the actual experience of being in Copenhagen is wonderful and can be magical!

This was an amazing course and experience because it was located in Copenhagen!! The class work prior to the immersion week was a lot more than expected and felt like busy work. It was great being in Copenhagen and visiting many amazing companies; however, the days were long. The learning objectives and takeaways were unclear but it's a great experience to take an international class
I would recommend the class, but would caution against the density and quality of the class material leading up to the week in Copenhagen.
Yes
Yes, definitely, if you are interested in Sustainability and Corporate Governance; great opportunity to learn and have fun at the beautiful Copenhagen.
The course is generally fun, there's not a ton of free time within the schedule though so do your tourist stuff on the weekend before/after.

Yes and I would absolutely take this class again given the chance. If you have any interest in sustainability, the Nordics, Europe, or anything social science related or international affairs, take this class.
Great course, highly recommend! I feel I learned a lot and my views were productively challenged. A lot of concepts came full circle for me being able to interact with companies.
Yes - great use of a break!
Yes, absolutely! He did a great job of teaching us this material and had a lot of knowledge

I would recommend this class! It is a great perspective setting and lets students analyze, benchmark, and experience a part of the world that has a lot to offer the rest. Robert helps to reframe the thinking around what it means to be a capitalist and an American.
Yes, I'd highly recommend. It's rare to have this kind of opportunity - expect to work hard:-)

Yes I think this was one of the coolest trips I've been on at haas and gave me a great insight to how the Nordics have done so well, I think it's a character building journey perspective growth type of class, not a hard or purely soft skills class. I really enjoyed it

I would recommend this course only if you have the bandwidth in the spring to take on 12-20+ hours of preparation material, as it has a lot of prework. This is not typical for other SIB and GNAM courses, and would be something I caution evening weekend students to when they plan their spring semester around. Otherwise, it does cover Nordic culture and sustainable capitalism very well and has effective course material. The site visits in country are very relevant, and immersion environment is very conducive to learning the subject.

Absolutely recommend this course! The subject matter of capitalism is so vitally important to be critiquing as citizens and business school students. It offers a wonderful way to benchmark US and international metrics to get a comparative view of the progress we have made and still need to go.

Prof. Strand is passionate, knowledgeable and so friendly to study with. His energy is infectious and encouraging. He puts a LOT of effort into the course and the trip is really worthwhile, with the different site visits. You do have to find your own way for housing and logistics, so be prepared to do some work on those fronts, rather than just sign up and follow the pack. It's an adventure, so bring a good attitude because a lot is fit into a short period of time. 10/10, totally recommend and believe this material should be core reading for MBA students ~
Yes, I would recommend taking this class but beware there is a lot of upfront prep before the immersion week so be prepared to spend 8-10 hours a week on reading assignments.
I'd recommend this course because it was a great crash course into sustainable capitalism and the Nordics as a region. It is not a challenging course, but very informative.
I would. I had some preconceived notions of how it is to live and work in the Nordic countries, but travelling there helped me learn what life is really like over there.
It was very useful to listen to a variety of journalists, executives, and educators talk
about their systems and institutions.
Robert is great! Very high energy and passionate about the topic.
Yes I would, Robert is clearly excited about the topic and wishes to help others dive deeply into the subject matter. His instruction style would only be improved by better organization
Loved the immersive nature of the class. Helped with connecting concepts to applications.

I think this is a really cool option for spring break, and a great way to get to know other people better. If you're interested in energy or sustainability, you'll find the site visits super helpful. If you're interested in what makes our economic system challenging and how it could be better, this course will also just interest you academically. I had some very deep discussions with others in the class about the Nordic model -- where we can learn from it, where it fails.

I do think this class is a lot more work than I expected -- the pre readings are very heavy and the discussion posts are pretty extensive -- it's much more work than other similar 2 credit spring break courses like the Innovation Sprint in Amsterdam. I also wished that there was a little more free time to explore Copenhagen during the day.
Yes I highly recommend it. You will take away a lot from this course. The connections you'll make is also wonderful. I loved it overall.

Yes! It is definitely one of the best courses I took at Haas. The reading materials were insightful and made me reflect a lot. Also the experience in Copenhagen, visiting and interacting with to Danish companies were very unique and rich to me!
Highly recommend for every student to take this course!
Yes, absolutely! Unlike other treks, this is a class with 2 units.

personally, I learned so much about capitalism, politics, and systems, and developed my critical thinking through real- world practice. I don't think I could have learned and applied these ideas so quickly in any other setting. I would recommend this class to any student who is interested in learning about the the nordic society, and what mechanisms work well in supporting capitalism in a democracy.
Of course!!

If someone is heavily interested in the climate and sustainability topics this is a good class. Oftentimes, the discussions were heavily policy based, at others it was focused on finance and renewable energy. I think this can be a lot to absorb if you haven't taken another course in sustainability

I'd recommend for people who are interested in learning about Nordic culture and way of doing business. It's not the same as visiting Copenhagen as a tourist. You really get to know how things are done in the Nordics.
However, coming to the week of the class in person is very demanding and requires preparation.

Absolutely, feels like this is one of Haas's marquee classes. The pre-work before the trip is not difficult but it is time consuming, so be aware of that. The trip itself is fantastic but the class size has recently increased (from 45 to 60) and that size of a group feels unwieldy sometimes. But those are small complaints compared to the experiences students get from the country visit

Yes. I thought this was one of if not the most thought provoking courses I've taken. At times it is hard to figure out how practical the information is in a US context, but overall it's very beneficial even just as a thought experiment. Plus, having the opportunity to explore Copenhagen allows you to see the outcomes of the system.

I would recommend but with some caveats. The class can be very useful for MBA students but may or may not be the most useful for understanding sustainability through a business/business model lens. Hearing the title of the course on sustainability capitalism, I didn't realize how much would be focused on sustainability as a function and industry and not necessarily on the business and financial models that make them possible. The class also has significant reading requirements leading up the immersion week, that other SIB class have not required.

I would definitely recommend this course to every person, as everyone is a participant in the imperfect capitalist system in the U.S., and we can all work to make it more equitable and sustainable for people and the planet. There is a decent amount of prework, which enables thoughtful discussion throughout the course. You will meet incredible folks across industries and the public and private sectors. The in country time is the best complement to the prework, and Denmark is an incredible country. It is helpful to see how change can be brought on at all levels, from internal carbon pricing to investing in the energy transition and alternative ownership structures and the power of a unionized workforce.

Robert is incredibly passionate and knowledgeable, and cares so much about his students and the class. He is wonderful to learn from. I am so grateful to have taken this class. It was one of the best I've taken!

Yes, must take. Skip other spring break plans for this class. The course is interdisciplinary and critically examines how economies, societies, and people can be better in different elements than the American way. Loved reading and preparing for the immersion week knowing that it would translate to fruitful and engaging conversations during the week. Even yet, it has provided me with a refreshed perspective that we (as a society) can change as long as we are intentional and focused on our priorities.

Yes, but be aware that the week in Copenhagen is very heavy towards environmental sustainability, not necessarily sustainable capitalism in general, so those who are not interested in this may have a bit of a learning curve to keep up. I enjoyed hearing about these topics, but would've loved to see more entrepreneurship and early stage innovation mixed in as well.

This was a 60 person class with masters of climate solutions students along with full time and part time students. Definitely recommend! This class served as a sort of capstone for me across several other classes. It brought together learnings from classes in economics, systems change, labor organizing, policy, capitalism and growth, etc etc. I really enjoyed the comparative analysis format of US vs Nordics to develop my knowledge of both systems. You will worry when bidding that you'll be bummed to be in class over spring break. Do not fear! It is a wonderful experience and you get to immerse yourself in the city with MBA friends between / after the sessions. I found this super worthwhile overall. Very high ROI on learning vs overall HW.
Yes would recommend, seeing real life application of school theory was very insightful

sections.goodFor: Students who need the AI Certificate credit and want theoretical grounding in AI fundamentals and future-of-work research; Toby Stuart's sessions are singled out as excellent.
sections.notFor: Anyone expecting hands-on AI/LLM use or practical business AI strategy - there is none; also too foundational for AI-experienced students, and there is overlap with the intro coding class.
sections.workloadNote: Identical comment set to the other MBA296-2 section. Half-semester, four professors; pre-class questions (often opened late), in-class quizzes, low-value assignments.
sections.gradingBasis: In-class printed quizzes, pre-class questions, assignments; quizzes called poorly prepared (typos, faulty structure, too few printouts).
sections.redFlags: Recurring (8+ of 17): first offering was 'a hot mess' - four professors with no handoffs, misaligned start date, unmaintained bCourses, no GSI, poorly prepared quizzes, theory-only with no hands-on AI despite the title.
sections.quote: There were 4 professors who each taught a few weeks of class separately... they never seemed to actually talk to each other or have a handover when switching to then next professor
comments: This class had a few interesting lectures but overall was a pretty chaotic overview of AI and the future of work. The technical foundations and future of work sessions were interesting but the class is very dependent on the professors and how many sessions you have with each of them. Hopefully it will continue to improve as the AI Certificate improves over the semesters.
Course is poorly designed. I dont feel i have learned anything. Very theoretical, not hands-on. Until the PO designs a better course, wouldnt take it.

No. This class was billed as a strategic class for non-technical people to learn more about how to leverage AI in workflows, and we didn't once use AI/an LLM of our choosing in class. I expected to become more more AI-literate as a result of this class, and I am coming away from it having no new skills other than knowing a few hypotheses of how AI may (or may not) impact the labor market.

The way it was this year, not really. I'm sure the fact that it was the first time this course was offered played a role but it was a complete mess. Start date was misaligned between students and professors (we all showed up to the first class, professor didn't show up and then emailed us saying the class actually started a week later), quizzes covered topics that were a bit irrelevant in my opinion and were very poorly prepared (typos, faulty structure, not enough print outs for everyone, etc), assignments didn't add much value, and content overall was too theoretical and not very practical. Hopefully all of this (and other problems we had) improve drastically for next year.

While the topic is important, the course needs A LOT of work. Having four different instructors for the course was a recipe for administrative disaster. I think this course will improve next year, so I would still take it, but I want to note that it may be too foundational for AI experts. Toby Stuart who hopefully remains one of the lecturers for the course is a great industry leader and makes you think.
I would not recommend, better off taking an LLM course. I am not sure what they were trying to do making us take this course.

Yes. This class should be a core class, right after Data and Decisions. It is crucial for today's market that every MBA students masterizes these concepts and is able to "talk AI" and understand the technology in a proper way Interesting course to get exposure to the nuts and bolts of AI and how it will affect workplaces and society from several different perceptives.
Yes, The course is useful and brings clarity about AI in the business world

I would recommend this class because I still got unique insights into what's happening in the space and readings I would not go looking for own my own, but not all the professors were equally good (Toby Stuart was great; Jonathan Kolstad was good; and Anastasia Fedyk was not as great; we haven't had the fourth professor at the time of this submission so can't speak to them) but the learning experience fluctuated a lot depending on who was teaching. If Toby is teaching his own class on this subject, I would probably just take that.

No, but I think this class can only get better (hopefully it will). Some general comments about how to improve the class (it didn't feel appropriate to write it down only for one faculty): stop relying on the "this is the first time we teach the class so things will go wrong" and actively try to prevent that from happening (Question the status quo, anyone?); if you ask us to answer the pre class questions before 11 pm, make sure to open them with enough time to answer (most of the times I would try to answer them on Saturday (closed), Sunday 11am (closed), Sunday 5pm (still closed), and then by 9pm it was open but it closed at 11pm), and several times they didn't even open the questions so you would be checking all the time until finally giving up; communicate with other faculty on a regular basis (e.g., it happened twice that the printed quizzes were not enough for the students); and in general, the class should be called AI foundations and not Business AI foundations, as there was little to no connection to the business side (eg., it explained how AI works when translating words into 0s and 1s, then doing some calculations for the error, distance, etc when it could have been explained much simpler and why this is relevant); if the class will continue to have this technical focus, then there is plenty of overlap with the Intro to coding class
It was ok- I hope they update it to be reflective of the feedback in terms of balancing how much time was spent on the content the students found most interesting
If you need the AI certificate sure. I'd like to see an iteration of this class with less professors. 4 in one half semester was way too much.

I think this course could be good but this year was not well coordinated and prepare given it was the first edition. Also, is important it is taught from a business/ corporate lenses, not so focus on research and academia but rather what kind of problems, challenges and decisions we are gonna have to face in the corporate world (even if we don't have a technical role) and what do we need to make them efficiently. I would think of the course as a guide for a student who is put in charge of defining the AI strategy of a company, what kind of tools they implement and how these are integrated, what factors to take into account, how do you train employees, what workflows should be redefined, etc. I would recommend this class because I learned a lot about how businesses are currently thinking about AI and what AI strategy should look like.

This course will give you a strong and broad understanding of AI fundamentals from the theory perspective, which is great. There is little content on its application, though, nor really content on policy/ how to handle it/ etc. There is also no hands-on learning with AI. So if you take this class, be well aware that what you get out is theory and understanding (which is a helpful thing, no doubt), not practical application.

Hopefully, from an organization perspective, this class will improve because it was a hot mess this semester. There were 4 professors who each taught a few weeks of class separately. This was great from a knowledge and perspective breadth POV. However, they never seemed to actually talk to each other or have a handover when switching to then next professor, which made the class disjointed as they didn't seem to know what was covered, where we were at, when quizes where, if past deck material was actually posted, etc.. Furthermore, they didn't seem to manage or update bCourses regularly, causing confusion, and there was no real GSI in tow to help keep up with this either. First year course with a number of different professors so it tended to be disaggregated. Solid material and deep dive into AI.

sections.goodFor: Mostly only students who need it for the AI Certificate, where it is required; a couple say individual instructors (Toby Stuart, Abhishek Nagaraj) were worth hearing.
sections.notFor: Anyone expecting practical business applications of AI - students say that is essentially absent; non-technical students, for whom success 'seemed out of reach.'
sections.workloadNote: Not quantified. Rotating lectures from four instructors (Zsolt, Thomas Lee, Abhishek, Toby Stuart) plus quizzes; students describe it as disjointed rather than heavy.
sections.gradingBasis: Quizzes students say test slide memorization or material not covered in class; attendance appears not to count.
sections.redFlags: Most comments: 4 rotating instructors, disjointed, no clear objectives; title a misnomer as business application is absent; too technical for non-technical students yet shallow for technical ones; unfair quizzes.
sections.quote: The name "Business AI Foundations" is a misnomer. We never really got into the practical business applications of AI in any meaningful way.
comments: As it stands right now, I cannot. I hope this becomes the class it should be (and a part of core), but clearly it was hastily put together and expectations the faculty had for the class were very different than what we had as students. If we want a technical AI class, we can go to a different school - we are here for a business class and this was not it. Additionally, the first two quizzes were mostly on concepts that were not even discussed (at least in detail) in class. No, not at all. And this is the only class at Haas where I'd say that.

The name "Business AI Foundations" is a misnomer. We never really got into the practical business applications of AI in any meaningful way. The course covered AI at a surface level from a technical perspective, but I didn't leave with any greater practical knowledge of how to actually use it. I think I got more value messing around on my computer during lectures than I did from the lectures themselves. Three of the four instructors I'd be interested in taking again, just in different classes.

So I'm left wondering what the point was. If this had been called just "AI Foundations," it was too surface level to earn the title. The business portion felt almost entirely absent. And the fact that it's required for the AI Certificate and costs a real chunk of points makes that worse, not better. The curriculum needs to change and the instructor team needs to be managed pretty dramatically before this is worth taking. Knowing what I know now, I wouldn't take it.

You have to take this for the certificate but if you don't need the certificate, you can probably get a similar amount of value out of just talking to other students, keeping up with the news, and taking Data Mining

Yes, this is an important class. Four instructors in such a short period was not idea. But in the future, one or two professors would be idea. Overall, this is an important class and i encourage everyone to take it to understand the AI impact and landscape in business.
Not as it currently stands - I recognize that the administration is revising the course to be more pertinent to stuent desires and to what the market is asking for, however.
The course give insights into the world of AI in bits and pieces, but it failed to bring it together, particularly difficult to see its business alignment.

This course has potential, but it's disappointing in its current form. The course spent a lot of time on technical topics that were too complex for non-technical people to understand, and not complex enough to add value for technical people. The rotating professors seemed cool in theory but made the class feel disjointed. If the curriculum was overhauled and focused more on practical business applications of AI and problems that businesses are encountering, it would be much more worth it.

If this course were more refined, I would recommend it - but in its current state, I would not. There is a lot of potential, and I believe the professors could be excellent, but the class needs stronger continuity across instructors, content, and the evolution of each lecture, as well as clearer connections to real-world business applications. The learning objectives were often unclear, and the quizzes did not meaningfully reinforce learning... they felt more like memorization of lecture slides than true understanding. As a result, I'm leaving the course unsure of what I actually learned. Given how rapidly AI is evolving, this is an incredibly important moment to offer a course like this at Haas, and it feels like the class didn't fully harness that opportunity.
For a Business AI Foundations class: Zsolt - Lean Yes, Thomas - No, Abhishek - Strong Yes, Toby - Maybe
no, but honestly this class is new, and I'm trying to give it the benefit of the doubt.
- You can't have this many professors in a course, especially because it doesn't seem like they had a lot of communication on how the class w as going
- What is the purpose of this class? That needs to be more clearly outlined
- Maybe include takeaways in each class so we can understand what we're supposed to take from all of this.

Interesting content, but definitely they are still figuring the structure out. I think with time it will be a really good class. Yes, I'd recommend it but it needs improvement. The overall course felt a bit disorganized.
Yes

All of the instructors were great except for Thomas Lee. He clearly knows a lot on the topic but struggles to communicate key concepts. He often reverts to highly pedantic and confrontational lines of questioning with students. This course needs some work. While the technical aspects of AI are interesting and important foundational knowledge, this course was too technical without linking that knowledge to business decisions. The quizzes were very difficult even if you did attend classes, while class attendance did not seem to be valued at all in the grading scheme. For people without a technical background, being successful in this class seemed out of reach. The last two classes were by far the best.
No. No one should take this class.

If Toby Stuart is teaching it yes. He was great. Really thought provoking and worthwhile discussion. Otherwise maybe not. Parts of the class were super technical and other parts just felt random? Feel like we need things to be more hands on and less theoretical

No, this class lacks practical applications of AI, and AI in business. This note is cross-professor and about the design and content of the class. Unfortunately, the added value from the class is currently very limited.
I don't know that I would take the course again in its current format. It felt very disjointed across professors and did not quite meet my learning goals for the course.

rows.title: Data Analytics
rows.ghostNote: Ten-week data analytics course aimed at general managers rather than analysts. No history under this number; the instructor's career record (6.03, 31st percentile) is the only signal.

rows.title: Special Selected Topics for MBA Students

sections.goodFor: Students with little or no prior exposure to entrepreneurship or VC, especially those newer to the Bay Area, who want a condensed experiential introduction to both worlds and connections with MBA students from around the globe.
sections.notFor: Anyone with real entrepreneurship or VC experience or prior coursework; several commenters said it will not move the needle for them. Remote takers should expect painful cross-time-zone group logistics.
sections.workloadNote: An intense one-week immersion: roughly 48 hours deep as an entrepreneur, then another 48 as a VC, with short-turnaround group assignments; be prepared to work very hard.
sections.redFlags: Recurring (3 comments): the compressed one-week format made group assignments across time zones very difficult on short turnarounds. One student found the VC-side instruction disjointed and hard to follow, and another flagged misaligned incentives because some students were not taking the course for credit.
sections.quote: The style of the class is to sort of throw you in to the deep end and let you figure it out. It can get a little intense, but it works.

rows.title: Haas@Work
rows.terms: 2021 Spring;2022 Spring;2023 Spring;2024 Spring;2025 Spring;2026 Spring

sections.goodFor: Students exploring consulting or design thinking with no prior client experience; strong practice at client interaction, insight generation and storytelling, and it stays local.
sections.notFor: Anyone wanting a true consulting class (it is framework/design-thinking focused), or anyone on a team that isn't bought in - several say a disengaged team makes it a slog. Team leads carry more.
sections.workloadNote: Not quantified and contested: one calls it a relatively chill Applied Innovation class, others say it requires substantial outside work. Load depends on the client project and is worst for team leads.
sections.gradingBasis: unclear; team client project and presentations are the visible deliverables
sections.redFlags: Experience varies a lot by project and team buy-in (3 students); team leads shoulder much more work (1); it is not a direct consulting class despite expectations (1).
sections.quote: But caveat, if people are not bought into the project, it can be hard work. I'd encourage team buy in from the beginning
comments: This was the most meaningful course of my first year. I absolutely loved being able to test and learn design thinking and consulting in such a growth-minded and fun environment. You will truly get as much out of this course as you put into it. The course's mantra of "trust the process, do the work", is something that I can't wait to apply for the rest of my life!
Yes
Yes, especially if you want a (relatively) chill Applied Innovation class that keeps you local
Yes - hugely applicable, great frameworks, repeatable process
Yes
Yes, absolutely! Both Haas and Ischool/ MIMS students should learn this method, how to work in diverse teams, the power of feedback, and would enhance their product design and management skills.
Great for someone that is looking to gain experience in engaging with clients

Great course. Highly practical. Good learning experience if you want to know how to present or interact to clients. It is not a direct consulting class, but if u have 0 prior experience this will give a good introduction. More a framework class to understand design thinking.

I would recommend the course. It's a great process to go through and understand. But caveat, if people are not bought into the project, it can be hard work. I'd encourage team buy in from the beginning

I would recommend this course as it helps get some relevant experience in design thinking and client work. However, some projects are more difficult than others, so it may require far more work. Be prepared to invest energy into this, especially if you are one of the team leads.

[REDACTED IN THE PUBLIC BUILD] A student described finding the team-lead role considerably harder and more emotionally draining than expected, and said they would not recommend it to others in their position. — Why: The original names the writer's race and gender. In a section this size that is potentially identifying, and it was written for a CalNet-gated audience.

This is a great course for any students exploring the consulting or design thinking spaces. It will give you plenty of practical experience and provide a boost to your resume when applying to jobs. This course does require a substantial amount of work outside the classroom, but it's worth it in the end!
Yes, helpful for navigating team and client dynamics.

Yes, it was great because you learn a ton about how to generate insights and communicate them, storytelling is a big part of this course and you get to practice it in real-time. It was also a great bonding experience with our team.

sections.goodFor: Students targeting consulting or wanting real client work, human-centered design/innovation methods, and practice leading through ambiguity.
sections.notFor: Anyone who can't absorb team-lottery risk or needs structured teaching - it is learning by doing, class time is unstructured, and instructors/TAs are reported not to intervene when teams break down.
sections.workloadNote: Semester-long team consulting engagement with a real client dominates the work; evening sessions are short lectures plus team working time. 'A fair amount of hands-on work.'
sections.gradingBasis: unclear
sections.redFlags: Experience hinges on your team/client (3+); one reports 'carrying a LOT of dead weight'; 2 call class time inefficient with instructors/TAs not stepping in; oneone student reported the team-lead role was unexpectedly draining.
sections.quote: Ultimately, your experience is far, far, far too at the mercy of who you get grouped up with on your team.
comments: The frameworks and thought process that I learned from this class were something I immediately started applying at my job, and I'm sure I will continue using them. It forces you to think in unconventional ways, to explore alternatives and to validate ideas. Working so closely with a team for a semester is also one of the best experiences I've had at Haas. I would definitely recommend the course.
I got a lot out of this course. I had fun, I learned a lot.

8 times out of 10, I would absolutely NOT recommend this course to a fellow student, unless they indicated to me that they would benefit from going through the type of consulting project that this course offers. Ultimately, your experience is far, far, far too at the mercy of who you get grouped up with on your team. While I had some great team members, I'm exhausted from carrying a LOT of dead weight.
Yes
Yes. This course is helpful in case you're looking for an internship and/or looking to work with a client without fear of failure

Haas@Work is a signature course at Haas for a reason and brings human-centered design and innovation principles into practice with real clients. The class combines consulting, product management, AI, strategy, and client work together in a hands on class. Even though it meets in the evenings, I found every class to be valuable time to work with my team and learn consulting and innovation skills that apply in any job context. I loved this class and highly recommend it, although it is a fair amount of hands on work with the internal team and client!

I highly recommend this course to anyone looking to work in the consulting industry. It involves real client needs and helps solve their actual pain points. The entire process closely reflects what real consulting work is actually like. Yes, absolutely; it was very hands on and helped me develop tools for dealing with ambiguous problems and helped in understanding how to " trust the process "
I probably wouldn't recommend the course. With the rise of AI tools today, I feel like part of the course's value proposition has become less compelling

Yes, this class is great if you're looking for hands-on client experience, experience with design thinking methodology, or growth in leadership (internal or client-facing). The experience can be mixed based on the client project you are assigned to, however. It's also less about structured learning and skill sets and more about learning through doing and getting comfortable with navigating ambiguous, complex problem spaces.

Yes, I would recommend both the course and professor. I appreciated the open creative space that was created for us to work in, the lectures were relevant and helpful, but short enough to leave time for group work. I enjoyed working on a real project with real clients and appreciate the structure of this course for making that possible.

If you are going into banking/PE, you should probably take this course regaradless of the below comments; if not, I would reconsider. This isn't a class where you'll build up your finance skills, if you're thinking that like I was.
I can't truly recommend this course for a few reasons:

- I can't recommend it as an online course. Could be different if it was in person, but engagement was poor. - The majority of the homework comes down to preparing weekly writeups or decks - which can take significant time - but count for almost none of the grade. In addition, no feedback is given on these assignments throughout - including a grade - so you have no idea how to improve.
- The course includes a lot of models being made - but no discussion of what the models should have been or how they should have been calculated.

rows.title: The Neuroscience of Communication and Embodied Leadership
rows.disagree: Modest rating, but comments are uniformly enthusiastic

sections.goodFor: People who genuinely want to practice leadership - nervous system regulation, boundaries, hard feedback - and will invest real time and personal vulnerability outside class.
sections.notFor: Anyone looking for an easy 2-unit elective, or who struggles with virtual/weekend formats - one says the Zoom weekend format is ineffective and an added strain.
sections.workloadNote: Substantial pre-class assignments plus daily embodiment practices; several stress it is 'A LOT of work' for a 2-unit course. In-class time is interactive partner and small-group work on Zoom.
sections.gradingBasis: unclear; the graded artifacts appear to be pre-class work and participation in experiential exercises, but no one states weightings.
sections.redFlags: Heavy pre-class workload flagged by 4+ of 13 ('don't take this if you just want an easy 2-unit course'); 2 say the Zoom + weekend format is ineffective or draining; requires real emotional investment.
sections.quote: I would recommend this course if it is a subject you are keenly interested in and willing to put in the work for! Do not take this if you just want an easy 2-unit course.
comments: yes, the class was slow to start but at the last day I really started to understand why it was important. Yes. The experiential format made the learning stick in a way that lectures alone never could. I am already applying what I learned to how I communicate at work and at home.

Absolutely, without reservation. This is one of the most practically impactful courses I have taken at Haas. Unlike many leadership courses that stay at the conceptual level, this one gives you a rigorous scientific framework, grounded in neuroscience and somatic practice, and then immediately puts it to work through structured partner exercises, group T-sessions, and daily embodiment practices. By the end, you are not just thinking differently about leadership; you are physically experiencing it differently.

Erica is an exceptional instructor. She models every principle she teaches in real time. When unexpected moments of vulnerability arose in class, she met them with warmth and adaptability rather than redirecting to the agenda. That consistency between what she teaches and how she shows up created a level of psychological safety that made genuine risk-taking possible for the whole group. Her 10 years of experience mean she anticipates where students get stuck and intervenes with exactly the right nudge.

The one honest caveat: the pre-class assignments are substantial, so come prepared to invest real time outside of sessions. That said, the in-class experience is worth every hour of preparation. If you are serious about developing as a leader, not just learning about leadership, take this course.

Yes, I would strongly recommend this course and Erica to other students.. This is one of the few classes that meaningfully changes how you show up in relationships and leadership: you actually practice regulating your nervous system, setting boundaries, and giving/receiving hard feedback. Erica models what she teaches with a rare mix of clarity, vulnerability, and rigor, and creates a level of psychological safety that lets you do real inner work, not just learn concepts.

yes i would recommend. This course offers personal insight that you do not find in other courses which will help understand how and why you personally react to certain threats. This will help you regulate how you react in stressful situation, and to connect with people in a deeper more meaningful way which can help your career tremendously. Absolutely yes. I highly recommend this instructor. I loved her teaching style, which allowed me to embody the skills I desired. I didn't even realize I was missing these essential tools until this class helped me develop them. I highly recommend Erica if you would like professional guidance on self reflection and reflecting on your interactions with others. The pre-class work is a lot but the in-class work is very interactive.

This course is a must for anyone who is or wants to become a manager or leader. This course should be a mandatory elective at Haas. It was much, much more valuable than Leading People or Leadership Comms. I highly recommend to anyone who wants to be successful, happy, and at peace in life, not just professionally.

I would recommend this course if it is a subject you are keenly interested in and willing to put in the work for! Do not take this if you just want an easy 2-unit course. I am happy I took the course, but I knew what to expect and it is a lot of work and certainly makes you reflect a lot on your own experiences. Just know what you are getting yourself into and it will be a great experience. Also, keep in mind if you will be able to handle the virtual learning environment, because this course can be difficult if that is not a good fit for you. That said, it is quite interactive with a lot of small group discussions on zoom.
Yes - brilliant for measured growth within leadership development

I think Erica is fabulous! To other students thinking of taking this course, just know it is A LOT of work. I can recommend the course to people that really read the syllabus, know that this is what they want to work on and are willing to invest a lot of time and "self" into the course. The outcomes and personal growth will be a great reward. This should be a required course! Anyone can teach hard skills. It takes a special person to guide you through carefully crafted and intentional exercises that connect your past, present and future self based on how our thoughts interconnect with our behaviors, actions, and others.

Yes but it's a lot of work. Please please don't underestimate it! Be prepared to put in a lot of work and to learn even more because the reward is incredible. It'll shift how you see people that are different from you, and give you new language and practices to connect across differences – something we need more and more in these times!
yes.
I would not the weekend and zoom format are not effective and can be an added strain on top of everything else.

rows.title: Human Rights and Responsible Business Strategy

sections.goodFor: Students interested in real estate development or land use who want a qualitative, conceptual survey plus CA policy/law context and cross-school interdisciplinary exposure.
sections.notFor: Students taking several other development courses (overlap risk), or anyone wanting quantitative depth - coverage is uneven, deep on some topics and skimmed on others.
sections.workloadNote: Light: few assignments and no final project, which one student warns makes it easy to lose track. Guest speaker in nearly every session. Thin evidence - 9 comments.
sections.gradingBasis: unclear
sections.redFlags: One says a guest speaker in almost every class was 'a bit much' and it could be a 2-credit class; one flags uneven topic depth; one warns of overlap with other real estate electives.
sections.quote: It's an interesting course. Not requiring a lot of assignements, no final project, so you can easily loose track. Overall worth it.
comments: Yes, I would recommend this course to anyone who is slightly interested in Real Estate Development or Land Use. Both instructors did a nice job covering the course contents.
If you want to learn about real estate development this class is a must take.
It's an interesting course. Not requiring a lot of assignements, no final project, so you can easily loose track. Overall worth it.

I would suggest this course to fellow students if they are seeking to learn more about land development and the reality of developing. This course introduces the fundamental components of developing property, which is usually not too easy. This course ties together policies and law quite well, especially in California.

I would recommend this course as a qualitative and conceptual approach to land development. There are great speakers across various land development practices that complement lectures from Linda and Evan, who have a wealth of knowledge.

This was a very unique and interesting class for me, and I generally recommend it if students are looking for a high- level introduction to land development process and an interdisciplinary experience. Getting different perspectives on a subject matter and getting to meet/engage with students from different schools was valuable. I generally liked the course content and felt we covered a wide range of interesting topics. I found the course content to be interesting, but sometimes we went a little too deep on certain topics while others we skimmed over too quickly. However, this may just be the downside of the interdisciplinary nature of the course, which I otherwise quite enjoyed. There was a guest speaker in almost every class, who generally were quite interesting, engaging, and informative, but it was a bit much. Perhaps could have been a 2-credit class?

Yes I recommend this course, but I would caution against taking this and more than 1 other development focused class for fear of too much overlap. However, both teachers bring a practitioner's mindset to the teaching which helps blend real world perspectives with the course material.
Would recommend the class

I would HIGHLY recommend this course IF you are interested in working in real estate after school. I have taken every real estate class offered by Haas and this class in particular has the most material that was not also covered in other classes. VERY helpful

sections.goodFor: Students wanting cross-listed exposure to land development alongside law and other graduate programs; one found the subject fascinating.
sections.notFor: Students without strong financial modeling skills or who need self-contained instruction - the pro-forma assignments outrun what class covers.
sections.workloadNote: Thin evidence - only 4 comments. Assignments include a pro-forma one student calls harder than any finance pro-forma they had done; work gets much harder at the end of term.
sections.gradingBasis: Assignments requiring in-depth pro-forma/financial model analysis; other components not described.
sections.redFlags: 2 of 4 commenters say class discussion, slides and guest speakers do not align, and that assignments require analysis the class never teaches (municipal code research, financial model setup).
sections.quote: the course material and class discussions don't align with guest speakers or course class slides.
comments: NA
It get WAY harder at the end make sure you ration enough time

No, the course material and class discussions don't align with guest speakers or course class slides. There were assignments that required in depth analysis for a pro-forma that was harder than any finance pro-forma ever completed. A lot more time could've been spent on finding the required material for each assignment to better enhance learning.

The course was fascinating and I enjoyed working with students from different graduate programs. I recommend every student take a cross-listed class. And while course objectives were clear, theories in execution were not directly transferrable for either MBA's or Law Students; more time in class could have been used to look up how municipal codes are searched and how best to set up financial models.

rows.title: International Business Development for MBAs, IP course

sections.goodFor: Students who want international consulting experience with a real client and travel; described as a once-in-a-lifetime, friendship-building MBA highlight.
sections.notFor: Students who need certainty or predictable load: you don't know your country, team or client when you sign up, and team leads do far more work with little recognition.
sections.workloadNote: Very heavy and back-loaded: spring class plus 80+ hour weeks for two weeks of in-country client work, and additional assignments/presentation in the following fall semester.
sections.gradingBasis: Team consulting deliverables, a blog post, a final presentation, plus a fall presentation for the last credit; guidelines unevenly enforced.
sections.redFlags: Recurring: credits do not match workload (fall assignments for spring credit), assignment instructions confusing and constantly changing, guidelines unevenly enforced, class time not relevant to all projects.
sections.quote: Project, team, and country dependent. Super MBA experience and would recommend doing it. Team leads should expect to do a lot more work with little recognition.
comments: Absolutely. Amazing opportunity to get consulting experience while traveling the world.
This is a truly transformative experience. A lot of work, a lot of hard work!! But you get to learn so much, experience so much, and explore so much! I highly recommend this course????
I would. This was a GREAT course!!

This course, as many people know, carries a lot of uncertainty. When you sign up for the course, you have no knowledge about what experience you are doing to get (country, team, client), so it is definitely a risk. But that said, I think the whole experience was worth it once you are able to go to your country, experience a new culture, and meet your client in person.

There were a few issues with this course throughout the semester that I hope are addressed: 1. The class time was not always relevant to all projects and it seemed not the best use of time for all teams. I think sharing a variety of resources that might or might not be applicable to projects would be rather, rather than providing only one framework or way to do things and assume that all teams can use this in their project. 2. Especially at the end, guidelines provided for some assignments were not followed by all teams. For example, we were told to keep the blog post at certain length, or the final presentation at 3 slides and these guidelines seemed almost "optional" and not really enforced by all teams, creating an unfair advantage for those teams who did follow the guidelines. 3. This class should be 4 credits if they still make us do assignments in the fall semester. I think it is ridiculous that we only get 2 credits in the spring for the amount of work we put in, including traveling in country and working 80+ hours for two weeks while in- country. All other applied innovation classes that have client-facing work are 3 credits. The fact that we also need to do a presentation in the fall to get the final 1 credit out of the 3 does not make sense at all, and this should be 1 credit IN ADDITION to the 3 credits we should already be earning for all our work from January to May. I hope this changes for future classes.
Yes if they are willing to work extra hours
Project, team, and country dependent. Super MBA experience and would recommend doing it. Team leads should
expect to do a lot more work with little recognition.

It's a great course with plenty of opportunity. Well-organized but not all projects are Go To Market strategy, and that is all the course focuses on. Instructors are very helpful, but instructions for assignments are confusing and change constantly
Yes, this was my all time favorite experience at Haas. The in country travel was a once in a lifetime experience, and I made lifelong friendships with my teammates.
Yes for the travel and consulting case experience!! Bang for your buck

rows.title: Pricing
rows.disagree: Modest rating, but comments are uniformly enthusiastic

sections.goodFor: Students headed into consulting, strategy, product marketing or pricing roles; several argue it should be core because it ties micro, marketing and strategy together.
sections.notFor: Students who bounce off a dry, insistent lecture style (one detailed pan says he cuts people off), or who dislike case-and-group-work formats and dated cases.
sections.workloadNote: One student states about 2 hours outside class per week; case prep plus group assignments each session. Class runs ~1.5 hrs case discussion + 30 min takeaways. Take-home final.
sections.gradingBasis: Case discussion and participation, recurring group written assignments, and a take-home final.
sections.redFlags: One long detailed pan of the teaching/communication style: dry content, poor transitions, cutting students off, syllabus hard to parse. 2-3 others note some cases are antiquated.
sections.quote: Be prepared for around 2 hours of work outside class each week.
comments: The course was a fascinating combination of pricing insight, business insight, and life insight. It was a true pleasure to attend and I felt I learnt a huge amount. Wasim was able to draw a vast wealth of stories from students, and encouraged everyone to get involved and share their opinions. A huge bonus to the class was the incredible speakers that Wasim was able to get in as well, they really made a massive positive impact!

This class is the cornerstone of the MBA, as likely, in one form or another, an MBA graduate will have to interface with Pricing. This course will provide you with a comprehensive view of pricing from the perspective of different products, pricing mechanisms and markets. The course was also well executed with engaging discussions and great speakers (we had a BCG senior partner, a Simon Kucher Pricing consultant, and a SaaS sales leader). Case workload was very manageable. Wasim himself is also a great guy.

Yes. 100%. In fact, I STRONGLY urge the program office to make this class part of the core. It blends microeconomics, marketing, and strategy in a way that is actually useful, practical, and real. All those classes in the core are very subpar. You could give students more opportunities to take electives by making pricing a rich, full core requirement, mandatory for all students.
Yes, i recommend this class to fellow students. This class gives you real life examples of pricing strategies that will be useful for anyone

Rethink at least three times before you bid for this class: 1) read the syllabus and imagine all the content and communication in the semester are presented similarly. Would you be ok with having to parse through information always like this by yourself? 2) Would you be okay with content being extremely dry and lacking good transitions from topic to topic? 3) Would you be ok with the professor always insisting on the point he's trying to make, and sometimes even cutting people off once he hears what he was trying to get?
TL, DR: I don't like his teaching and communication style strongly. Even given the rich content and its potential usefulness in my future work, I would have told my old self to take another class.

Yes! This course is the ultimate course if you are looking for relevant and useful content. It links and expands upon work done in ethics, strategy, micro, macro, and finance. It is among the few classes that I feel I will actually use in my career.
Yes its a must do for mbas

This is one of the BEST classes I've ever taken at Berkeley Haas for two years so far. Ton of insights and learnings. If you are considering your career at consulting or strategy ops at big tech companies, you should take this course as there are so much insights not only about pricing but competitive strategy in general.

To be honest, I first hesitated taking this course as folks left a review about "old-fashioned case" and "too much focused on SaaS pricing" - both being the main reason. However, those were NOT TRUE at all, at least in my personal experience. The cases were balanced between traditional business and SaaS, for some of them, you can hear what had happened actually from the professor. Cases are a bit old thou, you can still learn a timeless learnings, like pure "classics" in every field of expertise. During the semester, I really enjoyed this course with Prof. Azhar this semester. I wish we had more of this kind of practical classes during my two years.
I would recommend! It's different and very very important way to think about strategy
Yes, he explain the class concept well in and engaging way

Wasim is one of the most genuine professors I've come across at Haas. He truly cares not just about students' learning but their approaches and curiosity to think differently. His class has so many tiny anecdotes that add more to the MBA experience and makes it more human.
I highly recommend this course to those who enjoy not just pricing but comprehensive business strategies. A very worthwhile learning experience.

Pretty good class, would say that it is a bit more about overall strategy than solely pricing, which was a strength of the class in my opinion. Wasim is a great professor if a bit quirky - just takes some getting used to. The workload is really not that bad if you don't mind group work, plus the final is take-home. Overall, I would take this class again. I would definitely recommend this course. It touches on core business fundamentals that are relevant across roles like product development, marketing, and strategy. The case-based format (similar to consulting interviews) really sharpens your structured thinking, which is invaluable in corporate settings. Prof. Wasim keeps the class engaging by connecting business strategies to real-life decision-making, making the concepts easy and relatable.

Be prepared for around 2 hours of work outside class each week. The class typically runs 1.5 hours of case discussion and 30 minutes of key takeaways; personally, I found the concepts section could be a bit shorter, but it doesn't take away from the overall experience.

10000% yes. This has not only been the most relevant class I have taken at Haas, but it has remained so because Prof. Azhar keeps it relevant through his masterful lectures, cases and guest speakers. He imparts wisdom by the minute, is humble, kind, and strikes the perfect balance for an MBA course. Prof. Azhar was by far the best Prof. I have taken at Haas. He is not only incredibly gifted, but can convey that knowledge and wisdom through humor, in his assignments, lectures, and outside of class. The first speakers he brought in were the best guest lecturers and the most relevant ones to the context of the class and the current economy. He masterfully keeps the class engaged and interested throughout. Finally, he has been the kindest person overall in my entire Haas experience and the most understanding of my particular situation as a mother in her postpartum. I could not recommend him more.

I think this class is great if you're looking to get more knowledgeable on pricing methodology, some of the cases were a bit antiquated and made it difficult to connect to. but If you can get over that, Wassim is a great professor. I would 100% recommend this course. Core Strategy does not have a lot of frameworks to develop business intuition. Pricing helps you see many strategic situations through frameworks, so it serves as a great complement. The case work and guest speakers help you see how those frameworks work in the real world. Professor is funny and remembers a lot about students. He has many great experiences to share.
For sure. The way Wasim teaches the courses, he will ingrain concepts into your mind - making sure you are able to recall ideas well after you've left Haas.
I will say to get maximum value out of the class you need to put the work into cases - its of no use showing up for class if you arent doing the readings and contributing to the group assignments

Absolutely! I believe Pricing should be in the MBA core or advertised more by the academics offices. There are so many relevant frameworks and learning that I will leverage in my Product Marketing role in tech.

Yes - this course is extremely useful for anyone who wants to work in strategy/marketing/product or want to learn about pricing in different industries. This is not a low lift class but it isn't too heavy either - it is the perfect level or course load that pushes you to engage and come prepared. Also, Prof.Azhar lets everyone participate and is open to different perspectives which is great.

As long as Wasim teaches it, this class is a must-take. It's far better than managerial accounting, brand management, or any litany of similar courses that touch upon its topics. Take it as a capstone.

I highly recommend this class. Wasim is both highly knowledgeable and facilitates class in an engaging way; you'll both be interested in the material and also learn insights that you can apply in future real world scenarios. Absolutely! It's an extremely practical course with widespread applications across industries and roles. The various nuances of pricing along with examples of how companies are using them is helpful in approaching problems that we face in the real business world.

I would highly recommend this course to anyone who plans to go into a pricing or strategy-based role in the future. The cases spanned a wide variety of industries, with learnings and principles that are highly practical to anyone that will be in a senior management position in the future.

This was one my favorite classes at Haas. I felt like I learned so much that will be applicable in my career and just my day-to-day life. The professor facilitated engaging discussion, and there were so many valuable lessons we gained experientially and through case review. Cannot recommend more.
Great class with a decent amount of workload. You get as much as you put in as work on each case and each assignment.

Wasim clearly stated objectives and expectations right from the start and stuck by it. He is extremely proficient at understanding the class pulse and moving us through tricky concepts. He listens without judgement but has very strong opinions which he voices with utmost confidence and conviction. His course taught me the rigour of constantly learning and how to mould quantitative and qualitative information. I now feel I understand the moving parts of all functions in a business much better just through the lens of pricing!

The cases and course design was on-point. Fabulous mix of cases, lectures and guest speakers. We moved through content not only efficiently but also with key reinforcements from time to time. I only got better writing each assignment and I could see my thought process evolve.

sections.goodFor: Any function or industry - students frame it as a full strategy and market-research course, not just pricing; especially useful for founders and strategy roles.
sections.notFor: Non-quantitative students, who one commenter warns may struggle; anyone wanting AI-era content, since some frameworks and material felt dated.
sections.workloadNote: Not quantified. Case-based with guest speakers; students call it content- and math-heavy on the surface but well-structured and digestible as taught.
sections.gradingBasis: unclear
sections.redFlags: One student says some material and frameworks felt outdated and wants more current cases and AI tools; one bare 'No.' with no explanation.
sections.quote: Maybe - if you are already a quantitative person, this class will be a breeze. If not, this class might be a struggle.
comments: Yes, the class is very helpful for likely any position post-Haas, Professor Azhar is incredible overall, and I think I was the most intellectually challenged in this class.
Yes! This class was one of my favorite advanced topics and will be a strong value add regardless of function or industry you are going into. Highly recommend!
Yes, Absolutely.
Yes! Professor is one of the most caring professors I have met at Haas!
Absolutely 11/10 would recommend
Yes, I would definitely recommend this course. It's pretty essential in your toolkit irrespective of your post MBA industry.

Yes, absolutely. Professor Wasim is a highly effective and engaging instructor who brings strong clarity and structure to complex pricing concepts. He does an excellent job connecting frameworks to real-world applications, making the material both practical and memorable. The course is well-designed, with thoughtful case selection that reinforces key ideas, and the guest speakers add valuable industry perspective. Overall, it's a rigorous yet rewarding class that I would strongly recommend to anyone interested in pricing or strategy.

Yes I would. If you want to learn about differentiation, pricing strategies and go to market this is a great class. He is very experienced but stays on top of industry news. I really appreciated being able to discuss pricing strategies for OpenAI or Anthropic's products rather than the usual Coke or Airline cases that we cover on other courses

The class is extremely worthwhile. Beyond pricing you lose learn about strategy and market research. It is a very good aggregation of everything I have learned in the MBA so far. As a founder there were many insights I will take with me to my own company.

Yes, very much! A must-course in your MBA degree, seems content and math heavy but is really easy to digest and understand the way Prof Ashar teaches. In fact, he brings down complex concepts to intuition that you build through this course. He is a gem of a teacher, well-connected with a bajillion star alumni, and genuinely caring/helpful. Maybe - if you are already a quantitative person, this class will be a breeze. If not, this class might be a struggle. I also wish that this class leveraged AI tools and more current cases to stay at the cutting edge. Some material and frameworks felt outdated.
Yes, would definitely recommend
No.
Yes on course, yes on the professor. Thoroughly enjoyed the class and how Prof. Azhar managed class conversations with us.
Yes. He is well prepared and I learned a lot from his frameworks and way of analyzing industries and companies. Pricing is not just related to product elasticity, it's a full on strategy course,

I absolutely recommend this course to anyone considering working in business. Even if you won't be working in pricing directly, learning pricing strategy will make you a better business leader. Great class regardless of function or industry you are going into.
yesss

sections.goodFor: Students who want a current, well-connected overview of the impact investing landscape beyond just impact VC; the instructor is consistently praised as engaging and generous with office hours, and the guest speakers as high caliber. Best suited to those with basic finance under their belt.
sections.notFor: Students without finance fundamentals, despite the course being billed as entry level; several say it gets technically heavy and one had to run separate sessions to help classmates keep up. Also not for anyone wanting practical fund-building skills rather than a survey, or who dislikes cramming a broad topic into two Sundays.
sections.workloadNote: Repeatedly called a lot of work for a one-credit class, with substantial pre-reading and an intense group project squeezed between the two full-day Sunday sessions.
sections.redFlags: Recurring (10+ comments): the two-Sunday compressed format is too short for the breadth of material and should be a multi-week elective. Recurring (8 comments): assumes real finance background despite being marketed as entry level. Recurring (4 comments): workload is out of proportion to one credit.
sections.quote: It was a really useful, practical, and interesting overview of the impact investing landscape and trends.

rows.title: Systems Change for a Small Planet

sections.goodFor: Students wanting a reflective, values-oriented break from the MBA bubble - questioning capitalist assumptions, personal growth, and frameworks for dominant versus emergent systems.
sections.notFor: Anyone after practical systems-change knowledge (crash course, cases, implementation, pitfalls) - one points to the 1-credit Systems Change course instead - or averse to touchy-feely reflection.
sections.workloadNote: Thin evidence (6 comments). Reflective, discussion-driven work; one student says instruction was unclear and assignment expectations ill-defined. No hours or assignment cadence given.
sections.gradingBasis: unclear - one student says assignment expectations were ill-defined, but nobody describes how the grade is determined.
sections.redFlags: One of six says the course was under-thought and poorly delivered, with unclear instruction and ill-defined assignment expectations. One would condense it to 2 credits with more actual systems-change content.
sections.quote: If you are just looking for system changes knowledge (i.e., crash course, case examples, how to implement, pitfalls, etc.), then this class is not for you
comments: I'm so glad I took this class - it was such a breath of fresh air in business school. This class really challenged my worldview and self-view and truly nourished my soul.

Yes - I absolutely loved this class. It was so different from every other class I've taken, and was a much needed breath of fresh air to reflect on my values and how they are aligned or misaligned with how I am living, and how we are all encouraged to live in modernity. The class gave me some really useful frameworks to think about systems change and my role in dominant and emergent systems, and how to promote systems change. I really really loved this class. I would not. The course was a good place to reflect on bigger systemic issues and provided meaningful opportunity to reflect on my place and role within those systems, but the course overall was under thought and poorly delivered. I do think the course has potential, but instruction was generally unclear and expectations around assignments, expectations, etc. were generally ill-defined and again, poorly delivered.

Yes. As a business school student, this could be the most important course you take during your time at Haas, especially if you open yourself up to the questions and discomfort that will arise from it.

It depends what you want out of the class. If you are just looking for system changes knowledge (i.e., crash course, case examples, how to implement, pitfalls, etc.), then this class is not for you and would recommend looking at the Systems Change 1-credit course that's offered. Now if you are looking for that + a touchy-feely course that is different than anything else you've taken at Haas, let's you spend time to reflect (vs go-go-go that bschool is), and grow as a person (vs student, corp ladder climber, etc.), then this course if for you. It was a breath of fresh air and a safe heaven. I'm glad I took it, but also would have been glad if it was condensed to a 2-credit course and focused more on systems change knowledge, implementation, etc.
Yes! Even if it isn't being offered again, this class really helped me step outside of the MBA bubble and question a lot of the business / capitalist oriented thinking that Haas embodies.
Yes 100% recommend - this was one of the most intellectually expansive and introspective classes I have ever taken and would recommend it to everyone.

sections.goodFor: Anyone needing a microecon foundation for business decisions; strongest fit for students who already have some econ exposure and can attend section.
sections.notFor: Complete econ novices - lectures move very fast; also students wanting applied real-world data/analytics rather than theory (1 wanted problems, data, statistical tools).
sections.workloadNote: Problem sets and discussion sections; several say you must budget time outside class to process fast lectures, though one calls the load not prohibitively heavy.
sections.gradingBasis: Exams referenced (one student felt unprepared for the exam); problem sets discussed. Weighting not stated.
sections.redFlags: Pace too fast for those new to econ (3-4 comments); course tries to cover too much in the time available (2); one student felt unprepared for the exam despite understanding takeaways.
sections.quote: He's a great professor who is very knowledgeable but he goes way too fast for people who have never learned or seen any of this material before.
comments: Yes. He's extremely knowledgeable and a good teacher and fun to be in their class.
I do think Jim did deliver on teaching us the fundamentals of microeconomics, so I do overall recommend.
Yes. Jim is extremely smart, challenges you to think beyond the economic concepts. He also is very personable during office hours.

I would. Even though i said the class changed in a way i didn't like, there is no denying he is a great lecturer and that doesn't come easy. He can dissect topics and concepts to make them feel incredibly manageable.
Yes! Jim clearly cared about our learning and I appreciated his tone and humor. He made it clear why we should care about the content and tied it back to our everyday world well

comments: I would recommend this class. It was a really nice complement to so many of the quant-heavy types of leadership classes that tend to focus on content rather than connections. I think what Erica is teaching is resilience and adaptability that is helpful in any sort of work environment and often missing from many management style courses. sections.goodFor: Students with the emotional bandwidth to be vulnerable and reflect deeply, who want real practice at feedback, conflict, reading the room and building trust.
sections.notFor: Anyone closed to discomfort or self-disclosure - students say flatly it will waste your time and degrade the experience for classmates. Also those who dislike long remote sessions.
sections.workloadNote: Pre-work and assignments plus long hours of self-reflection; called a lot of work where you get out what you put in. Sessions mix short frameworks, live exercises, peer coaching and reflection.
sections.gradingBasis: unclear; pre-work, assignments and in-class exercises are described, but grading itself is never discussed.

sections.quote: Expect to embarass yourself a little bit, step out of your comfort zone and have really deep conversations. If you are not open to these types of experiences, don't take the class.
comments: Absolutely. Erica creates one of the most meaningful learning environments at Haas. Grounded, human, and deeply reflective. This course helps you slow down, reconnect with your values, and lead with more presence and authenticity. It's not just another class; it's an experience that stays with you long after the class/session ends. You notice immediately in your interactions with others, you remember concepts and practices from class, and your practice with the people around you.
This is a life changing course if you are willing to put in the work. It pushes you to self reflect on a very deep level and gives you real practice in interacting in various situations.

I've been working for eight years, and I think taking this class now has a very different impact on me compared to if I had taken it eight years ago. Back then, I had just graduated, full of dreams and ideals, and my way of thinking was very straightforward. But over the years, I've encountered many complex and indirect challenges — especially in interpersonal relationships, whether with colleagues, leaders, or family.

Although this class was short, every simple metaphor in it suddenly helped me understand things that once confused me. For example, the metaphor of the rubber band reminded me of the times when I was under a lot of pressure at work and felt unsatisfied with my own performance. Now, I understand that I need to forgive myself, because I am human, not perfect. I need to accept both the good and the imperfect parts of myself — they're all part of who I am. I want to embrace that imperfect self, give myself space to breathe, adjust my mindset, and then move forward bravely toward the next destination.

Transformational course, if you come in with an open mind, the right level of curiosity, and a desire for personal change. Erica is an amazing instructor and manages the course really well. A bit of research into what touchy-feely looks like for me before I signed up was important.

You should take this class if you 1) are willing to devote long hours reflecting on yourselves and practicing interpersonal skills, 2) are willing to practice vulnerabilities by putting yourself out there and sharing them with your classmates (who you might not know), 3) want to be more conscious about your senses, deeply rooted assumptions / preconceived notions, and how to lead with intuition. If all the above conditions satisfy, this class would be a gratifying experience and has a long-term positive impact.
100000%. This is the type of class that adds true value on an MBA.
Yes! Absolutely. I learned about making deep connections through this course, which is a life skill.

I absolutely recommend this class. It has been the most impactful class at Haas and probably has changed the way I relate with myself and others forever in a very positive way. Recommend in the highest terms! Erica is a highly valued resource of the university and I wish her course could be offered to all students.
