I would absolutely recommend taking this course - I benefitted from it immensely and think it should be required for everyone. This class will change your life!

1000% yes! This course is transformative if you commit to the work. It's not a passive class; it challenges you to slow down, reflect, and engage deeply with yourself and others. Erica creates a space where you can safely explore discomfort, vulnerability, and growth with peers in ways that connect directly to real-world leadership. The pre-work and assignments are meaningful and build toward a powerful in-class experience. If you're willing to show up fully, this class will change how you lead, listen, and connect.

Every Haas student should take this class. You practice real-world people skills that show up daily like giving/receiving feedback, navigating conflict, reading the conversation dynamics, and building trust. The format mixes short frameworks with live exercises, peer coaching, and structured reflection, so you're not just learning concepts, but you're applying them in the room. It's a course where trusting the process matters. You'll be asked to lean into discomfort, try new behaviors, and debrief what worked. I walked away with practical tools that I now use in everyday life.

It takes a lot of work to manage a portfolio and learning to do so takes time. I would add a lab component and make sure the class is well enrolled. I would have found it useful to have more lab practice on using resources like Bloomberg terminals, Facset, CapIQ, and the myriad of other resources available to us for this course. But learning is best done by doing, so more hands on experience would have been useful. Highly recommend, but I believe there are much more to improve, like how to apply our skills early on, how each lecture and speaker could be paired with more practical tasks. Despited these, I still learned so much that it changed my way of thinking about how to create impact.

I would! I met and learned from so many amazing people, not just Gloria and the speakers she brought in, but my fellow classmates. It was a really great community to be in!

It depends on what you're looking for. I expected to leave the class with more tangible ways to challenge capitalism, but in retrospect, the class is called "reinventing capitalism," which implies working within existing economic structures. I think a course more focused on challenging and deconstructing capitalism would have been more interesting. That said, I did learn a lot more about innovative social impact business models than I knew before, which is useful to know as I continue my career post-Haas.

I would recommend it - it did a good job of opening my mind. I wish we were able to dive even deeper into how to implement some of these concepts, but learning about them in the first place was a fantastic start.

sections.goodFor: Students who want an overview of alternative models of capitalism, enjoy reflective/experiential assignments and value the guest speaker roster.
sections.notFor: Anyone wanting concrete business content, rigor or debate - critics call it surface-level, an echo chamber, with infantilizing activities; skip if you already agree with the premise.
sections.workloadNote: One student reports routinely 4-6+ hrs/week for a 2-credit course: dense readings, weekly experiential activities plus write-up reflections, and a semester-long project.
sections.gradingBasis: Weekly reflections/activities and a semester-long project; 2 say deliverables and grading were unclear and changed mid-semester.
sections.redFlags: 3 detailed critiques: surface-level content and messy delivery, shifting assignment instructions, semester project first raised in March, an unannounced Easter-weekend simulation, unresponsive prof/GSI.
sections.quote: This course also had far too much work for a 2-credit course. I have routinely spent over 4-6 hours a week in preparation for this class.
comments: I would want this course to be redesigned for greater impact and a more challenging approach before recommending it. The material was sped through and was surface-level at best. I don't believe we redefined anything. Gloria is passionate and enjoyable to interact with, but the presentation of the material was messy, the grading and deliverables unclear, and the weekly reflections are infantilizing at best and offensive at worst.
No. Many of my classmates were very engaged with this class, but I really don't think anyone coming to Haas for tangible and concrete business would get a lot of use out of it.

This was the worst class I took at Haas. If you feel like you already understand that the current state of capitalism is bad for us, you're not going to get anything more out of this class, so stay far, far away. Gloria is a perfectly nice person and I took it because the title seemed interesting and because I heard from people who liked her other classes. But it feels like she has no idea what she wants this class to be yet. It had so much potential and started strong, but I don't feel like it ever got around to the actual "reinventing" part beyond the first two classes where we talked about alternate forms of capitalism. There were also just WAY too many activities that felt extremely middle school ("go spend time in nature!"). I ended up skipping a lot of the very dense readings because the reflections took too many hours between doing the activities and doing the write up every single week. The classes also sometimes seemed to have no aim and it felt like we were just killing time until the guest speakers came. A lot of class time pre-speaker would be us sharing our feelings from the reflections and very little conceptual lecture. When we did have conceptual lecture, it felt very elementary. In general, it felt like the course content was aimed at changing people's minds about capitalism = good when in reality most of us took this class because we were already there. This class shouldn't be offered again until she has a better idea of what she wants to do with it, besides making it a speaker symposium class. She and the GSI were also pretty unresponsive. All in all this class was a huge waste of my time and credits and I really regret taking it. Feels bad saying that because she's such a nice person, but it's true.
Yes, if you want to change the world, this is a must-have course! If you wish to change the world while keeping your core values as you navigate capitalism, this is a mandatory course!
Would recommend - thought provoking class that gives a helpful overview of the menu of options that exist to build a capitalist system.
Good learning if you're willing to invest in the readings / class discussions. Great speakers.

No I would not recommend this instructor or course to a fellow student. I had much higher expectations for this course. By nature of this class being an elective with a somewhat provocative course name, the students in the class already largely all had similar opinions despite coming from various different schools at Berkeley (ie- Haas, Goldman, etc) and having different backgrounds. During discussions, the class quickly became the same repetitive echo chamber praising and complaining about the same topics in very similar ways. At the beginning of the semester, multiple students suggested that the professor and GSI implement anonymous " devil's advocates ": 1-2 students assigned (via email before class) to pressure-test assumptions and opinions voiced in class by respectfully disagreeing or dissenting and bringing up alternative thought processes instead for discussion. Despite the professor and GSI nodding and taking this into consideration, it was never implemented.

Ironically, this class on reinventing capitalism for a sustainable, humane, and equitable world was one of, if not the most, economically dissonant courses I have taken at Haas. There were several weekly assignments that were significantly disconnected from the reality of people's everyday lives in a way that was derogatory towards others. The most notable one being to interview a service worker about essentially why does life suck for the average American worker. The assignment literally said " Bonus if you have the conversation over coffee or a meal, your treat " as if essential workers should be oh so thankful so as to accept the gracious charity from some super duper smart fancypants Cal grad student in exchange for a conversation where a random nerd gawks at their life situation. This course also had far too much work for a 2-credit course. I have routinely spent over 4-6 hours a week in preparation for this class. The instructions for weekly assignments and for the semester-long project would change in the middle of the semester which was confusing especially when the syllabus and bCourses announcements gave different instructions. There was not an introduction to the semester-long project back in January when the class began. Instead, the prof brought it up as an aside in March to remind us that our semester-long projects should be about halfway done. This blindsided many individuals in the class who were barely aware of the project or that was supposed to be treated and planned differently than a " final project ". For another weekly assignment, we were told on a Monday in class that we needed to clear our schedules at 12pm and 5pm the upcoming Friday, Saturday, and Sunday for a simulation that was not scheduled in the syllabus or mentioned at all previously. This caused multiple people in class to have to change pre-scheduled weekend plans on short notice, and the icing on the cake was that this was Easter weekend as well.

Between unclear assignments, barriers to completing assignments, an echo chamber of students without prof/GSI encouraging different perspectives, and lack of in-depth deep dives on any topic, I did not enjoy this course nor would I recommend it to others. To barely ever mention how wealth in the U.S. is currently distributed by race because of historic and present-day racist policies and to have never mentioned anti-consumerism was a shock to me. This course lacked diversity of thought, and because of the self-selection of students who choose this course, I had at least expected to learn more deeply about any topic at all instead of glossing over a topic for barely an hour to then have a random guest speaker there to promote their business.
YES HIGHLY RECOMMEND! Gloria is an amazing professor who is humble, genuine, and incredibly well connected:)

sections.goodFor: Students already in or entering biotech/pharma/healthcare who value direct access to big pharma, small biotech and VC leaders; better after an M&A class.
sections.notFor: Beginners with no pharma/biotech or pharma finance background - 2 say it is not taught as an intro; also those wanting quant depth or teaching rather than speakers.
sections.workloadNote: Two Sunday sessions only one week apart plus project work in between; 2 students say the load is too heavy for a 1-unit class and ask for the Sundays to be spaced further apart.
sections.gradingBasis: Project work and assignments between the two Sunday sessions; specifics not described.
sections.redFlags: Runs like a speaker series with little actual teaching and does not match the syllabus/course description (2 comments, one calls it 'a waste of time and money'); workload too heavy for 1 unit (2); light on quant.
sections.quote: It was more like a speaker series or a seminar where we heard from different speakers (all great) but there was not much teaching involved.
comments: Yes
Yes I would but with a caution about lack of hard/quant learning
Yes, the learning and insights you get from the instructors and guest speakers were truly inspiring, highly recommend if you are in biotech, or consider a career in this field.

Kim and Shalini were great. But the course format can be improved a lot. Loved that we got to hear from a lot of different prominent leaders in big pharma, small biotech, VC. But the course load was a lot. One recommendation is to split the two Sundays further apart so that there's enough time to do the project work. This is a heavy lift for 1 unit class with just one Sunday apart.

Yes, the most engaging classes I've been in. The wealth of experience provided by the guest lecturers was amazing. Having industry leaders in class made it very easy to understand the practical applications of theory. Their unique backgrounds provided excellent perspective on the biotech industry as a whole.
Yes - recommend any of Kim's classes - I always leave with a new perspective and resources that help me in my career. Yes but would recommend an M&A class before to get the most out of it

I would not recommend this class. The syllabus and course description was completely different from the actual class format. It was more like a speaker series or a seminar where we heard from different speakers (all great) but there was not much teaching involved. For someone who doesn't have a background in Pharma/Biotech or Pharma finance and is looking to learn as a beginner, this class is not it. The workload was also too heavy for a 1 unit class. No
10/10 if you are in bio/pharma/healthcare world
Yes!
Yes, if you are at all interested in the space, gives a great overview and practical application of it through the course work and assignments
Definitely. Bot Shalini and Kim are amazing professors with incredible experience and bring amazing speakers that bring great value to the class.
Not at all what a waste of time and money felt like a conference

sections.goodFor: People new to startups or deep tech who want climate/energy networking, consulting-style experiential work and a resume project, and who genuinely have time to invest.
sections.notFor: Anyone who has already launched a product (too basic), or who is time-constrained. One student calls it impractical, admin-heavy and geared to a 'fluffy' summit, saying better options exist.
sections.workloadNote: Very heavy; most work happens outside class - stakeholder interviews, entrepreneur meetings, assignments, and a final C2M Summit presentation. 3-hour sessions several call long or redundant.
sections.gradingBasis: Team project with an assigned startup client plus presentations culminating in the C2M Summit; explicit grade weights not discussed.
sections.redFlags: Startup matching is a 'complete blackbox' (one gave 96 of 100 pts to a choice they didn't get); long/redundant 3-hour lectures; heavy admin time; startups often not climate-focused enough; team luck dominates.
sections.quote: The whole course is dependent on how good your team and your startup is. It would have been nice to have some content that didn't depend on those two factors
comments: Yes, if you're interested in climate technology. In particular, building out a network in climate/energy and/or thinking through how tech can scale are the core strengths of the class. The guest speakers and networking opportunities in this class are fantastic. And the teaching team does a good job introducing how to interview stakeholders, how to approach techno-economic analysis, and preparing you to present. However, while I have some frameworks to think about how tech scales (TEA, Competitive Analysis, TAM), these concepts are introduced then left up to us to really apply them in-depth. Because of this (as well as all the stakeholder interviews we have to do), the class can feel like a lot of work.

Yes! This is a great course for anyone, even someone with no experience in clean tech. It'll give you exposure and there's tons of investment that the course makes in you as a professional regardless of your industry vertical Yes, depending on what you are looking to get out of it and how much time you have. This is a great class for consulting experiential learning, plus startup and deep tech real-world experience -- both of which are great things. If you're looking for a safe environment that's flexible in terms of workload and has team members to lean on, this class is a great fit. If you're looking to learn lots by doing, want to learn quickly, and want to learn broadly, then an in- semester internship is likely more effective from a time-effort perspective -- but this is a much larger commitment than a class.
Yes I would

This is an awesome class and clearly a lot of time and energy has gone into perfecting it for students. My main recommendation is to choose more climate-focused technologies and companies. All of our eggs are in one basket re the company we're paired with and I wish I was able to work with a company more focused on GHG emissions
reductions.
Yes. I learnt a lot about the operation and key factors impacting clean tech startups
Yes. These instructors are really helpful not only delivering the program but also navigating related issues and problems

I would recommend this course to anyone who is interested in learning the challenges early-stage deep-tech startups face. There is a considerable amount of work that takes place outside of class meetings in the form of interviews, meetings with entrepreneur, and assignments. You do NOT get to choose the startup you wish to work with; you are asked to distribute 100 points to your top 5 startups. I was not selected to work with my top choice, to whom I assigned 96 points. The matching process is a complete blackbox.

You will work with people outside of Haas, people who are a lot busier than your average MBA students. They, understandably, will not be as available to put in the work as you would and FT or EWMBA students will be responsible for carrying the team.
Yes. It's chaotic but gives valuable insight into what it might be like to work at a clean tech startup. Awesome networking opportunities within cleantech.
I thought the lectures were helpful but they were very long considering the value I got out of them.
The whole course is dependent on how good your team and your startup is. It would have been nice to have some content that didn't depend on those two factors
I recommend splitting the class back up into 2 different class sections
I think this class is helpful if you've never launched a product before but if you have, it doesn't help you delve much deeper into it.
I wish that the startups felt more like clean tech - more energy related startups or solutions that, if scaled, would address bigger climate problems.

I absolutely have and would recommend this course. It's easily my most well-organized, well-facilitated class. This inspired me in turn to be involved in this class above and beyond, and I used many of the lessons I learned in this class (especially in effective storytelling and presenting) even in other courses. I also feel grateful to now be connected with my amazing team, who I can now call my friends.
I am not an MBA, and do not come from a business background. This course has been a welcoming, intensive intro into Haas, where I will certainly try to take more courses.
Difficult but gratifying class. A lot of effort expended and the C2M Summit helps deliver a gratifying end. yes, helpful for understanding early stage cleantech

I would recommend to people who want to do a ton of work, who are really interested and doing this type of work, and don't have experience. The main thing is it is a ton of work, and takes a ton of time, not really all of it super useful - I was jealous of those who skipped class because so much of it was redundant

I would recommend this class to those who are interested in working in the clean tech space or working with startups and founders to shape their go-to-market strategy. However, I would also like to mention that the workload is probably one of the heaviest among all classes I've taken as a third year MBA student. Additionally, you don't get to choose your teammate - you kind of do by selecting the same company but not really know who will be on your team till the team is formed - and your teammates will have a huge impact on your experience with this class, positive or negative.
Maybe. I would prefer if the course is again split into two classes every week because 3 hours is too much with me (and I learnt that)

It depends on your desires/priorities. This is a heavy lift class and the type of class that you get out as much as you are willing to put in. Also, I feel like non-MBA people might have gotten more out of this than MBAs (except for those specifically looking for consulting experience in a deep tech/climate tech field) since the business portion is not extremely advanced (which makes sense considering the class has students from other schools with no prior business experience).

Yes, I would recommend this course. It offers a rare mix of real-world industry exposure, structured guidance, and hands-on teamwork that helps you build both technical and commercial skills in cleantech.
Absolutely recommend. This course gives you real exposure to cleantech startups, investor thinking, and
commercialization. The team is incredibly supportive, and the final summit is a unique, high-stakes experience that pushes you to grow.
For people who have limited startup or entrepreneurial experience absolutely for those with might be a little too basic It is a lot of work, and a lot depends on if your company is cool.

Yes, I would recommend this course if you have the time to really invest in and engage with it. The class is very time- consuming, and most of the learning happens outside of the classroom. If you don't have the capacity to give the course the attention it deserves, you likely won't learn as much and won't be able to contribute effectively to your team.

No. Way too much time spent on administrative matters, not practical enough. Not close enough to real world experiences and more geared towards a "fluffy" summit presentation than for actually providing useful inputs to startups. There are much better classes available (including on Coursera).
Yes, but only if you need the credit

I would recommend this class to students who want an interactive class that works with an external client. It is a great resume builder but it is A LOT of work. Also the experience is very dependent on the group you are placed with and the startup.
I would recommend this course though it is heavy workload, so be prepared when you enroll in this course. It is really worthy!!
The teaching team is solid, experienced, competent, helpful, responsive, interactive, and supportive. They help you get through a very difficult and intensive course/project.

sections.goodFor: Students new to entrepreneurship/VC who have an idea they are genuinely passionate about and land on a committed team; the VC pitch and ecosystem exposure are the payoff.
sections.notFor: Students who need organized instruction and responsive staff, or who lack a project they care about - motivation reportedly collapsed class-wide after Darwin Day.
sections.workloadNote: Weekly written assignments/essays plus a semester-long team venture project that ramps up heavily at the end; several call the weekly write-ups busy work with little value.
sections.gradingBasis: Weekly write-ups, GSI-tracked attendance sign-in, and team deliverables ending in a VC pitch; final expectations called unclear.
sections.redFlags: Disorganization and busy-work weekly essays (3+); slow/unreachable TA and professor, GSI rigid and wrongly marked attendance (1-2); team formation drives groupthink; mid-semester instructor swap hurt quality.
sections.quote: I would, but this course is pretty disorganized and has a lot of busy work.
comments: Absolutely!

YES!! This course is one of my favorites so far. You get practical experience to test the entrepreneurship journey along with solid advice, clear examples, and team support. It is a lot of work if you are truly passionate about your chosen project so do be aware of that. Especially if you are new to the VC/entrepreneurship space, I HIGHLY recommend taking this course. I learned so much that I can now directly apply as a possible entraphsip or really any new project. Both professors are so willing to help and also honest with their feedback which I so appreciate!
Great experience in taking that first step into becoming a founder. This class is a safe environment to test your VC's ideas, again VC ideas!

Yes, I would highly recommend this course to any MBA student, or those considering entrepreneurship. Its extremely hands on, so only take it if you are ready to engage and put the work in, especially at the end of the semester. The learnings are invaluable and whether or not you have an idea or business you want to work on now, this will help you learn how to think about problem spaces, validate ideas and progress through bringing a product/service to life. If you do have an idea or business now, this will be an opportunity for guided strategic development.

The course began on a strong note, with the first 3 – 4 weeks offering well-structured and valuable content. However, the quality and coherence of the course declined significantly afterward. The structure appeared to unintentionally encourage groupthink and popularity-driven decisions, often at the expense of better ideas. Strong projects were sometimes overlooked, while weaker or duplicate ideas advanced. While the professors aim to stay neutral in team formation and idea selection, some degree of intervention — especially when multiple teams are proposing near- identical or clearly underdeveloped concepts — might improve the overall experience and outcomes.

A more flexible team formation process would also be beneficial. Forcing students to join groups they may not be genuinely interested in, rather than allowing them to pursue topics they are passionate about, can limit engagement and stifle creativity.

Also I really want to emphasize how the GSI was unnecessarily strict and annoying about random things when they themselves were so disorganized. Many students, including myself, found the GSI to be overly rigid and

unapproachable. For instance, I was incorrectly marked absent from a session I clearly attended and signed in for. When I raised the issue, the GSI dismissed it without considering a correction. This kind of inflexibility and lack of responsiveness undermines trust and adds unnecessary frustration to the student experience. Given that most graduate students are working professionals, a more respectful and collaborative approach would have been more appropriate.

If you have not done anything in entrepreneurship before I think it is helpful framework. The final deliverables lacked clarity on what was expected and the fact that the class was a simulation goes against the seeming expectation for you to actually build a company. It is hard to tell if the expectation is an educational endeavor or for you to actually build a company which makes assignments difficult.

I would 100% recommend this course. It's fantastic from a learning perspective, I loved how the course was structured layer by layer to build up a business plan. I've already taken an entrepreneurship course, but this landed in a much bigger way.
I would say you get out what you put in. And your team is so important to making this an enjoyable process, so keep this in mind.

100% recommend it. The EWMBA version has more interesting students, and the teaching staff are both legends too. If you want to learn how to synthesize an and take it all the way to pitching it to VCs from Lightspeed, a16z, etc, this is the class for you.
Only if they have an idea that they are passionate about and want to launch.
Hands down I would certainly recommend this class to other students interested in exploring the world of entrepreneurship or VC.

I would, but this course is pretty disorganized and has a lot of busy work. They need to get rid of the weekly assignment/write ups because I didn't get much value from those. Instead, have check points related to our main project to keep teams on track. Also, it was really hard to reach the TA and professor, slow replies, and not always getting quality time

Definitely recommend. Even if you don't see yourself as an entrepreneur, this course can be helpful in understanding the start-up ecosystem and gaining knowledge about funding, business model, strategy etc.
I absolutely would. This should be a required course and is full of invaluable lessons for all.
yes, I would definitely recommend the class to someone interested in learning about startups and wanting to get a holistic view on the process of startups.
I would not because I could have learned so much more by having devoted class time to learn by doing rather than listening to lectures.
yes

No. The class was helpful the first few weeks when we were all working towards our own ideas and pitch. The class took a nosedive once Professor Beyer had to step out and Shiva stepped in. We didn't learn anything during the weeks Shiva instructed. The class workload is too heavy (essays every week) and wasn't helpful. This class would be more effective if each student continued working on their ideas throughout the semester.

There is a 35% chance I would only recommend this class to my fellow students. For most of them, it would be a no. Maybe this is because I had a sub-par experience with my team after Darwin Day, but after speaking with many of my fellow classmates, there was a lack of interest in the class across the board after Darin Day. The motivation to come to this class went down substantially for me and many of my classmates after Darin Day, but we all still came and felt unmotivated through the end of the semester.

sections.goodFor: Students who want exposure to Lean Startup methodology for validating a new venture and to hear from a couple of successful entrepreneur guests.
sections.notFor: Anyone wanting step-by-step guidance on actually starting a venture; 1 of 2 commenters attended every class and says they learned nothing beyond one framework.
sections.workloadNote: Only 2 comments - very thin. Pitch your own startup idea in one day, then work in peer groups on the ideas selected by professors or student vote, with little supporting instruction.
sections.gradingBasis: Group startup project and assignments; no other grading detail given.
sections.redFlags: 1 of only 2 commenters: lectures ramble on topics unrelated to assignments, only 'blue ocean strategy' actually taught (and googleable), group startup work unsupported, 'waste of credits and money.'
sections.quote: Majority of class does not teach anything, its more of rambling on topics unrelated to assignments or how to actually step by step start your own venture
comments: I would not recommend this course unless you are looking to hear from a couple of successful entrepreneurs. Majority of class does not teach anything, its more of rambling on topics unrelated to assignments or how to actually step by step start your own venture. Only one class "blue ocean strategy" is explained, and I could have googled it. We did not learn anything unfortunately. You create your own startup one day-which may or may not be chosen. You then are told to work with peers on the selected group ideas the professors pick or are based on student votes, and are not taught anything to help you with these startups. I have attended all classes and walked away learning nothing but the definition of blue ocean strategy. Waste of credits and money.
Yes, the focus on the "Lean Startup" methodology makes this course essential for anyone serious about validating a new venture.

rows.title: Business Communication in Diverse Work Environments

sections.goodFor: Students pivoting into climate/impact VC who want real client work, investor network access and interview material; one landed an in-semester internship through their client.
sections.notFor: Anyone wanting a structured introduction to impact investing - learning is self-driven and peer-to-peer. If your client is unfocused, the project drifts and you learn less than peers.
sections.workloadNote: Not quantified. Almost all work is the semester-long client project; a lot for 2 units if scope isn't set with the client. Class sessions sometimes cancelled to give project work time.
sections.gradingBasis: unclear; the client project and its deliverables dominate
sections.redFlags: Experience varies heavily by client and team (5+ students); 2 say there is little real lecture or teaching from the instructors; 1 reports classes cancelled at the last minute for 'project work time'.
sections.quote: This class is entirely based on your client project, with little to no lecture or deep learning coming from the professors. In fact, class is often cancelled (at the last minute)
comments: Absolutely - specially if you're interested in getting real life experience more about impact and climate investing and/or working with it.

I learned a lot with this course, but I think part of it was because of the client we were assigned to. Potentially this is a class that the more you give the more you get, and part of it depends on the clients engagement and organization to support the project.

Amazing opportunity to connect with the impact and climate investing space - we got to know a lot of the clients and part of them (not only ours) joined the final happy hour and we were able to network more.
Yes, this was a fantastic class for anyone that wants hands-on experience in impact investing

Yes if you're interested in hands-on experience in impact investing. Like most experiential classes, your group and project idea will have a big impact on your actual experience, but I found the ROI on project time very high and would have invested more time in this class if I could do it over. Both instructors are very willing to share their expertise and time with you, the lectures themselves are very informative, and I highly recommend this class.
Yes
Definitely would recommend the course! I thought this was a great experience working with a client and learning real world applications of what we learn in the classroom.
Yes, especially for future investors! It's fun and meaningful to work with real VCs/investors.
Yes if you already have experience in this industry. If you are new it is how much you put into this class.

I would recommend this course with the caveat that what you get out of it really depends on the client and project you get. If you get a client who doesn't really know what they want or how to utilize your skills, the project may end up being very unfocused, and you may not learn as much as your peers. A lot of our project felt self-driven, and we kind of lost the benefit of working with someone who works in the industry- we didn't really get to know what he does on a day-to-day basis. That said it was useful to speak to my experience in interviews and gave us credibility to have conversations with some really influential people in the industry.

Yes! Your experience will be somewhat colored by the client youre paired with but regardless, the class is an incredible value add. You'll also have a lot of opportunities to learn from your classmates' projects.

This class is entirely based on your client project, with little to no lecture or deep learning coming from the professors. In fact, class is often cancelled (at the last minute) to give us more "project work time." Honestly, I was hoping to learn more about impact investing from the professors who are such seasoned professionals in this space, but they seem to believe that it's only worthwhile to learn by doing through our client projects, which are highly variable depending on the assigned client and topic.

This was a fantastic class! We had the chance to work with real-world clients and could select them during the first week. I really appreciated how dedicated Etter and Liz were to our growth and supporting us throughout the process. Coming in with no understanding of impact investing (or investing, in general), I felt like it helped to provide me with a deeper understanding and real-world skills.

If you want to work in VC, TAKE THIS CLASS! As someone who is looking to pivot into Climate VC, this may have been the single most impactful class I took in my first year at Haas. Landing a first role in venture is hard, but this class gives you the practical experience to make it easier. The connections with your client are also very helpful, and mine led to an in-semester internship with a fund my client connected me with.
I would recommend this class as it does a great job of tying in the real world into Haas. It was also extremely interesting to see all the other projects other teams were covering.

Good class, very hands-on, but like any applied innovation, the workload and overall class experience depends heavily on the group and client you are assigned. I feel like the class can end up being a lot of work for only 2 units if you don't set a clear scope with your client or get a hard to tackle problem. A lot of the class is self-driven and learning is meant to be peer-to-peer, so this might not be the best class if you are looking for an introductory overview of the impact investing space.
Absolutely, fantastic instructors that bring deep industry knowledge and a great network
Yes fun class and engaging

I would definitely recommend this course if you are interested in climate investing. The projects themselves vary, but Liz and Etter are great resources if you are willing to engage with the class and put in the time.
Yes I would especially if you have never thought about impact investing (applications, capital structures etc.)

Interpersonal Skills and Embodied Systems Leadership

sections.goodFor: Students who want deep-tech commercialization exposure with real early-stage clients, plus unusually high-quality networking nights with VCs, serial entrepreneurs and operators (~3 per term).
sections.notFor: MBAs seeking consulting or entrepreneurship practice: one warns business students hard-carry teams of masters students with 0-2 years' experience, plus an age gap and heavy unpaid labor.
sections.workloadNote: Thin evidence (5 comments) but consistent: extremely heavy - one says ~3x the time the unit count suggests, covering interviews, weekly assignments, deliverables and several rounds of presentations.
sections.gradingBasis: Team client project with mid-term presentation, alumni night and final demo day; grading not otherwise discussed.
sections.redFlags: Team composition: the MBA is often the only business student and ends up carrying and coaching much younger masters students (2 of 5). Workload far exceeds the unit count. Experience hinges on client and team.
sections.quote: That said, be ready for an extremely heavy workload. The class easily takes 3x the time suggested by the unit count
comments: Not if you're a business student, unless you are making a hard pivot and are seriously in need of a hands-on client project on your resume, and you're willing to put in the time and unpaid labour for it. It's a good project to talk about during interviews, but that can easily be achieved through other Haas Experiential Learning courses or an in-semester internship. The workload is much higher than you think, because the teams are usually Masters students who are fresh out of undergrad with <2 years of work experience (often 0 or 1 year), so it's much more work than you'd think to coordinate with them and work with them to get the material up to a standard that you're willing to present and put your name on. The projects are usually a business question at its core (market entry, commercialisation, pricing, etc) and most groups this year had max 1 business school student, so as a business student you'll be hard-carrying most of the analysis and being a pseudo-coach for the rest of your team trying to grapple with business content that they might be learning for the first time.

Also be aware that there is usually an age gap, so if you're above the median age for business school students, be prepared to have sufficient patience to work with other students in the 22 to 25 year old range.

One advantage of this course is that the networking nights are truly impressive. Lots of VCs, serial entrepreneurs, and folks from all backgrounds (e.g. ex-military, someone who used to work at a large insurer and now is a GTM specialist for healthtech startups). The quality of contacts here is higher than the average business school networking event, so it does have value if you're interested in continuing in the deep tech space. Networking nights happen ~3 times per term (mid-term presentation, alumni night, and final demo day, though along the way you sometimes get connected with one-time "mentors" that you can speak to about your project too).

The course is a great opportunity to leaarn about the path to commercializing frontier "deep tech" innovations (frontier technologies). Profs Rappaport and Bowman are great and have experience, especially on the patent and regulation side of things. The course is a great opportunity to connect with industry professionals and experts that may open up future opportunities. That said, be ready for an extremely heavy workload. The class easily takes 3x the time suggested by the unit count and requires managing interviews, project deliverables, weekly assignments, and several rounds of presentations. The experience is also heavily team-dependent and teams are formed based on interest and past experience (plus availability)

I think this course has a lot to offer. It gives you exposure and experience to working at an early stage startup. Prof Rappaport and the GSIs offer a reasonably laidback class, and I think any complaints of the course are probably centered on their teams or startups. I enjoyed the course and would recommend it whole heartedly.

From a business student perspective, if you are eager to support early stage startups in whatever challenge they might have, this class is for you. If you are interested in practicing consulting skills or entrepreneurship, there are probaly better options out there.

Startups come in various development stages and industries, so you should come prepared to work in industries you did not want/expect to work with and with founders with differing levels of engagement.

If you want to work on the commercialization of deep tech with real clients, this is a very good class. However, be prepared for a heavy workload. Also, as you might expect, the experience can vary significantly depending on the client and your teammates.

sections.goodFor: Students without a finance background who want a 30,000-foot survey of asset management and a map of the career options in it; guest speakers are a draw.
sections.notFor: Anyone who has worked in the industry, or who wants specific financial concepts applicable in a role - coverage is broad and stays shallow.
sections.workloadNote: Not discussed. Very thin evidence - 8 short comments, several one-liners, no mention of assignments or readings.
sections.gradingBasis: unclear
sections.redFlags: 2 of 8 say the breadth of asset classes keeps everything at a high level; 1 of those also calls the classes not particularly engaging. Small sample, so treat as directional.
sections.quote: Covering such a broad range of asset classes is an ambitious goal, and as a result each asset type was explored only at a high level.
comments: 100% SAM OLESKY IS AN INCREDIBLY EFFECTIVE TEACHER AND THE MATERIAL IS INTEGRAL FOR ANY STUDENT
INTERESTED IN FINANCIAL MANAGEMENT WHETHER PERSONAL OR PROFESSIONAL.

Yes, great for a general overview of asset management, especially if you don't have a background in finance. I would recommend this course to any students who want an overview of the different career options that exist in asset management as Sam does a good job providing a 30,000 foot view. For anyone that has worked in the industry, I wouldn't say it's necessary to take the class.
Yes. He is the best
Yes

I would not recommend the course. Covering such a broad range of asset classes is an ambitious goal, and as a result each asset type was explored only at a high level. Combined with classes that were not particularly engaging, it was difficult to gain a deeper understanding of the material.

I would recommend it if you're interested in learning about different parts of asset management from a professor and guest speakers who have had very successful careers in the industry. Professor Olesky has a wealth of knowledge and passion for asset management, which makes the course more interesting. However, if you're trying to learn specific financial concepts that you can apply in a future role, I would probably recommend a different course.

rows.title: Design, Evaluate, and Scale Development Technologies

sections.goodFor: Students with a food-system idea they genuinely plan to pursue after graduation, who value community, reciprocity, and diverse speakers from across the food system.
sections.notFor: Anyone without an idea they are excited about - both commenters say the value depends on bringing one you intend to deeply pursue outside class.
sections.workloadNote: The class is what you make it; teams matter but some students worked alone and still produced strong final projects. Only 2 comments - no workload detail at all.
sections.gradingBasis: unclear; a final project/business idea is the visible output.
sections.quote: Yes, but only if you have an idea for a business that you are planning on deeply pursuing outside of class/after graduating.
comments: Yes, but only if you have an idea for a business that you are planning on deeply pursuing outside of class/after graduating.

I would recommend this class to folks who are really interested in improving the food system. The class is what you make it, and it definitely helps if there's an idea you're super stoked about pursuing. Your team is important, but folks also worked alone and so many people ended up with amazing final projects and business ideas. Will is a phenomenal connector and community builder, and puts a lot of care into creating a positive, systems-change focused

environment within the class. He brings in diverse speakers from all nodes of the food system. I value the space and community this class provided, and the opportunity to reach out to and learn from so many talented people. I love Will's focus on reciprocity and am carrying that into my future work and projects.

rows.title: Haas Sustainable Investment Fund
rows.terms: 2021 Fall;2022 Spring;2022 Fall;2023 Spring;2023 Fall;2024 Fall;2025 Spring

sections.goodFor: Self-directed students who want real portfolio and impact-investing experience and can tolerate a very small, loosely structured cohort.
sections.notFor: Students who need structured hands-on practice with Bloomberg, FactSet or CapIQ, or a properly enrolled class - the section dwindled to about six people.
sections.workloadNote: Managing a real portfolio is described as a lot of work, but nothing is quantified. Only 2 comments - very thin evidence. Students want a lab component added.
sections.gradingBasis: unclear; lectures, speakers and portfolio management work are described, but grading is not discussed.
sections.redFlags: Both comments raise execution gaps: enrollment collapsed to about 6 students, there is no lab component for Bloomberg/FactSet/CapIQ practice, and lectures and speakers are not paired with practical tasks.
sections.quote: The class in theory is so great, but the execution was short of my expecations given my classmates were only 5 others by the end of the year.
comments: Yes and No. The class in theory is so great, but the execution was short of my expecations given my classmates were only 5 others by the end of the year. It takes a lot of work to manage a portfolio and learning to do so takes time. I would add a lab component and make sure the class is well enrolled. I would have found it useful to have more lab practice on using resources like Bloomberg terminals, Facset, CapIQ, and the myriad of other resources available to us for this course. But learning is best done by doing, so more hands on experience would have been useful. Highly recommend, but I believe there are much more to improve, like how to apply our skills early on, how each lecture and speaker could be paired with more practical tasks. Despited these, I still learned so much that it changed my way of thinking about how to create impact.

sections.goodFor: Students targeting sustainability/ESG or consulting careers who want real client experience with big-name companies, exposure to strong guest speakers, and instructors commenters describe as experienced and well worth knowing; best for the self-directed who can handle a variable, team-heavy workload.
sections.notFor: Anyone expecting to be taught consulting skills or deep sustainability content in class; the experience hinges heavily on your assigned client and team, remote and mixed-program teams frustrated many, and several 2024 Fall commenters flatly called the current format a waste of time.
sections.workloadNote: Heavy and unpredictable: the client project can balloon when clients give little direction, and several found it unmanageable stacked on a full-time job or other demanding courses.
sections.redFlags: Recurring (7+ comments): outcome depends on client and team luck, with vague or absent clients and disjointed mixed-cohort teams derailing projects. Recurring (5+): class sessions and speakers do not teach consulting skills or connect to the project. A few (3): class content felt shallow for people already in the sustainability field.
sections.quote: I would recommend it to someone, but the quality of the course is very dependant on the group and the project you get

sections.goodFor: Students aiming at impact investing or asset management - works with or without an investing background, and gives real exposure to selecting managers.
sections.notFor: Students who need a clear syllabus and week-by-week structure (format is still new), or who are skeptical that secondary-market impact investing is meaningful.
sections.workloadNote: 'A fair amount of work' with hands-on investing, asset manager selection and speakers; students report the sequence is scattered and you don't know what's coming week to week.
sections.gradingBasis: Hands-on fund/investment work including selecting asset managers; not detailed further.
sections.redFlags: 2-3 of 11: unclear structure, expectations and week-by-week sequencing in this still-new format; one rejects the premise outright - impact investing in secondary markets 'is just a joke'.
sections.quote: you will learn a lot but the knowledge is kinda scattered around throughout the course, not knowing what's coming at you week-by-week
comments: I would recommend this class. It's an interesting class with a focused topic, and lots of practical topics and speakers. It is relatively new in its current format, so I think it will get better through time.
Yes great course to learn about sustainable investment and apply it in practice
No. Talking about sustainable and impact investing in secondary market is just a joke.

I would recommend this course to another student if they are passionate about learning the topic. It's a great way to experience hands-on investing and learning about sustainability. The opportunity to select asset managers and hear about what they prioritize is invaluable. The course is a fair amount of work, and you have to be keenly interested in sustainability. I think despite the sustainability lens it is also a great way to gain exposure to the asset management / stock investing world in a hands - on manner.
Yes! Excellent learnings from world-class professors!
the class needs clearer structure and learning perspective from the beginning and the expected engagement with the students
you will learn a lot but the knowledge is kinda scattered around throughout the course, not knowing what's coming at you week-by-week
Yes!Anne & Peter are great to learn from as professionals doing the work in the space. Panos passion on subject matter and research is a great compliment to them both. Great class!

Great experiential learning experience with professors with both deep academic and professional backgrounds Yes! Have already recommended it to friends. It is a great class for folks both with and without an investing background, and especially for those who want to pursue a career in impact investing or related fields.
This course gives a phenomenal look at both asset management and sustainability - for anyone interested in either, I'd highly recommend taking this course.
Yes I would recommend this class. It was a brand new topic for me and although I felt intimidated at first, by the end I felt like I was up to speed and had learned a lot!

sections.goodFor: Students who want a live client consulting project and a sustainability speaker series, can self-manage without guidance, or need the applied innovation credit.

comments: yes
I would recommend this course - the opportunity to work with a client on a real business challenge is really great. There is also a good mix of guest lecturers and class-voted discussion topics.
Absolutely... YES! I learned a lot and the experiential part of it was invaluable.
Yes, recommend this class for those looking to get into a consulting career. It provides solid foundation and familiarizes you with real work in the consulting realm.
The experience to work with a real company is really valuable.
yes- both are very personable and I would recommend that students get to know them personally as well.
Honestly no, it's a bit unorganized. Your experience is very dependent on who is in your group, and instructors aren't able to step in to adjust if thinks are truly back

The course experience is highly dependent on the group project. There's a lack of guidance on the consulting framework and implementation of the framework from professors (while the framework is given, it does not seem like projects have to align to it/not enough check-ins to ensure that teams are on track using the framework). The other half of the course are really great guest speakers that gives an overview of various sustainabiltiy topics throughout the semester, however there's a lack of structure on teacher-led content.
I don't know. If the course materials continue to be so unorganized then i wouldn't recommand to anyone. Yes

Take this course! Great way to link theory and practice - completing the consulting project throughout the semester with a real company and real clients made it feel very hands-on and valuable learning experience where we actually made an impact. One of the best courses I've taken as someone with a sustainability background who had grown tired of redundant theoretical sustainability classes - this one was actually worth it and I learned new things. Fine class if you need the applied innovation credit, but don't take it for fun. Despite good topics, deep disorganization and over-indexing on consultant nonsense made this feel like a waste of time. Very disappointing.
Absolutely
Yes, very interesting course and the instructors were awesome!!

I would not recommend it. The class seems very spontaneous, without proper planning, and the consulting projects have no guidance, and no hierarchy so it it so hard to actually do them adequately. I think this should be a speaker series. That part was nice. But the consulting project felt like I was doomed to fail from the start. So bad. I would not recommend this course. Some of the guest speakers were interesting, but the teachings didn't build on top of each other well and depth of content was severely lacking. Lectures were very basic and I don't think the format took advantage of the instructors' wealth of experience. I walked away without any clear value-add to my education or professional toolkit.

Highly recommend. This Strategic Business course blends core strategy frameworks with a live consulting project, amplified by relevant guest speakers and candid, actionable feedback, you'll leave with sharper problem-structuring, stronger storytelling, and client-ready deliverables.
I would recommend this class to a student who would be interested in hearing lots of interesting guest speakers, but caution them on some of the concerns I raised in the previous section.

[REDACTED IN THE PUBLIC BUILD] A student said the course is not worth the tuition and that comparable material is freely available elsewhere, and criticised the quality and originality of the teaching material. — Why: The original makes a specific unverified factual claim about how a named instructor prepares their material.

rows.title: Real Estate Investment Analysis and Sustainability
rows.terms: 2021 Spring;2022 Spring;2023 Spring;2024 Spring;2025 Spring;2026 Spring

sections.goodFor: People serious about commercial real estate - already working in it or recruiting for it - who know the terminology or will put in extra time to catch up on fundamentals.
sections.notFor: Casual learners, personal real-estate investors, and those expecting deep sustainability content: beginners get thrown into commercial jargon and one EWMBA student found little peer knowledge-sharing.
sections.workloadNote: Half of nearly every class goes to guest speakers, much of the rest to student presentations toward the final project; pro forma work sits outside class, assignments often posted 2-3 days before due.
sections.gradingBasis: Almost half the grade is the final project (pro forma model plus research) per one student, plus progress presentations.
sections.redFlags: Guest speakers consume ~half of most classes, crowding out teaching (4+). Disorganized: assignments posted to bCourses 2-3 days before deadlines with vague expectations (2). Little concrete pro forma guidance.
sections.quote: 90 minutes of almost every class was scattershot guest speakers talking about their various developments across the country that didn't add much to my learning.
comments: Highly recommend this course to those who look to learn fundamental and systematic real estate investment and development
Nancy has a lot to teach, but i think half of the time was spent on guest speakers which ate up the time to learn some really practical skills in real estate investment/finance

I would recommend this to folks who are serious or seriously curious about going into commercial real estate, but not for anybody else. I came in thinking this would be a nice foundation for future personal real estate investments, giving me the ability to evaluate the profitability of, say, buying a house or a small set of apartments. I also was hoping for in depth evaluation of the state of the real estate industry in the climate transition and where / how it needed to move faster. Unfortunately, neither of these were the case. We quickly dove into jargon and nuances of commercial real estate, which was good for the half of the class who had taken real estate classes already, but which made it difficult for me to engage. I do think the lineup of speakers were quite cool (e.g., the developers of Hudson Yards in NYC), but again, very focused on larger scale commercial real estate.

There's a slight disconnect among real estate classes. We learn how to build a proforma multiple times. There should be a foundational pro forma building course, giving other courses more time to go deeper into their specific real estate topic.

"Highly recommended! If you're a student interested in project development — whether from the business side or the engineering/architecture side — this class is extremely valuable. It equips you with the tools to plan, execute, and finance a project effectively."

Yes. It is definitely tailored for students already working in real estate or pursuing jobs in real estate, but it was well taught and the guest lecturers and panels were all incredibly additive to the course experience.
This class is worth what you put into it. I found immense value in the guest speakers, and as a gateway to the real estate industry.

I recommend taking this class for anybody interested in commercial real estate development. Professor Wallace is a great professor and has her pulse on the market, able to convey difficult concepts simply. Ed McFarlane supplements Nancy's lectures well, as an Architect he adds a practical element to classes and between the both of them can answer any question you may have. Each class starts with guest speakers, who are industry practitioners. This alone is great exposure and worth attending the class. What you get out of this class is very reliant on what you put in. As someone working in Real Estate, I can firmly say I learned some new things and got some great ideas.

Yes I would recommend this course to fellow students as think the insights from professionals were great to have in class and the exercises in the class helped develop real estate analysis skills I didn't have before.
Yes, good class to learn how real estate development numbers work
Would definitely recommend for anybody interested in real estate finance and how to view it from a sustainability lense!
Yes, I would, if the person was interested in pursuing a career in real estate. The material can be a bit overwhelming if a students does not know about the fundamentals of real estate investments.

This is good class to take if you are interested in learning more about real estate - the professors are both experts in this field - and are willing to look towards the future of where it should be going. However, the first few weeks will feel like getting thrown into the deep end - but it's actually quite manageable! I'd recommend. Real estate is something you should have given a bit of thought before graduating from business school (it is the biggest asset class in the US after all).

I loved Nancy Wallace as a knowledgeable professional but I would not recommend this course. I had hoped to get more practical financial skills in this course, but felt that ultimately very little teaching happened. 90 minutes of almost every class was scattershot guest speakers talking about their various developments across the country that didn't add much to my learning. And the other 90 min was often student presentations advancing towards the final project...but that left little time to do any real teaching/skill-building.

Also the course felt disorganized. The curriculum felt haphazard with topics not often progressing logically from one to the next, and assignments (and their accompanying details) wouldn't be created on BCourses until often 2-3 days before they were due. We would often have to remind the teaching team to post assignments (things that were vaguely labeled in the Syllabus like "Progress Report 2") and to give us details about what to submit, and then scramble to get those materials together on time. This is especially surprising in a 30-person course with two Readers that could have been supporting.

I would recommend as a very introductory class for real estate. It goes through most of the topics, but if someone wants something more technical or specific about the financials, this is not the class. Overall, speakers were great. Would liked to have more concrete learnings about applying sustainable features into real estate.

Yes. This class is a must for whoever used to, wants, or is about to work in the Real Estate industry. Professors are super professional and knowledgeable in this area. This class provides a hands on experience in Real Estate and cover almost every aspect of the industry from financial pro-forma to sustainability. If you don't have any finance or real estate background like me, this class might be a bit challenging but still manageable.

I would recommend this class as a great intro to real estate development and understanding the high level levers that could be utilized. Covers key topics and familiarizes you with different projects and companies within the ecosystem. I would recommend this course if you are interested in the built environment. That said, if you are only casually interested then this may be too technical/heavy on the finance side of things. The course has some heavy hitters as guest speakers who have implemented projects all over the country.

I would recommend this course for students who already have a good understanding of real estate or who are willing to put in extra time and effort outside of class to get up to speed on the concepts and fundamentals. Instructors were not the most organized and often were delayed in communicating expectations for class assignments. Half of the lecture time for almost each class was reserved for guest speakers, which was sometimes useful and interesting but not always. Almost half the grade is based on the final project and there is very little guidance on how to actually work through the pro forma model, complete the research, etc. (guidance is very high level).
I would recommend this course to students who want to dive deeper into the financial side of sustainable

development. This introductory course would require someone to have heard certain terminology from real estate to make this course more worthwhile. Other than terminology, coming from an engineering background, I was able to share sustainable strategies and was able to correlate how efficiency affects financial results.

I wouldn't recommend this to an EWMBA student. I didn't enjoy the low opportunity to share experiences and knowledge that other students had. This course is great prep for some one seeking a career in commercial real estate. However, as a someone with no background in real estate this course lacks breadth. I still don't understand how to develop a commercial real estate project. I get a few concepts like pro-forma and pitching projects to LPs.

sections.goodFor: Students targeting real estate or curious about the built environment and sustainability; strong networking via well-connected professors and industry guests.
sections.notFor: Students with no modeling/finance background (called VERY difficult), and anyone wanting professor-led lectures - one says most class time is guest speakers and advises auditing instead.
sections.workloadNote: Heavy for 3 units: pro forma case studies plus a final team project, with 'A LOT to absorb very quickly' including industry lingo; guest speakers fill much of class time.
sections.gradingBasis: Case studies and a final team real-estate project/pro forma; heavy guest-speaker component.
sections.redFlags: One student says the two professors hardly lecture and it is mostly guest speakers, recommending auditing rather than paying; steep unforgiving ramp for those without pro forma experience.
sections.quote: If you don't have much modeling experience or finance background, this course could be VERY difficult for you. There is A LOT to absorb very quickly
comments: I would highly recommend this instructor and course, especially for students interested in real estate. Regardless of whether you have a prior background in the field, the instructor is very supportive and makes a strong effort to help students understand the material. The course includes a project based on real-world scenarios, which provides a valuable and comprehensive experience of the real estate process. It allows students to engage with the challenges, opportunities, and complexities of real estate development in a meaningful way. Overall, it is a very rewarding and insightful course.
Yes, highly recommend this course. This course helps student to understand the real estate principle a lot if you are interested.

Whether you're interested in a career in real estate or just want to understand what defines a good real estate investment, you should take MBA280. This is a foundational course for anyone curious about the built environment. Nancy Wallace and Ed McFarlan are Berkeley's best and are complemented by an excellent roster of guest speakers. This is an experiential course so students should come prepared to work hard because they'll only get as much out of the class as they're willing to put in.
Yes, if they are interested in GP/LP real estate side of the business. it is very useful to understand the incentives for the built environment.
Yes, for the connections and networking opportunities the class affords.

Terrific course, the professors (especially Professor Wallace) add so much insight and context atop the great guest speakers. If you're interested in sustainability in the built environment and/or real estate development I highly recommend this class
Yes, if you're interested in real estate. this is one that should be taken.
Yes I would. The professors and guest speakers were wonderful and really deepened my understanding of the real estate industry.

I would not recommend paying for this class. If you are able to audit it, that would be much better. Most of the class is listening to guest lectures and the two professors hardly do any lectures themselves.

Yes, I would recommend this class if you are interested in a career in real estate. It provides a solid introduction to pro formas and financial modeling, taught by two stellar professors who are genuinely passionate about teaching and eager to help students learn. They emphasize gaining hands-on development experience while incorporating

sustainability principles. I learned a lot despite having very little pro forma experience when I entered the class, and my knowledge of pro formas grew significantly during the course through practice with case studies and the final team project (the Professors provided a lot of support). Both professors are very approachable and make themselves available. office hours, responding promptly over email. They are thoughtful in bringing a stellar lineup of industry guests, developers, investors, and other professionals, who share their experiences. This greatly enhances the classroom experience and offers a valuable opportunity to connect with industry leaders. You will leave with useful tools, industry terminology, and connections, as both professors are well-connected and encourage students to reach out to speakers and contacts. This was my favorite class during Haas, and I only regret not being able to take more classes with Professors Wallace and Ed.

I definitely recommend this course to folks, especially if you are looking to develop or hone your real estate skills. If you don't have muc h modeling experience or finance background, this course could be VERY difficult for you. There is A LOT to absorb very quickly, including industry lingo but also concepts. This is definitely a 3 unit and requires a lot of time and effort. Make sure you have a good, collaborative, communicative group because you will need to lean on them a lot with the case studies and projects. I'm not kidding. But it is worth it and you will feel prepared to talk shop about real estate after this class. I took away a lot, even if I don't plan to go into a real estate job after my MBA.

Absolutely. I think someone interested or keen in understaning board governance and how to approach these roles. Its a great way to start with it.
I would recommend this instructor. He brought in great experiences to the classroom and lots of material that will benefit anyone who is in a future non-profit board role.
Sadly not because of the arbitrary grading and lack of feedback and clear instructions.

sections.notFor: Anyone drawn by the 'Finance & Infrastructure' in the title - it isn't emphasized; students who took several climate classes find it repetitive and law school options better.
